Love willed that Death should occupy the house— ' Not host ilely—but like a generous foe E. Who, guest perforce, inflicts no needless throe, And scorns to jest and gibe, and hold carouse. , And when the leaves were tender on the boughs, And white the maytree shone, and thick like snow, Death entered softly where Love bade him go, Obedient to the suzerain uf his vows. • And unto one whom wordly strife perplexed, Whom sickness grieved and care made tremulous, . The foeman, pitying, brought the boon of peace. "Or e'er these things his soul have greatly vexed" (Death spake, benign, compassionating us), "The Master hath ordained that they shall cease."

L . White lilac, sweetest may, exotics white, Gifts of dear hearts), made beautiful the gloom, And breathed of blessedness to us on whom _ Had fallen regret:and longingtinfinite. Yet still we wept. Till One arrayed in light, .7 II Magnifica], more sweet than may in bloom, More white than lilies, filled the darkened room, And, through our tears, beamed glorious on our sight. ' "My liegeman, Death, I sent to take him home," For Death is kind, and life laborious, 1 The way is difficult, the travail sore. "Now Death and he are gone—but I am come " (Love spike, benign, compassionating us), "And, 10, with you am I for evermore." —Sunday Magazine. E. 11. CnirmArr.

The cue that all drowning men want.—Rescue. What trade never turns to the left P—A wheelright. The only real secrets of trade are ;industry, integrity, and knowledge. It is said that a blind woman can knit faster than one with good eyes. She doesn't look out of the window

every five minutes. Grandpa was telling about some one who was very heavy for his size, and he said, "He is the biggest man -I ever saw for his size." At this all smiled, so he tried it again. "I mean, he is the heaviest person for his weight I ever knew." Then, after a pause, "What are you all ?laughing at?" and grandpa walked off in indignation. Elderly gentleman (who has been talking to young Tellow from Philadelphia, and has taken a great fancy to him): "By the way, where are you staying? I wish you would come and visit me." Young fellow (who is a friend of elderly gentleman's son) : "Why, I am staying at your house; I have been there a week.' An old acotch worthy who had lost his case in a court of justice was asked by his wife, when he got home, how he had got on. "I've lost," said he, "but I gie'd the Shirra up his fit." "Bit, Tammas," she asked, "cud he no punish ye for that ?" "I taen guicl care o' that," said Tammas, "for I was six miles on my road hame afore I

opened my 'moth." It is told of a certain Dr. Kenrick,-a man held in high regard for sanctity, that one day he missed his hat from the sacristy, and rushing into Plunket-street, adjacent— the Monmouth-street of Dublin—he detected a woman in the act of disposing of it. "I only wanted It as a relic of your reverence," said the ready-witted culprit. "You seem very anxious to get rid of it, then." "I was only asking the value of it," replied the female, with unshaken self-possession. I heard from an old New Englander, who was brought up with Daniel Webster and enjoyed his friendship, a story abut the great statesman's first ascent to Mount Wash- ington. It was in the days when the trip up the moun- tain meant a tiresome tramp, without the assistance of railroads and other modern improvements. When the party had returned to the restarting point, someone asked Mr. Webster how he had enjoyed the trip. His reply was, "I wouldn't have missed it for 5,000 dols., but I wouldn't make the ascent again for 50,000 dols." Wife (reading the paper) : "Well, I declare, if that isn't the queerest thing I ever heard of!" Husband: "What's that?" Wife: "Why, here in the paper is an account of a wedding up in Manchester, and among the wedding presents was a bull-terrier, given to the bride by her father." Husband: "I don't see anything odd about that. She was the old man's youngest daughter, wasn't she ?" Wife: " Yes ; but what's that got to do with it?" Husband: "Why, of course, if she and all the rest were married, he had no further use for the dog." A lady has a pony of which she is very fond, but not long since she thought that he was a little "dull," so she called in a veterinary surgeon, who prescribed a powder for the equine favourite. The next morning she said to her man-of-all-work, "Pat, did you give the pony his medicine?" "Faith, mum," answered Fat rather rue- fully, "I got a big glass pipe, an' put the medicine in it, an' I backed the pony in the corner. I put the pipe in his mouth, an' was just goin' to blow it down into him; but he breathed first, an' I have the powther in me in- stead of him!" _ .

It is announced that Messrs. Appert, of Clichy, France, have discovered a process that will make glass-blowing by the mouth unnecessary. ManyNatlempts have hitherto been made to get rid of`t, his7painTul process in the operation of glass-making, but to this 'day in every bottle-house may be seen pale-faced men with their cheeks hanging limp in folds, the result of years of glass- blowing by the mouth. Cases have been known in which teen's cheeks have been worn so thin that:they have actually/cracked ; and it is a common sight in a bottle- hcuse to see blowers at work with their thin cheeks puffed out like the fingers of a glove. The works of the immense clock which has been put -up in the Board of Trade building in Chicago are pro- nounced a most perfect reproduction of those of the great Westminster Palace clock, London, but with some improvements and additions. It is constructed of iron, bronze, and steel, and weighs ten tons without the bell, the latter adding some 4,500 pounds more. The pen- dulum alone weighs 750 pounds. The hammer that strikes the bell weighs 80 pounds. The clockwork is be- low the dials, which are 10ft. 10in, in diameter, and the bell is above them, or 250 feet above the ground. The pendulum swings one way in two seconds. Sorr SOAP.—According to the Abbe Hue, Eastern monarchs are gullible. He says, "Once it happened that a Frenchman came to the Khan of Tartary, and the Emperor asked him what offering he had brought him. The Frenchman replied, I have brought you nothing, for I did not know of your great power.' How,' said the Emperor, did not the very birds, as they flew over your ccuntry, tell you of our power?' The Frenchman replied, 'Sire, perhaps they did; but as I do not understand their language, I do not know what they said.' And thus the Emperor was appeased." The Squire of Western Lullington, in Shropshire, has a coachman whose mental lights are not as bright as his lamp-light. He is a good man in his way, but he often thirgs up rather more than is pleasant. Some valuable plants were expected at the station, three miles off, by a certain train, and care had to be exercised .in their conveyance. So John was told to take a message to the station-master that the plants were to be kept at the station till the donkey cart arrived for them, and that the Squire himself would come down to see them loaded. "Now, you quite understand ?" asked the Squire. "Oh, yes, sir," replied John, "I'm to say they are to wait for the donkey, and you'll be down about four o'clock!" LAST FOND Loaes.—When a lady (we are talking of S. lady in the full height and breadth of fashion) has got her bonnet and gloves on, and is perfectly ready with her parasol in her hand, she always goes back to the looking glass to take a last fond look. Upon our asking a dear handsome duchess" if this was not the truth, and the beautiful truth, she had the charming candour to state—" Yes, my dear sir, it is the truth, but not all the truth. No woman, take my word for it, is satisfied 'with ope look. At least, I know that lam not, for (and here our duchess laughed, as though she was pleased with herself and all the world) I aon't mind telling you, I invariably tal,-e four—four g00!1 ones. The first look in the glass is for myself, that's fair; the second i.s for my husband, that's nothing but just; the third.is for my friends, that's only generous; and the last is _ for. my rivals, that's human nature. If the last lcrkisatisfies me, then I know it is all right, and I assure ou I never take any more!" . IN A ITOPELESS MlNORlT7.—Everyone in the small town in which the following circumstance happened knew o.ld Joe, the wheelwright, and those that didn't know him ecarcely need to be told that Joe was not a bigoted teeto- taller. The Salvation Army had its headquarters for the district close to Joe's favourite hostelry, and one even- ing, having his usual "load on," Joe by some means or other drifted into the meeting-room, where the warm air and the "Captain's" dry discourse caused Joe to yield himself to the drowsy god, and he soon sank into a pro- found slumber. At the close of his discourse the evan- gelist wound up with this fervid appeal—" Will all of you who want to go to heaven please rise ?" Of course everyone except poor Joe rose, and then sat down. "Now I want all of you who want to go to hell to stand up," said the "Captain," and Joe catching on to the last word or two of the request, stood up as well as he could, to the horror of some of the older soldiers. Steadying himself against the seat, he looked at the " Captain" an instant, and then said, "Well, Captain,' I don't know exactly what we're voting on, but you and I seem to be in a hopeless minority."—Mechanical Pro- gress.

TOuGIt ENOTIGII.—Hugh Gough, of Borough, Was a rough soldier on a furlough, but a man of doughty deeds in war, though before he fought for his country he was a thorough dough-faced ploughman. His horse having been houghed in an engagement with the enemy, Hugh was taken prisoner, and I ought to add was kept on a short enough clough of foOd, and suffered from drought as well as from hunger. Having on his return home drunk too large a draught of usquebaugh, he became intoxicated, and was laughing, coughing, and hiccoughing by a trough against which he sought to steady himself. There he was accosted by another rough, who showed him a cough which he had caught in a clough near; also the slough of a snake which he held at the end of a tough bough of a eugh tree, and which his dog had found and brought to him from the entrance to a sough which ran through and drained a slough that was close by in the neighbourhood. A GIANT SEWING MActriNn.—We have mentioned one of the tiniest machines made by the Singer Manufacturing Company, and we-may now go to the other end of the scale and give a brief description of the largest machine they have yet produced. This gigantic stitcher weighs over four tons, and embraces some striking novelties in its working parts. It is adapted for general manufacturing purposes of the heavier sort, although specially made for stitching cotton belting, which has during the last few years come much into use as a serviceable substi- tute for gearing or ordinary leather belting. The ma- terial used for the belt is of great strength and tough- ness, and is sewn together in layers, the aggregate thick- ness in some cases exceeding an inch. The cloth is first carefully arranged fold upon fold, and then fed into the machine between iron rollers, nine inches in diameter, and over eight feet in length. There are two needles employed, and two shuttles, and the shuttles can be re- moved from their races without disturbing the overlying layers of belting.—Cassell's Great Industries of Great Britain.

IRISH SEWED MUSLIN.—A FUGITIVE TRADE.—Specimens shown at the Great Exhibition of 1851 attracted wide attention to Irish sewed muslin, and at that time it was a highly fashionable article of adornment with the ladies, not only of this country, but of the United States and various European kingdoms. At the Exhibition referred to, a handkerchief sewn in Newtownards for a Scottish house was considered one of the finest specimens of this kind of work ever produced. It was valued at twenty guineas. One Glasgow house paid to Irish sewers alone in the first six months of 1851 no less than £63,400, and for the same period of 1853 they paid £90,000. At that time, and for several years after, no town in the north of Ireland, from Derry to Dublin on one hand, and from ! Belfast to Sligo on the other, was without its sewing , agent, and in some towns five or six agents were re- quired. It was estimated that no fewer than 80,000 women and girls were employed in the muslin sewing business in Ireland at this time, and their earnings , ranged from 3s. to 10s. per week. Dark days were at hand, however. Many persons had rushed into a busi- ness which was regarded as being highly remunerative, and the result was over-production. Every market became gorged, and the low price at which the em- broidered goods were sold made them so common that they palled upon the popular taste, and went out of fashion. In the commercial crisis of 1857 the trade suffered severely, and the Irish peasant girls found that the occupation which had been so irksome to learn was gone. Great hardship ensued, as might be expected. At intervals since then a limited demand for hand-sewn muslins has been experienced, but that the trade will ever reach its former extent is extremely unlikely. Em- broidering machines have been invented which turn out work as beautiful, if not more so, than the hand used to do, and as that work is comparatively cheap it is likely to meet most requirements. The machine embroidery, it must be said, however, is not so durable as that pro- duced by hand.—Great Industries of Great Britaia. WOOD CUTTING IN EPPING FOREST.—In Theyclon Bois, ' up to a very recent period, the privilege of wood- cutting inaugurated each year in so singular a manner was continued. But the increasing timidity of the in- habitants, and the power of the lord of the manor, led at length to the almost entire cessation of the practice, which was not exercised, except in a very furtive manner. It has been seen that in the parish of Loughton alone did the curious custom continue to be exercised with full vigour, until extinguished by recent Epping Forest legislation: and the long exercise of the right was owing in a large degree to the sturdy determination of the commoners; for it is a curious fact that, although for many years, until the existence of the legislation re- ferred to, the whole of that portion of Epping Forest in- cluded within the Manor of Loughton was enclosed— illegally enclosed, as the Court of Chancery decided—yet the poor inhabitants of the parish, relying on their Royal Charter, each year, at midnight of the llth of November, went over the enclosing fences, and commenced their top-lopping of the trees, continuing the practice during the stipulated period. Even in Loughton, however, an attempt was once made—similar to that practised suc- cessfully at Waltham in 1641—t0 rob the poor of their right. It fell out in this way :—An invitation to a great banquet in the Manorial Hall at Loughton, on the 11th of November, was sent out to all the poor in the place. The feast was fixed to commence late in the evening, and, as at Waltham, on the occasion already referred to, all who were able came to partake of the gord cheer provided. Everything was done to mate the guests for- get the progress of time—wine being passed round with- out stint. But some of the men assembled wisely re- frained from partaking too freely of "the flowing bowl ;" and when the hour of midnight drew near, they rose to go. Eagerly they were pressed by their host to remain and finish out the feast. But when, refusing his blandish- ments, they began to move towards the door, a curious and significant expression passed over the countenance of their entertainer. Truly he was a cunning plotter; for, anticipating the possibility that two or three of the assembled commoners might determine to drink spar- ingly, in order not to forget the necessity for the mid- night excursion to the forest, he had taken the pre- caution to lock and heavily bar the door of egress. But the host had this time reckoned without his guests ; and great was his amazement, to hear, from his seat at the board, the sound of heavy crashing blows from the direction of the hall. Rushing there in consternation, his dismay was extreme at beholding his wooden out- post shivering and splintering before the lusty onset of half-a-dozen brawny woodmen, armed with gleaming hatchets, which at each blow told with effect even on the oaken panels of the massive door. These men, either anticipating the possibility of a ruse, or anxious to save themselves the trouble of going to their homes to fetch their axes after the banquet, had ingeniously concealed these effective instruments about their pc Ts ons ; and lucky was the chance whin made them do so, as the event proved; for the barrier which their treacher- ous host had thought to be—as it would have been to unarmed men—impregnable, was not long in yielaing to the heavy and repeated assaults which were actually made upon it. It came down ere long with a thud and a crash, and, with a wild shout af triumph, waving their hatchets high in the air, the dauntless woodmen made for the lonely forest glade to exercise their curious mid- night custom.—lllustrations. lIARRISTERS—whose professional labours necessitate long In- tervals between meals—nothing will be found so exhilarating, comforting, and capable of sustaining exhausted native as Cadbury's Cocoa, guaranteed absolutely pure. Beware of Imitations.—Aclet.

div.p: hobbledehoy-hood, and they need to be well supported with good and nourishing food, as the strain upon the system consequent upon the formation of the adult feathers is very great. To provide for this they must be well fed, and should have some bone meal in their soft food every day without fail, and as much liberty as can be given without actually allowing them to fly all over the country. It must also be remembered that the day very soon dawns and that the chicks are out and about by three o'clock in the morning, so that if they have to wait until seven or eight o'clock before they get any- thing to eat they will suffer in consequence, and it is as well, thereforp, to scattar about a little corn, such as dari or buckwheat, the evening before. Care must be taken that too much is not put down, or it will be wasted; but just sufficient to stay their appetites until the proper feeding time, which had better be as early as possible.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

In favourable localities early Potatoes will be fat for I use, and the question is—How can the ground they occupy be turned to the best account? In the neigh- ' bourhood of Lancaster, which is noted for its allotment ! gardens, we observed at the end of last week that this crop had been cleared, and the ground was already ! planted with Celery, and Lettuce on the intermediate spaces, which will be fit for use long before the soil is re- quired to place round the Celery. Those who wish to keep the whole of the Potatoes for their own household use could not very well carry out the above arrange- ments, as the Potatoes are taken up from day to day, as required, and two or three weeks will have transpired before there is room for any Celery, which would be rather late. If, however, a row is taken up here and there space would be set at liberty for Celery, and the Potatoes not required for immediate use may be buried in the ground, in order to preserve their freshness and prevent the skin from setting. In a few days another row might be served in a similar manner, to give space for more Celery. Our plan, however, is to plant some kind of winter greens or Broccoli' between the Potatoes, and follow these with Celery and Lettuce. In the gar- den plots referred to several patches of spring Cabbage had been also cleared, and the space they occupied planted with Celery, which was well established. Here, again, it is easy to squeeze a row of Celery here and there in the Cabbage plot by pulling a row of the latter up as soon as ready, and if they have been planted the usual distance of 2ft. between the rows it will allow about 18 inches on either side of the trench to lay the soil on, and by the time the Celery requires earthing to any extent the whole of the Cabbacte should be off the ground. For winter crops, various. Kales, Savoys. Broc- coli, and late Cauliflowers should be planted as soon as we get rain to soak the ground. The latter and the Dwarf Savoys may be 18in. distant, but all the others re- quire to be 2ft. each way. The plants should be closely examined as they are taken up to see if they are "blind" —a term applied by gardeners to plants of the brassica that fail to form central buds—as all that are in that con- dition should be discarded. Where the rows of Onions are gappy advantage should be taken of moist weather to transplant others. from. where they are thick, so as to make the crop as regular as possible. These have been very scarce and dear this spring, and those who had their spring sown forward have made money out of them. The finest we have seen were on some plots in what is occasionally designated' as " Cronswell's Meadow," situated on the west side, of Lancaster, and, as evidence of their health and vigour, we- were assured that one plot owner had realised from three beds; 24ft. by 4ft. each, the sum of 205,, and the beds when we saw them appeared as if two out of three of the plants should come out, so it must have been a remarkable crop in the first instance.

THE FaoNT GARDEN.—One of the most delightful re- dolents flowering at the present time in the front garden is the Pink, and our-favourite-is-the white one, which we think is not surpassed by any other variety in florifer- ousness, beauty, and fragrance: There is a row of it several yards in length along the side of the platform at Croston Station, which cannot fail to attract passengers' attention and delight their olfactory organs if they stop there. In order to increase the number of the different varieties of Pinks, pipings or cuttings should be inserted without delay in sandy soil, with-glass protection,if pos- sible under the shade of a wall or-hedge, where they will escape the direct rays of the sun,during most of the day. Plants that are not too large may betaken up soon after flowering and planted deeper than they were before, which will be the means of their forming roots along their naked stems, which, if taken up and divided, the following year would give. any number of plants. If large flowers such as are seen at exhibitions are ex- pected, the plants to prodUce them must be from cut- tings rooted the previous years,. and cultivated in pots or prepared beds, or wintered inpots and planted in the- open ground in March. THE CrnErmetrsE.—SeedS of herbaceous Calceolarias should be sown during this -month in pots or pans pre- pared in the follbwing manner. Whichever is used it is essential that it should be clean inside and well drained: —The soil must be fresh, and may be composed of three- parts loam and one part leaf mould; with a sprinkling of sand, which should be well mixed and passed through a riddle. The rougher portiom should be placed over the crocks to within 2in. from. the top, so as to prevent the finer particles mixing with the- drainage and ob- structing the free egress of water. The remaining 21n. must be filled with the fine-soil, and pressed with the bottom of a flower pot or a round flat piece of wood with a handle in the centre. This will reduce the depth to which is tioite sufficient- for the seedlings to grow in till they are. ready to prick out The seeds are- so small that it is difficult to tell where they have been dropped, and to guide us inthismatter we sprinkle the wirface with and,; and press- the seed in and cover- ever with a piece eisglass andpinzein.a shady position.

Carman OFT, Dt INDIANS.—A romantic Indian story comes from the Pacific Coast. The affair came to a cul- minating pointabont June 20th, when a desperate encoun- ter took place between the Indians and a small band of Mexicans, nearrNogalee,, Mexico. It seems that on April al!th the Indians, undee Geronimo, made a descent on the place of Mr. 3eek, killing Mrs. Peek and her child, and , taking into captivity Mr. Peek and his niece, a girl of years of age. The Indians beleng to the Apache tribe, and ' have been Wetly purstted ever since, both by the Unita States troomand Mexican civilians. It is to the credit of the latter that the 'rescue of the capeive girl is due. The band of Mexicans, hut 10 in number„struck the trail of ehe Indians and. followed it up with great determination and energy. There were 42 hostile Indians. When near the summit ot the mountain on which. was the Indian encamp- ment the Mexicans were fired on, and three fell dead, a fourth being severely wenn:led. The remaming six sprang into the bushy and endeavoured to outflink the hostilee, and obtain an equal elevation. One of the chief's sqpaws in charge at the girl Peek was sleeping in a creek near to the spot gained by the Mexicans. One of the Indians ran out to call the squaw in, but she waved him back, and with a rifle fieedion the Mexicans. She was shot dead y and to save herself, the girl fell to the ground, feigning death. The Apaches, hearing the firing, ran out. The loader was shot dead. In attempting to career off the body six others were- shot dead also. The Indians carried ofi their com- rades, bat could not regain the bodies of the women. The Mexicans had taken up a position over the bodies of the sqnaw and the girl Peek, both of whom were supposed to be dead. The Indiana were put to flight, and it was then feund that the girl was alive. The poor creature was. naked from the waist upwards, and appeared quite dazed. , She could scarcely remember auything, but that she had been captured somewhere near Nogales, a long time ago. Her eves were sunken in her head. She had lived on raw horseflesh, and had never tasted bread since her captivity. Her body was mach lacerated by riding through thorny bushes by night. She had been dashing almost constantly through bush, rocky creeks, and over mountains day and night ever since her capture. She had always slept on the arm of Geronimo's squaw, and apart from the sleeping place of the Indians. The squaw bad been detailed to guard and protect her. The girl knew nothing of the fate of her uncle, who was captured the same day as she was; but it appears he escaped from the Indians. The girl was being brought to Magdalena by her brave rescuers when the despatch was sent oft_ Her uncle was then on his way to receive her. I'd visions o" 'greatness swlmmin' before me like silver cleauds wi' M.P written on 'em i' letters o' gowd,. Pd eaur Sal's last words- ringin' P my ears—" I towd thee thy time would come if tbeau'd follow my advice. Ifs-come neaw." Preparations wur at once begun for howdin a media' i'th owd Bell fowt. As there war to be no opposit:on, Pd no 'casion to put cant a printed address. I could erplain my "policy" at th' meetin'. But just to please some folk, at liken a bit of ado undo on 'em I'd better canvas th' elevistun an' see heaw th' feeling war upo' sich an' sich things. SO I started on my reaunds. Th' <mowers I geet war very en- caaragin' an' bad moostly to be gan by women. I never knew beforee heave mony henpecked husbants there- wur Hazelwith. Ther a good lot war cbickenpecked as weel. They had to be for quietness, they said. Ther nobody wanted anytbin, nobbat a bit moore wark, an' a bit moore brass for dooin it. I promised 'em I'd see they had it. Has for" Home Rule," they conldno' get deawn to it. Jack o' Planter's wife said-if, it, would bring their Jack <whoara a bit sooner of a neet he mit have a voice i' thing* awhoarn. But if it wouldne' do that they'd better keep as ,they wur. Ther no better "Home Ruler" than the rowNtivin, and hoo knew heaw to use that when it wur badly wanted. Billy Softly'a wife's notions o'" Home Rule " weir rayther furr cant at sae. Theywanted no rulin' at their heause. When th' lads went to skeo th' skoomester ruled their copy-books wi' a lead spoon, an' a piece of a brash stall. Bat they'd getten o th' larnin they, wanted, so they'rn nowt short nobbut a bit o'' wark. I promised her they should have as mich as they wanted ;so hoo towd Billy he must mote for me. Ther an owd-bachelor would vote for me if I'd promise to put a heavy duty on p'rambilators,becose, he said, that ever sin' women begun o' em they'rn mans full o' childer. counry war o'errun wi 'em. I'd go tura. than that, I said. I'd put a duty on rackin-tintber. I'd his vote. My canvas wur a march o' triumph. I premised every- thing to everybody, an' that smoothed my way like nubbin' it wi' sond paper. Heaw th' performance would be I couldno' tell.. Happen when I geet to th' ileum of Com- mons I should find the?, somebody else tkeere beside me. But that doesno' matter when yo're on th' stamp. I pro- mised a good decal e' things when Pre coortin ut never come off.

Th' day fixed for the, meetin' coome, and browt a creased with it. Th' owd Ball fowt war never so throng sin' th' last rashcart, or sin' that day I made my speech abeaut chop beef. They sang "Rule Britannia," an' "Wait till the clouds roll by," while Pre gettin my courage up i'th' kitchen; an' when I meannted th' waggin at I war to spice eant on, th' saeaatin war sammat to be remembered. But it wur nowt to th' sheet nt4 war set ap when th' owd rib's bonnet war seen noddin bsheend me, an' her face, like a bunch o' summer bloom burst into th' front. My happiness wur fall messar. Sich like sheantsor "Brayvo, Ab !" " Thean's getten a rare backer l"' " Theau'll win in a tenter= !" " We shall have beef for fotchin, neavr," war gooin on. "Three cheers for th' owd stockenmender." "Hurray, hurray, hurray !" "one moors,"" Hurray." Th' owd, lass carchied as nicely as any lady could, ha' done ; an' then a cheearmon war elected. Two cheearmen war named, one a Liberal-Tcry, an' th' tother a Tory-Liberal; bat as nobody could tell.th' difference o' th' 'two, thl naeetin' agreed that one would represent booath parties. After sayin' a bit alvant hiasel, atV'th' importance o'th' occasion theyr'n met on, which war principally made up of,"'Prn,sure, I'm sure," an' makkin' his.speech last eaat till ererybody war gettin' anyessy, he finished up be introducin' me. After another sheant silence reigned. Eaar Sill trimmed my shirt collar, ut war a GOsM. shape; an' when I'd getten my sideboards gradely fixed,lstrode forrad to th'.fronb. I'd my speech written on a slate witheant frame, so reeled it off. I begun "Fellow Friends. Anybody at comes afore th' country at this time man have a policy. If he hasno' one it's no. nse offerin' hissel. Pre gettin' a policy, but it's a borrowed an. I have ne gone to Gladstone, nor Salisbury, nor Chamberlain, nor Churchill, an' astt 'em for bits o' theirs. It isn' made o' petches o' dif- ferent aorta. It's o bin raade eant o" one piece, hond-sewn, an' whcana-wesht. Th' raakker on't is stondin' beside me. (Hurray-ay-ay.) To this owd blossom here I'm i' debt for what I have to offer to yo. Woman like, hoo thinks abeaut herseran' her sex th' fast, an' goes in for women's rights. (Hero I wondered what war up. Folk war laafin an' , eheaatin like mad-locks. I'd made no p joke; so I wiped; my face for t' see if ther any soot on it, an felt if my pare war risin. 0 bein' reet I looked reannd, an' seed my owd aalYa- tion wi" nay knee-breeches in her boat; an' hoo're &nein' 'ern as if they'ra bein' offered, for sale. Thoose war women's rights.) Ay, if trhey'n tit, (I went on). That's tbi pee. amble of her bill. If a woman doeeno' put 'ern on neaw an' again hoo isno' fit to be a mon's companion. Wear 'ern their turns is as fair for one as another. But hoo objects to women gooin' to parlyment. Nobbat just fancy if yo con a parlyment o' women. Six hundred women, an' happen three handera childer i'th' arms, Fancy four hundert talkin' at ono 0 for I never seed six women t'gether but four en 'em war Whin'. Then th' skrikin' o' th' childer, an' th' sraackin an'—well, th" trouble wouldno' end theere. They'd ha' to keep a gang o' women i' livery for t' look after th' nussin. "Ladies of the totty bottle." (Loud laughter and cheers.) Beside, in a close atmosphere like th' Heause o' Commons, they'd have to ha' three or four doctors % ready for faintin and other emergencies. They mit look forrad to some very young members Wu' elected without opposition. (Here I'd my eloquence cat short by a hoist bein' slapped on my meanth, an' a mani- festo bein' sheanted ray ear,—" That's noane i' my bill, Abram.") It's one o' my amendments. Neale, then, for th' array,—women as sodiera. I believe they'd make better feighters than th' men. Whoaever seed a woman flinch fro' danger? Why, 11°1)11 run into it sometimes, speshlv if another woman has bin sayin' summat abeant her. Then it's war to th' knife. One o' th' two has to be damaged. There'd be an advantage i' women being' sodiers I that's bin o'erlooked. We could put mothe i'th' rs-m- aw front o' th' battle; so at when th' feight war o'er some I sons•in.law mold Inv a bit o' Oleic own road. Heaw Emmy

"Thank, you, ma'am," said he, " but where is yours ?" An old editor of Harper's told me once that just after he came to,New York he got so hard up that he needed • a hundred dollars very badly. He did not dare ask Fletcher Harper, who was a great friend of his, for so small anamoune as a hundred dollars, through fear 111 might he looked on as a petty borrower and sort of &at' beat. So he walked in,on his friend and said :—" I want SOO dollars. Can you let me have it ?" The re- sponse. was" certainly:" He got the money, put 400 dollars of it in the bank, and when he scraped together the hundred he spent, he paid it all back. Years after: ward he asked Harper what the latter would have crel?, if he had asked for the hundred dollars. Fletcher ho should probably' have let him have it, but shouldhas:ar kept out of his way thereafter. "I thought so," Sal Seaver; and then he told Harper what he had done. , • A curious anecdote is told of that remarkable and /ant officer, Admiral Cornwallis. - F)REIGN NEWS.

DISTURBED STATE OF BURMA H. RANGOON, BLTURDAY.—The country about Mandalay is 'very disturbed. The flotilla steamer Kadz,e, while descend- ing the Myiltugo, was fireel on by insurgents, and one of the &pop guard was wounded. The Myentzein Prince holds the country to the south-east of Mandalay, and his forces are said to be increasing. Until the Myentzein Prince is captured or driven from the field there is no prospect of a pacification of Upper Barmah. All the other insurgent leaders profess to be fighting in his interest. Much surprise is felt that more vigorous measures have not been taken against the Myentzein Prince. RUSSIA AND BA.TOUM. CONSTANTINOPLE, SATIIRDAY.—A Note of the Russian Government announcing that Batoum has ceased to be a free port has been presented to the Porte. It states that in view of the then circumstances the character of a free port was given to Batoum at the time of the Berlin Congress by the spontaneous action of Russia; but now that a Customs .cordon has beers established around the place the existing condition of affairs causes serious prejudice to the commerce of Russia, and the Government of the Czar has therefore been impelled to decide upon withdrawing the declaration making Batoum a free port. Batoutn, will remain, notwith- standing, an essentially commercial harbour, and will not •become a place of arms. BERLIN, MONDAY.—For the first time s'nce the opening •of the Batoum question the Norddeutsche Zeitung, Prince Bismarck's organ, makes editorial references to tho pubj..ct. After simply alluding to the Government's decree closing the free port, the semi-official writer says.:—" With this act the Batoum question, which has lately given rise to so much discussion in the press, will probably soon.disappear from the order of the day." TU RKISH DISARMAMENT. CONSTANTINOPLE, MONDA Y. An Imperial Irade has been issued sanctioning the reduction of the regular army to the peace footing. The military and naval reserves will also be disbanded. Several Turkish vessels are now at Salonica in readiness to bring back the troops. FIGHTING BETWEEN MONTENEGRINS AND ALBANIANS. CONSTANTINOPLE, SKrunDt.Y.—lntelligence received here reports fresh conflicts between Montenegrins and Albanians in the direction of Motsa Planina in the Gassinje district in which the Albanians lost one man killed and three wounded, and the Montenegrins two killed and four wounded. M. Bacics, the Montenegrin Diplomatic Agent, at an interview with Kiamil Pasha, has pointed out that this state of things is dangerous and likely to lead to armed in- tervention, unless order were maintained by the Turkish authorities among the Albanians on the Montenegrin fron- tier. On the last occasion hut one on which the fighting occurred the Albanians lost seventy killed and fifty pri- soners. The Porte claims the release of the latter. Monte- negro insists that an inquiry ahould first be held, in order to punish the aggressors. ALLEGED PLOT TO ASSASSINATE THE KING OF II ALY. Roue, MONDAY.—A. Sergeant of the 88th Regiment of infantry, in garrison at Monza., to-day nvnie an abortive attempt to commit suicide by shooting himself with his rifle. Among his papers a letter was discovered addressed by him to the King. In this letter he stated that he had been deputed by a secret society to take the life of the King, but that he preferred to die himself. He commended his mother to the ears of the King. Taken before a magistrate the sergeant adhered to the statement made in his letter ; but refused to name the members of the secret society al luded to. It is gener4llY - believed that the story is a fabri- cation. King Humbert is reported tn have said, on reading the letter, The man must be a lunatic, who desired to im- part an interesting character to his suicide." THE CHOLERA. Ro}m, SATURDAY.—The cholera returns for the past 24 hours show that there were 135 cases and 46 deaths in the province of Brindisi, including 15 cases and 5 deaths in the town of Brindisi, 32 cases and 15 deiths at Lai iano, 59 cases and 21 deaths at Francavilla Fontana, and 12 cases and 3 deaths at Sin Vito. One case and two deaths are an- nounced front Venice, and 8 casLe and 1 death frecn Codi.

goro. Rons,lownev.—The cholera return for the past 24 hours report 06 cases and 35 deaths in the Province of Brindisi, Seim; a decrease of seven in the number of cases and of 14 in the deaths as compared with the preceding day. TRIESTE, ISIONDAY.—FrOM ROOll on Saturday to the same , hour to-day eight persons, including two infantry soldiers, have been attacked by cholera. One of the soldiers and one civilian have succumbed. • THE EXILED FREN'CII PRINCES. Pants, MONDLY,—The Due' D'Aumale having received official notice that he had been struck off the Army List, has appealed to the Council of State, and at tbe same time addressed the ftillowing letter to the Presidtnt of tbs Re- public Chaiatilly, July 11. M. le President, —Three years ago. without pretext or precedent, you inflicted upon me the aeverest of disciplinary punishments. / remained silent. To-day, in striking nay name off the Army List, you inter- fere with the chirter of the at my without taking into account the title won in battle. Your Ministers strike men without reproach and honoured by their services and tbeir tradition il devotion to the country. I leave to my counsel the task of defending a cause which is that of all officers. As for me, doyen of the Uenerat Staff, it is my duty to remind you

that military grades are beyond your powers." M. Brisson, the late Premier, called upon M. de Freycinet this morning and expressed surprise that the Government bad not ex- pelled the Duc D'Aumale immediately on learning tl.e con- tents of the Duke's letter. M. de Freycinet, in reply, stated that the matter would be considered by the Cabinet to-morrow. It is believed that the subject will be brought forward in the Chamber of Deputies by several members of the Left. PARIS, JteSDAY.At a Cabinet Council this morning the expulsion of the Duc d'Aumale from France was decided upon. It is believed that if the Duc de Chartres pursues the same line of action taken by the Due d'Aumale, a large number of deputies will propose the confiscation of tbe property of the Orleans family. RIOTING IN FRANCE. PARIS, MONDAY.—Serious rioting took place yeeterday at Armentieres, in the department of the Nord, both before and after the meeting at which M. Paul de Cassagnac spoke in favour of maintaining the Conservative union, which would "result in a fresh liberation of the territory by the expulsion of the Republic." M. Paul de Cassagnac had, in driving to the meeting, been the object of a hostile manifes- tation; but when he left it the disturbance assumed a more serious character, for, in his speech, he had said that tha time had long passed when the Republic could be accepted by honest men. In the conflict which was engaged in be- tween the 8,000 people who had attended the meeting and the Republicans, Socialists, and roughs, several shots were fired with revolvers. It was not till 11 o'clock at night that the gendarmes, with the aid of 300 soldiers, who were sent to Armentieres from Lille, succeeded in restor- ing Order. Five people were arrested. FRANCE AND TRADE PROTECTION. PARIS, SO/MAX.—The debate in the Chamber on the Corn Tax ended on Saturday, when M. de Ville, Minister of Agriculture, made a short speech on behalf of the Government. He entirely agreed with the Committee on the expediency of raising the duty on corn from 3f. to 5f., or even higher if it were found necessary for the protection of agriculturists. However, it was best to wait until the corn law of 1884 had time to produce its full effect. The importation of foreign wheat had almost entirely ceased, and could not meanwhile become a cause of alarm. M. de Ville asked the Chamber to postpone voting on the bill until next session. The motion was carried by 273 against 254. The bill has thus been cleverly disposed of so as to give offence neither to the Protectionist peasants nor to the more Liberal working classes. FRENCH NATIONAL FESTIVAL. Pints, WEDNESDAY, 8 P.M.—The national fete is being celebrated here to-day in the usual manner, and the streets present an animated appearance notwithstanding the un- favourable weather. Up to the present the rejoicings have not been marred by any untoward incident. The review of the troops at Lougchamps in the afternoon passed off in accordance with the official programme. MURDER OF A FRENCH JUDGE. ; An Exchange Company's telegram from Paris says :—A I telegram from Aubusson annomnces that M. Bourdery, the judge of the local tribunal, has been shot dead by a neighbour in revenge for the loss of an action tried before him.

THE FRENCH NATIONAL FETE. PARIS, THURSDAY, 8 A.m.—The National Fete was kept up with much spirit throughout the night. There have been fewer accidents than in previous years. The church at Ivry has been partially destroyed by fire, the woodwork of the belfry having become ignited by the illumination lamps placed around it. Two persons were injured. RENEWED FIGHTING IN TONQUIN. PARIS, THURSDLY.—The " Temps " this evening states that the latest Indo-China mail brings unfavoutable news from Tonquin. Some piratical bands, composed of former Chinese regulars who bad returned to Tonquinese territory, attacked at the end of May the French posts at Thatke and Thanmoi. In the fighting that followed the French had several killed and wounded. Thanmoi was completely sur- rounded, and Commander Servieres was marching to the relief of the garrison. Two French merchants had been assassinated. SCENES IN THE NEW SOUTH WALES PARLIAMENT. SYDNEY MONDAY.—The Legislative Assembly has been sitting for '56 consecutive hours discussing the Tariffs Bill, the proceedings being marked by great disorder. Three members were suspended. and it was found necessary to clear the strangers' galleries, which were unoccupied dur- ing the greater portion of the debate. The Opposition, headed by Sir Henry Parkes, refused to sit on Sunday, and left the Rouse at midnight. whereupon the Ministerialists passed the clauses of the bill. TrIE VOLCANIC ERUPTION IN NEW ZEALAND. Nzw Yozz, MONDIY.—The steamer Alameda arrived at San Francisco on the 11th. bringing further particulars of the volcanic eruption in New Zealand. Numerous small native villages were totally destroyed. Wairsa was covered to a depth of ten -feet with dust and ashes. Rahtomahana was engulfed, and also other small villages. Twenty-one persons are known to have lost their lives, among whom are several English residents. The loss of cattle, starved from the destruction of pasture by the dust, is very great. Much distress exists in all the Auckland lake district. An old Maori chief at Ratarna was dug out alive. He bad been buried in the ashes.for,lo4 hours. At the date of the de- parture of the Alameda from Auckland the volcanoes were still very active. Mr. Johnston, Government Agent in Auckland. reports that Rotana House, occupied by Mr. Haztrd, was borne down by the weight of the debris Mrs. Hazard was dug out alive, but four of her children were dead. Mr. Hazard is missing. Detailed reports as to the foreign residents at other points who were killed have not yet been received. MADAGASCAR. TAMATIVE, JULY 5. The Malagasy Government has granted a charter to Mr. Abraham Kingdon for the estab- lishment of a Royal Bank in Madagascar, with the right of coinage and of issuing bank notes. Tne total capital of the bank is fixed at £2 000,000. The Government has agreed to contract with the bank a loan of £BOO,OOO, tearing in- terest at 7 per cent, secured on the Customs revenue. CATHOLIC INTERESTS IN CHINA. ROME, WEDNESDA Y.—The convention under negotiation for some time past between the Chinese Government and the 'Vatican for the direct representation of the Holy See has been concluded, and Monsignor Agliardi has been ap- pointed to the post of Internuncio thus rendered necesaary in the Chinese capital.

_ _ • THE WIDNES DIVISION ELECTION. TELE RESULT. The poll on Friday. was a very heavy one consider- ing the migratory nature of the population. Only 535 less votes were recorded than in November, the total poll being 6,646. Mr. Moss polled 80 fewer votes than he did on his previous election' and Mr. Birrell 377 more than were recorded for Mr. Masi:watt, Mr. Moss's majority having undergone the substan- tial reduction of 885 votes, notwithstanding the split in the Liberal camp. Last election the figures were —Moss! 4,527 ; Muspratt, .2,650; Conservative ma- jority, 5.377. The result of the poll was declared from the L9cal Board 1 Offices shortly after noon on Saturdly as follows -M : T. C. Edwardsoss (C) ...... 3,719 Augustine Birrell (L) ..... .... 2,927

Majority .............. 792 The declaration, made by Alderman John Hughes, of Liver- pool, the deputy sheriff, was received with loud groans mingled with cheers from a crowd of about 600 persons who had assembled. Mr. Moss sac the.first to leave the building accompanied by his election agent, Mr. W. T. Husband, and the Rev. George Bond, and then Mr. Birrell, accompanied' by Mr. E. R. Muspratt and Mr. E. Carey, emerged and was loudly cheered. They walked to the Central Committee- room in Victoria-roed, where from the window of an upper room Mr. Birrell addressed the crowd below. ' Mr. Bezaßea, &Aid : I can at all events congratulate the electors of Widnes itself with baying done their duty faith- fully at this great crisis—(hear, hear, and cheers)—for I believe that all of you who have votes have honestly gene to the poll and polled them for me. (Cheers.) But stone the less, we have to face the fact that we have been beaten by a majority, which, though lareely reduced, was still sub- stantial. While last time my opponent, a gentlemen for whom personally I have great respect, got in by the Irish vote, this time I think he has got in—At all events his ma- jority has been enormonsly increased—by the greet number of Liberal abstentions. (Hear, hear.) But, gentletnen, there is no occasion for you to feel any alarm in this matter, be- cause the great question which has been before the country at this election, and which I know is very dear to the hearts. of many of you, the cause of justice to Ireland, hes now been espoused by a great party in Ecgland. It has been transplanted from Ire- land to England, and has as its leader the present Prime Minister of this oountry • and it will have in the new Par- liament a large number Of persons of great importance, great responsibility, and great eloquence, whom you may be satis- fied will never rest until the cause they have espoused is brought to a satisfactory conclusion. (Ceers.) Personally Ido not feel one little bit discouraged—(bear hear)—be- Cause the cause I laave been advocating is one Of truth, jus- tice, and good sense, and it will be advocated in the new Parliament by men of greater ability than myself ; and therefore I beseech you all to be perfectly cairn, good na- tured, and good tempeted, feeling properly eat'sfied that be- fore very long Ireland will have a substantial meesure of self-government grantee?, to her, ar ci that the unity of the empire of which we have beard so much will be not a whit impeired, and we shall live and die bound together by every substantial tie. (Cheers.) lam very much obliged to you for the kindness with which you have listened to use throughout the election. Personally I have enjoyed myself exceedingly, and I ehall go back encouraged by the thought that I have received such large hearted support from many, and made so many dear friends. (Cheers.) Mr. Moss also addressed his supperters at the Conserva- tive committee-room as follows :—Gentletnen,—l am very much obliged to you for again electine me as your mem- ber. I can assure you that I very fully appreciate the re- sponsibility that you have put upon me in this matter; and I only hope tbat I shall represent you properly in the next Parliament. (Cheers) We have won a great N ictory. (Cheers.) We have stuck to our principles, which I think are right, and you have done what the other divisions of Lancashire have done—you have returned one who will maintain the Union. (Cheers.) I think this contest has been fought on 'my good terms. We have not quarrelled with our opponents. We leave differed with them in pelitice, but have not quarrelled in any other way—(bear, bear)— and now that we have won I hope we shall make friends with them, and think no more about it until next election.

div.head: EXAMINERS, SATURDAY. JULY 17, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINERS, SATURDAY. JULY 17, 1886.

I hope I shall not only represent those who supported me, I but the Liberals as well, and that I shall give satisfaction to all the inhabitants of Widnes, and do all I can to pro- mote any local interests. (Cheers.) MR. MOSS AT GAKSTON. Having addressed the electors at Widnes on Saturday, Mr. Moss, accompanied by Mr. Gilbert Moss, proceeded to Gars- ton by the 1-32 train. He was met by a good nurnher of friends at the Central Station, who accorded him a hearty reception. He drove in his private carriage to the Conserve tiye committee-rooms, receiving as he passed along the greetings of his' friends and supporters. A large crowd assembled near the committee-roorns.—Captain in introducing Mr. Moss from the window of the committee - rooms, expressed his pleasure at the result ef the poll, and said they had been fighting for the good of the country and the unity of the Empire. (Cheers.)—Mr. Moss, who WAS received with prolonged cheers, thanked his supporters for the assistance they bad accorded him. He was satisfied that the larger part of his majority had come from Gars- ton. It the last election they were told that they had won because of the assistance of a certain party. This time, how- ever, they bad shown that party that they could win without their assistance.—Mr. Moss then drove home to Otterspool. MR. F. H. GOSSAGE ON THE ELECTION. At the termination of the business at the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Mr. F. H. Gossage, who presided, said he should like the press to give publicity to a few remarks he had to make concerning the state of the town on Satur- day, at a time when the inhabitants might naturally be ex- pected to labour under considerable excitement, owing to the declaration of the poll. He was gratified to be able to state that Inspector Wood, who was in charge of the Widnes Police Station, had only to report one case of drunkenness as happening on Saturday night. The town was in a very quiet and orderly condition; and Mr. Gossage had plea- sure in congratulating his fellow townsmen on this happy state of affairs.

TFIE GENERAL ELECTION- Last Saturday the Conservatives were slightly ahead of the other three parties combined, but they have since lost that position. In the polls announced since our last the Conservatives have made several gains from the Minis- terialists and in constituencies lately represented by Unionists. The Unionist Liberals gained two Ministerialiat seats and one Nationalist seat, white the Ministerialist gains numbered six from the Unionist party. Among the latter ware defeated Sir George Trevelvan. in Hawick Burghs; Sir John Ramsden, Osgoldcross 'Division, Yorks.; ar.d Mr. Albert Grey, Northumberland, Tyneside. The Unionist success which dispossessed a Nationalist—Mr. Timothy Healy—is interesting in that it admits to Parlia- ment the first Liberal member since 1885 from Ireland. It is also noteworthy that Mr. L. 11. Courtney retains his seat for the Bodrnin Division of Cornwall by a large majority, and Sir Robert Peel has failed in ousting Mr. R B. Finlay, the Unionist member for the Inverness Burghs. On Tuesday the returns were announced in two contest a in which Conservatives and Liberal Unionists were opposed. In the Torquay Division of Devonshire, Mr. R. Malloch, a Conservative, turned out the old member, Mr. L. Mclver, by a majority of 80 votes; while in the Peters- ield Division of Hampshire Viscount Wolmer (Liberal Unionist) held his own against Mr. W. Nicholson (Con- servative) by 111 votes. Viscount Wolmer obtained his seat in the last Parliament owing to two Conservatives fighting, being in a minority compared with the mixed Conservative vote of 18. On the whole, the elections we are noticing have gone against the Unionist Liberals. Considering the defeats in the counties which the Minis- terialists have suffered, it is pleasant to note the success of Mr. W. S. B. McLaren in the Crewe Division of Cheshire; Mr. Rathbone in Arvon, Carnarvonshire ; and Mr. C. J. S. Foljambe and Sir B. Samuelson in divisions of Nottinghamshire and Oxfordshire respectively. York- shire, which has been so faithful to the Ministry, has been the scehe of one defeat which will be regretted by many— that of Sir Matthew Wilson in the Skipton Division by the small majority of 134 out of a poll of 8712. Sir Matthew is 84 yews of age, and he was one of the minority of seven who voted for Mr. Villiers' motion for the immediate re- peal of the Corn Laws. His first contest was in 1841, when he won Clitheroe by five votes. Sir Geo. Trevelyan arrived on Tuesday morning in Lou-

_ don from Hawick. At Castletlaney a man named Flanagan has been com- mitted for trial, charged with having attempted to personate a deceased voter. Stimulated, perhaps, by the example of his brother (Lord Randolph Churchill), *he Duke of Marlborough intends to devote himself to politics. The Wesleyan address to Mr. Gladstone, promoted by Mr. Isaac Holden and the Rv. J. R. Hargreaves, has been signed or approved b, 700 ministers. Toe Doily Telegraph kindly suggests that in the circum- stances in which they are placed the Liberal party should unite themselves under the leadelehip of Lord Hartington. Some curious stories are told respecting the operations of the Primrose League. It is said that in certain constituen- cies dames of the Order have been urging the exercise of physical forte and intimidation. The Nationalists have determined to petition, on Mr. Justin McCarthy's behalf, against Mr. Lewis's return for Londonderry on the grounds of alleged impersonation and of certain persons who voted being minors. It is the intention of Mr. David Davies, the Liberal Unionist•candidate for Cardiganshire at the recent election, to petition for a recount and scrutiny, Mr. Bower Rolands, Q C., having been returned by only nine votes. The Pope has requested the Congregation on Extraordi- nary Ecclesiastical Affairs to give attentive examination to the whole Trish question, in order to determine the course to be followed by the Irish Catholic clergy in certain con-

tingencies. Once more the Times has been caught napping. On Monday it published a biography of Mr. James Lowther as the successful Tory candidate for a division of West- morland. As a matter of fact, it was another and a younger member of the Lowther family who won the

seat. The •Sterndard gives prominence to a letter signed "A," who confidently states that Lord Salisbury desires to act in concert with Lord Hartington in forming a Government, and that this desire will be frustrated, if frustrated it be, only by Lord Hartington himself regarding the difficulties in the way of its fulfement as insurmountable. Mr. Gladstone has addressed the following letter to Dr. Foster, the defeated candidate at Chester :---" Dear site—l thank you for your kind letter. You made a gallant fight, and in your defeat I regret the loss cf your aid in the House of Commons,the loss of Chester, and the action of the Duke of Westminster, which I conceive to be a fresh blow struck at the aristocracy by hint" It is stated that Mr. Timothy Healy has no reason to fear that be will be left out in the cold. He has been defeated it is true, but a seat will be found for him. He is too useful and capable a member of the Parnellite party to be spared. Mr. Sexton having been elected for two different con- stituencies—namely, Belfast and Sligo—there should be no difficulty about satisfactorily disposing of Mr. Healy. Many of the people injured by the police after the decla- ration of the poll at Cardiff have so far recovered, as to be able to get about, and the appearance in the streets of men, young and old, with heads bandaged or arms in slings is a familiar sight. Only two windows were broken in the whole town. The Mayor has called upon the bead constable for an explanation to be presented to the Watch Committee on Wednesday. The Wesleyan address to Mr. Gladstone has received in three days 400 signatures of ministers. One hundred and fifty others approve of it. but decline to 'sign, as they feel. bound by the general understanding not to mix in political action. It has been decided not to print a list of the signa- tures, but to present the address by a deputation to Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Isaac Holden, M.P., and the Rev. J. Richmond Hargreaves, Keighley, are the acting secretaries. The following telegram has been received from Mr. Gladstone at Mr. John Wilson's committee rooms at Sunder- j land :—" I heartily wish success to Mr. Wilson, who has already proved himself a worthy representative of labour in Parliament.. The county of Durham has so far, like the North generally, shown great judgment on great questions submitted to the country, and I hope the Houghton-le Spring Division will confirm that judgment.—GLADSTONX." The Central News says :—With reference to a letter signed "Onlooker " in the " Times " of the 12th July, ask- ing whether or not it is true that some time ago Mr. John O'Leary was privately summoned to London for the pur- poses of consultation, and that while there he was seen aed interviewed by the Prime Minister, Earl Spencer, and Mr. J. Morley, we are officially requested to state that there is no foundation for the insinuation thus conveyed. No one of the Ministers mentioned ham either seen or had any communication with Mr. John O'Leary. One of the most unique elections on record was that of South Carnarvonshire, the polling for which took place on Saturday. The successful candidate, Mr. John Bryn Roberts, was a Ministerialist, and his opponent. Mr. George Farren, a Liberal Unionist. Mr. Farren fought under the great disadvantaged feeble health, and was cruising about the coast in his yacht throughout the entire contest. The only meeting he addressed was from the deck of his yacht lying off Cernarvon harbour, his hearers meanwhile rocking in small boa, sin as close proximity as circumstances per- mitted. The majority against Mr. Ferrets on Saturday was 2,977—the figures being respectively 4 244 and 1,267. Mr. Bright, replying to a letter from an elector at Cleck- heatoo, calling attention to some remarks made by Mr. Wm. Anderton at that place on June nth, writes as follows: "One Ash, Rochdale, July 7, 1886.—Dear Sir,—Mr. Ander- ton cannot understand veliat he reads. The Irish have a right to ask for repeal or to incite insurrection if they please. and to take the consequences; but it may be wrong to grant it, and might be injurious to them. I have never said a word in favour of repeal or a Dublin Parliament, and my goodwill to Irelaed makes it impossible for inc to sup- port the wild plans of the Government bill. As to nay age and mental criticism, I say nothing. Mr. Anderton may be a Strong supperter of Home Rule, but he is not a geutle- man.--Yours very truly, Jones BRIGHT." Mr. Gladstone has sent the following. letter to Mr. James Kitson, of Leeds:—" Hawarden Castle, Chester. July 9th, 1886.—Dear Mr. Kitson,— to suff,r in a goof cause is a thing so honoarable and noble that I wiil not condole with you, but I am sorry that after so much of most intelligent and patriotic exertion you should not form one uf our Parliamentary band. We have Scotland, Ireland. York- shire, and I hope the North, and we have with us the civilised world. From this moment it is probable that our cause will visibly move upwards. It has indeed enormously moved upwards during the last twelve mouths, and is fin ml triumph is certain. The only qaestion is, how much will there ko of unhappines for Ireland, of difficulty and delay,

of pain and shame for England before the consummation will be reached. But I earnestly hope that you may yet be enabled to take your place amongst us. In any case, I am sure it will be felt that your high character has been raiied even higher by yeur conduct duting the present straggle.—With our best and united compliments to Mrs. Kitson, I remain, very faithfully yours, W. E. GLADSTONE."

LANCASHIRE DIVISIONS. GORTON.—The polling in the Gorton Division took place on Saturday, and resulted in the return of M. R. Peacock, the Ministerial candidate, and first member for the division. Viscount Grey de Wilton was the champion of:tbe Conser- vative cause. Carriages were freely used, and there was a good display of reel and blue colours. Tne result was made known on Saturday as follows : .

R. Peacock (G L) Lord Grey de Wilton (C) 4,135-457 The result was hailed with loud and prolonged cheering by the immense crowd which was gathered outside the building. On the last occasion Mr. Peacock headed his op- ponent with a majority of 1,748. RADCLIFFS•CIIII-FARNWORTIL—The polling took place on Friday and the counting on Saturday, in the Congrega- tional Schools, Radcliffe, before Mr. J. B. Edge, the return- ing officer. The result of the poll was declared from the balcony of the Local Board Offices shortly after one o'clock as follows

Robert Leake (G L) Sir F. Milner (C) Last election: It. Leake (L), 5,092; W. W. B. Hutton (C), 4,579. The announcement was received with enthusiastic cheering by the supporters of Mr. Leake.—Mr. Leake. ad- dressing the wed, saki he had been made a proud man that day. He stood in the centre of a real Liberal constitu- ency. (Cheers.) A very difficult political question suddenly brought before the constituency had not divided them as it had some of their neighbours. They, at any rate, had given their verdict on the great issue in favour of Ireland govern- ing herself so far as her local affairs were concerned. (Cheers.) Their victory would be received with the great- est delight throughout South-East Lancashire. (Lona cheers.) Afterwards Mr. Leake drove te The Dales with his Election Committee, being greeted with continuous cheers on the way. Wilms DIVISION.—The polling took place on Friday, and the votes were counted on Saturday morning. Par- ticulars are given elsewhere. The numbers were— 'l. C. Edwards-Moss (C) Augustine Birrell (G L) HRYWOOD.—The votes recorded in tte polling for this division on Saturday were counted on Monday, at the Municipal Buildines, Heywood. The returning officer was Mr. J. Molesworth, coroner for the distric'. of Rochdale. By about twelve o'clock the public outside were made acquain- ted with the fact that the old member, Mr. ((mac Hoyle, of Prestwich, was again elected. Mr. Molesworth declaleal the result as follows:— Mr. Isaac Hoyle (G L) 4.206 Mr. John Grant Lawson (C) 3,762-444 Mr. Hoyle proposed a vote of thanks to the officers who had conducted the election.—Mr. Lawson, the defeated candidate seconded the motion, and it was passed with ac- clamation.—At the election in November the numbers polled were Hoyle (L), 4,538 ; Kenyon (C), 3,955. Since then 140 voters have died, and the proportion of deaths in Hey- wood has been in the ratio of two Liberals for one Conserva- tive. The registered number of voters is 9,269, but the actual number of voters is under 9,000. Mr. Hoyle, M.P., thanked the workers of every rank and degree for their un- tiring devotion to the Liberal cause in the present contest. They had achieved a great victory. That victory was theirs, and they were entitled to the honour. Mr. Gladstone had shown what could be accomplished by generous treatment of Ireland, and it would be recorded in history that his at- tempt to turn bitter into sweet and cursing into blessing drew the Irish race to him, and that throughout the world Irishmen were in sympathy with him and with his work. (Applause.)—When Mr. Hoyle left the Reform Club the horses were taken from his carriage, which was dragged by the crowd to the residence of Mr. Isherwood, where he again said a few words. Cheers were then given for Mr. llsherwood and his family. at Mr. Hoyle's request, and also for the "Grand Old Man." NORTH LONSDALH.—The polling took place for North Lonsdale on Friday. The number of votes was 781 less than those recorded in November. The candidates were Mr. William Martin Edmunds (M), secretary to the British Home Rule Association, and Mr. W. G. Ainslie (C). the old member. As was anticipated, Mr. Edmunds was defeated. He was not only late in taking the field, but he bad the whole of the Cavendish influence against him and that in North Lonsdale means much. Mr. Edmunds fought a plucky fight, and during his week's acquaintanceship with the constituency be made a very good impression. Had he commenced his candidature earlier there is great probability that the poll, if it had not resulted in his favour, would at any rate have shown a considerable smaller majority against him than it has. The countiog of the votes com- menced at ten o'clock in the morning, and the work was got through with all despatch. Mr. Edmunds, although de- feated, is not in the least disheartened. The result of the voting was— Ainslie (C) Edmunds (G L).., 3.263-800 At the last election the figures were—Ainslie (C), 4,166; Sir F. Herechell (L), 3,941. ROSSENDALE.—The whole of the electoral machinery of the Conservative party was set in motion in order to pro- mote the return of Lord Harrington. But so zealously did those who approve of Home Rule Bills labour for Mr. New- bigging that the other side found it necessary also to set to work with great vigour. Though there has never, in the opinion of some, been any likelihood of Lord Hartington being overthrown, apprehensions were entertained by many of the Liberal Unionists towards the middle of last week that the majority in his favour would not be large enough to be satisfactory to them. This feeling stimulated both them and their Conservative allies to greater exertions, and they had their reward when the poll wee declared on Satur- day night. Both candidates being Lioerals, it became necessary for their active adherents to adopt some mark of distinction; accordingly, while Mr. Newbigging stuck simply to red ribbons and red rosettes, those who were work- ing for Lord Hartington displayed a combination of red, white, and blue. A great deal of good-humoured chaff was indulged in by the Liberals who were working in opposition to each other, and many of the conveyances used by the friends of the Ministerial candidate furnished food for much jocularity to Lord Hartington's followers, who had at their service a better class of vehicles. Good temper, however, prevailed throughout the division. The polling was very regular, and there were not many signs of keen public excitement, except at Bacup and Rawtenstall. The former place was crowded et night by people who wished to know the result before they went to bed. The votes were counted at the Mechanics' Institution there, and the result was declared at 10-55 p.m. to be— Lord Hartington (U) 5,399 Mr. T. Newbigging (G L) 3,949

Majority The election in November last gave the followinz return : Lord Hartington (L), 6,060 : Mr. W. F. Ecroyd (C), 4 228 ; majority, 1,832. On that occasion 10,288 ne,sons voted; the number who did so on Saturday was 9,343. If the 060 who Voted for Lord Hartington seven months ago may be assumed to represent the full Liberal vote, it is evi- dent that Mr. Newhigging secured 65 per cent anti Lord Hartington over 30 per cent. When the poll was declared Lord Hartington was absent, for after the dissrderly scene at the me.ting at Bacup on Tuesday it was thought ad- visable by his lordship's friends that ha should await the result at Crawshaw Crawshawboeth, the residence of Mr. T. Brooks, the chair man of his committee. CHESHIRE DIVISIONS. -

HYDE.—The result of the polling at Hyde on Friday was the defeat of the Liberal candidate, Mr. Thomas Gair Ash- ton and the return of his opponent, Mr. Joseph Watson Sidebotharn, by a majority of 443 votes. Mr. eidebothatn polled 218 votes below the numoer recorded for Mr. Ashton last December, and Mr. Ashten received 661 less, 4,546 being recorded for the Liberal candidate at that time and 3,990 for his oppouent, Colonel Legh. 323 fewer votes were recorded on Friday, and there is little doubt that a large number of Liberals abstained from voting rather than support Mr. Sidebotham. The votes were counted at the liede Town Hall on Saturday morning, and at half-past twelve the deputy returning officer. Mr. Henry Taylor, of Chester, announced the numbers from the balcony. The name of Mr. Ashton Quite first, and many Liberals naturally came to the conclusion that Mr. Ashton was returned, and rushed oft to the Reform Club with the news. When the mistake was found out their disappointment may be imagined. The numbers given were— Mr. Josept W: Sidebottorn (C) 4.328 Mr. Thomas Gair Ashton (G) • 3,885-443 Last election: Mr. T. U. Ashton (L), 4,540; Colonel Legh (C), 3,090: CREWE.—The polling in the Crewe division of Cheshire took place on Monday. The bulk of the voters are en- gaged in industrial pursuits, though there is a good spriek- ling of those engaged in the agricultural intetest. At the last election Mr. G. W. Latham defeated his opponent, Mr. 0. L. Stephen, the Tory candidate. by a majority of 808, and was returned as the first M.P. for the newly-formed Crewe division. But on account of continued ill lealth Mr. Latham was unable to stand as the candidate at this election. Mr. Stephen also declined to contest the division again. The Liberal party thereupon selected Mr. W. S. B. MiLaren,worsted spinner, of Bradfoid, and a nephew of Mr. John Beight, as their crindidate, whilst the Tories chose Mr. P. R. Twemlow, barrister, of Peatswo, d and owner of estete in the neighbourhood, as theirs. Mr. Melearen on Monday drove through the whole division, extending over twelve miles, and was well rec,ived. In their rounds both at Crewe and Nantwich the candidates met each other, and made cordial salutations. After the pell the ballot boxes bed to be brought from places dietant nine or ten miles, and the counting could not be begun until about 9-30. The numbers were declared as follows : Mr. W. S. B. NPLeren (1.1) 4,690 Mr. P. R. Twemlow (C)
tire of the Northvrich Division of Cheshire, was made kaown at Northwicb as follows : • Verdin (U L) Brunner (L)

Majority 458 The declaration was received with mingled groans and 1 cheers, which having subsided, the successful candidate proposed a vote of thanks to the returning officer, which was briefly seconded by Mr. Brunner. MACCLESFIELD.—The polling for the Macclesfield Divi- sion took place on Wednesday, the candidates being Mr. William Cowie Brocklehurst (Liberal) and Mr. William Bromley Davenport (Conservative). The contest has been , fought with remarkable vigour on both sides, and up to the last both parties made certain of victory. Beyond a profuse ; display of party colours, sad the employment of large nem- bers of vehicles, there was nothing noteworthy in the poll- ing, which was carried on briskly from morning till night. The polling was declared on Thursday as follows : Mr. W. Bromley Davenport (C) ... 3,283 Mr. W. C. Brocklehurst (G) 2,756-527 , At the last general election Brocklehurst.(l..) polled 3,311 votes, against 2,846 given to Sir W. C. Brooks (C). EDDISBURY.—ProbabIy the most exciting and strenuous political contest that has been fought in the district of Ed- disbury for some time was the one which took place on Thursday between the popular candidates for Parliamentaiy honours. Mr, J. Tomkinson, J.P., of Willington who is a landowner and a banker at Chester, was the Gladstone Liberal candidate, whilst Mr. H. J. Tollemache, J.P., of Dorfold, Nantwich, contested the division again in the Tory interest. They are cousins. On the last occasion Mr. Tollemache succeeded in obtaining the seat by a ma- jority of 121 over Mr. L. Irwell. Mr. E. Brassey, agent for Mr. Tomkinson, issued a circular to the tenants of certain farms complaining of the influence exerted against the Liberal candidate on the Eaton Hall estate, and announcing that if his allegations could be brought home he would in- stitute a prosecution under the Corrupt Practices Act. Fol- lowing upon the duke's action, mach correspondence his transpired. However, the voters of the division were left to judge the position of parties, and were educated nightly by Mr. Totnkinson, as Mr. Gladstone re- marked at Chester Station on Wednesday evening. The polling commenced at eight o'clock on Thursday morn- ing at the polling booths which numbered nineteen. The division is an exceptionally large one, and contains about 10,000 actual voters. The following were the polling sta- tions in the division; Boys' National School, Acten; Parochial School, Audlem; Boys' Old School, Great Bough- ton; a shop, Bradwall ; Mixed School, Bridgemere ; Egerton Arms Inn, Little Budworth ; Girls' National School. Bun- bury; Magistrates' Room Chester Castle; Schoolroom, Cbolmondelev ; Schools, &Church Minshull ; Schools, Dun- ham; Schools, Farndon ; Schools, Kingsley- Endowed Schools, Malmo ; Public Hall, Tarporley ; National School, Tarvin; National School, Tattenhall; and the Board School, Wrenbury. The following were the presiding officers for the respective booths :—Aston, Mr. C. S. Brook, solicitor, Nantwich ; Audlern, Mr. J. J. Dixon, Northwich; Great B ,ughton, Mr. J. H. Yearaley, solicitor, Warrington ; Tarvin— Station No. 1, Mr. A. Fletcher, solicitor, Northwich, and Station No. 2, Mr. J. E. Fletcher, solicitor, Northwich ; Tattenhall, Mr. G. A. Marcus, solicitor, Chester; and WrenburY-cum-Forth, Mr. J. Tibbite, solicitor, Chester. At Chester, where the Central Committee Rooms of the candidates are, a considerable, quantity of electioneering literature was observed on the walls: and at every polling district and the gates and barns on the highways of the county bills of various descriptions were placarded. Vehicles to a great extent were employed in conveying voters to the poll, and amongst those very prominent were some feom Eaton Hall. The voters of the estate farms were conducted to Chester Castle booth. Frodsham, the largest town in the division, was somewhat animated by political paties, and there is no doubt that Mr. Tomkinson received a goodly number of votes. lattenhall village was the most lively throughout the day, and small demonstrations were held at intervals. An amusing incident happened when Mr. Tollemache was passing through. A few free fights took place, and were speedily stopped by the police; whilst in one case Mr. Tollemache was the means of persuading peace. Mr. Tom- kinson afterwards paid a visit to the committee-rooms, and met with a good reception. In nearly all the districts party favours were worn. The ballot-boxes were removed to Chester after the poll closed. The result was declared on Friday as follows: Tollemache (C) 4,359 Toinkinson (G L)

Warrington batted first, and J. C. Lawton and W. A. Bettesvrorth made a good commencempat. Den- ton was at the wiket nearly three boars for 32 runs, and was ably upheld by Armstrong and Fairclough. The War- rington fielding was exceptionally good, and the bowling was also good. Armstrong kept wickets in his usual style, and took three. Williamson and Price succeeded best with the bat.
