and Major Windus presided. Mr. SETON-KAnn, who was received with cheers, said they were met together under very satisfactory circum- stances. He was glad to have that opportunity of again meeting what might very well be called the backbone'of the Conservative party in Sr. Helens. They had had a series of meetings lately, bat that was the most satisfactory, be- cause the election was over and the victory won. (Ap- plause.) What had struck him during the two elections, and particularly during the last campaign, bad been the way in which their canvassers, and chairmen, and committees had worked to secure that very admirable result. He believed it was a test election in that borough, and he believed they had to a great extent consolidated the constitutional party in St. Helene. (Applause.) They had proved that the borough was not swayed by the Irish Nationalist vote. (A Voice: "They have no votes," and laughter.) He de- sired to say nothing in any way offensive to the Irish Nationalist party in that borough or elsewhere. It was satisfactory to show that they had proved it to be a true Lancashire borough, not sacrificed to party feelings, and when a great national crisis arose they could put party differences aside and return a true expression of Lanca- shire opinion. They all had his most eincere and hearty thanks. (Applause.) Passing to general questions Mr. Seton-Karr said be thought it very instructive indeed to look at the figures in the newspapers wite regard to the re- turns. They in St. Helens did their best to put the issue plainly and squarely before the electors, and be believed the contest was fought in a fair and straightforward man- ner. It was satisfactory to them to think that the opinion of St. Helens bad been backed up in such a satisfactory manner by the verdict of the rest of the constituencies throughout the United Kingdom. If they looked at the re- turns, they found that the majority was against Mr. (Sled- stone's Home Rule Bills. (A Voice: "Three cheers.") Yes, three cheers for the majority. (Applause ) The majority, which was thirty against those bills, had then increased to 124, and they had reason to think that there would be something like 400 Unionists returned to the next Parliament. His own opinion was that Mr. Gladstone might at once proceed to put up his shutters—(laughter and a Voice: "It would have been a good job if he had done that long since "). If they took the vote of the masses, they would find that the popular vote had pronounced most unhesitatingly against Mr. Gladstone and his Home Rule. Mr. Gladstone had been sending out.a most extraordinary shower of letters and telegrams to all parts of the country. but it was a most curious thing that the candidates to whom he addressed them had invariably been defeated. Mr. Seton-Karr afterwards proceeded to say there was no doubt the Irish question must come on for consideration when Parliament met, and that would be pretty soon. What course events would take he would not pretend to prophesy. Whatever Government was formed—and he believed the leaders of the Conservative party would form a very strong element in that Government, he would like to pee a man like Lord Hartingten taking a post in that Government—he (Mr. t.4eten-Karr) believed he should be doing his duty to that borough if he did his utmost to. support not only the Conservative party, but also the Liberal Unionist party. (Applause.) He did not wish to be bound down by narrow party feelings in a great question of that kind. He thought in supporting a Government formed of the Conservative and Unionist elements he should be doing his duty to his constituents. It seemed to him that the formation of such a Government would probably be the great question which would arise. He thought it well that they should realise that that was a parting of the ways—that the election was a practical split up of parties in the coun- try, which divided them into different Hues. He thought the Conservative party might consider that in some respects they were changing their cloak—that they were not iu com- mon with that old fossilised party which existed fifty or sixty years ago; but that the modern C insersettive party was a party of enlightened progress, and desired to enfold in their embrace and join in their forces all ti ose enlightened Liberals and Whigs who found they could unite their prin- ciples and forces with thoseof the modern Conservative party. ',Applause.) It seemed to him that they might as well face that fact, and consider it well, and as far as possible so work their own party in that borough, directly and indirectly, as to consummate that union and join with them the moderate Liberals, some of whom he benieved had given him their votes on that occasion. He wishid to give horiaur where honour was dee, and he believed it was only fair and right to say they did owe something—he did not know how much —to the Liberal Unionists of that borough, but he firmly believed the Conservative party had proved itself to be the dominant party. (Applause.) Mr. JOSEPH MASSEY proposed, "That this meeting desires to record its high appreciation of the ability and energy with which Mr. Henry Seton-Karr fought the recent election contest in St. Helene, and heartily congratulates him and his constituency on the success of the Moionibt party in the borough." (Applause) Councillor LONGTON seconded, and Mr. F. FARRAM supported the resolution, which was carried amid loud ap- plause.

THE Elections are now virtuallyover, and politicians are in a position to review the sit- uation,, Last week the Tories were'-in high feather at the prospect of having a majority over Liberals, Liberal Unionists,-arixt Nation- alists combined; but things were not what they seemed. The Tories were gaining seats here and there in consequence of- disunion amongst Liberals; but not at.suc.h a. rate, it transpires, as to enable them to have a clear majority. They are still dependent upon their Liberal allies—who are with them on one question only—and they cannot now look forward, as they were doing, to acting able, whilst riding into power, to snap their fingers at everybody else.' Mr. GLADSTONE has, too, unquestionably failed to secure thesupp.ort up- on which he counted; and it will be for the Cabinet, when it meets next,week, to decide whether the Government will at once resign, or wait until they are compelled to do so by an adverse vote in the new House of Com- mons. It is open to the PRIME MibIISTER to take either course; there is no qqestion of principle; it is a matter of expediency. The constitutional practice is for a. Ministry to hold office until Parliament makes it clear that it has forfeited the confidence of the majority of the House; but, on, the other hand, Mr. DISRAELI, in i 86,8, established the precedent of resigning without waiting to meet Parliament, when it was made clear that the country had decided against him. The same course was followed after the General Election in 1874 and ino;., but last year Lord SALISBURY held on to .the Treasury Bench, although the result of the polls showed that the Tories - were in a minority of over So as, compared with the Liberals, and ,;of over 179.,c.ounting the 'Nationalists as liiberals. But, Lord SALIS- BURY, for reasons then known to himself and now knowm, to the country,. treated the Nationalists as,.allies, and .met: Parliament, though he could( not reckon upon a working majority. Mr.- GLADSTONE, might now take - the same course—leaving it to the Liberal Unionists, combined with the Tories, to com- - pass his overthrow. He is. indeed being. urgently advised by some Liberals to take-, this course, but we are:inclined.to think that, ;as his followers are inn undoubted minority,. ; he will take., the earliest opportunity of resign- ing. As the Tories see so, little of officer they may be excuseclfor desiring to enjoy its - sweets as long as possible. Mr. GLADSTONE, is happily beyond any such consideration, and may, be relied), upon. to- take the course- ' which he believes will best serve the in- terests of the State.

Assuming that the Government resign, who is,to be senfor ?. "The rimes "strenu- ously advocates a 1143TINGToN-SALLAITRY: Coalition; but, there are two or threo,little- difficplties in the way. In the first place, judging from, the various references, which: Lord HARTINGTON has made as to the sug- gested alliance with the Tories, it is exceed- ingly unlikely that he would enter 24. Cabinet along with Lord SiIsIJRY, even if it wero conceded that he should be Prime Minister ; and in the second, place the Tories are in no mood to make what they would regard as a great sacrifice in order to. humour :the Liberal Unionists. Their represen- tative organs are already enlarging on the doctrine that the spoils belong to the victors, and urging that they are the victors. The Liberal Unionists have certainly as a .body cut a wretched figure in the electoral contest. It always seemed to us absurd in them to expect that they would ever be anything but "in the way" as between the followers of Lord SALISBURY on the one hand, and Mr. GLADSTONE on the other; but we were not prepared for their losing, as they have done, 73 to the Conservatives, and 25 to the Gladstonians. They have gained 8 seats, and lost 38 ; in other words, they have gone 30 to the bad. The Tories, with these results before them, may well be averse to offering them place and power- But what are they to do? If they form all Administration, they will he in office by al.!' grace of Liberal Unionists; while they I'm; be opposed by a solid body of Liberals Nationalists directed by a leader who Is a , host in himself. If they fall back upon the policy of the 26th January—the policy 01 " suppressing the National League tbY will be unable to obtain the support of th! bulk of the Liberal Unionists, who afie utterly opposed to coercionr If they ou

nothing, they will not be allowed to remain idle for long, whilst their inactivity will, meanwhile, be looked upon as a standing 'confession of cowardice or incompetence. If they decide upon framing some measure of local self-government for Ireland, they will Split either upon the HARTINGTON rock, or the CHAMBERLAIN rock, or some rock of their own. Turn which way they will, the Tories will be powerless. Unable to com- 'nand a majority, they will hold office upon sufferance ; they will neither be able to govern Ireland nor reform it; and will inevitably be required before a year is over to make way for Other and better men.

THE result of the Election for the Widnes Division of South-West Lancashire is grievously disappointing, for, although the Inajority for the Tory candidate has been reduced by 1085, he has still a majority over his Liberal opponent of 792. It was thought by tho3e who were best acquainted with the Population of the division, that there could he no question of the return of a Liberal candidate, assuming that he could count up- on the Irish vote. At the last election, the Irish vote was given for the Tory candidate, and that in itself was taken as sufficient to 'account for Mr. Moss being returned with a rnajority of 1877. This time Mr. Moss has had no claim upon the Irish electors; on the 'Contrary, he voted against the Home Rule Bill, and yet he is elected by what the Liberal candidate truly calls a substantial majority. 'Granted that a considerable number of Liberals have abstained from voting, and that some, like Mr. HOLBROOK GASKELL and Xr. JOHN BROCK, have supported the Tories, the figures are still of a character to give us Pause. There have been 531 less votes polled thisielection than last; but, as the Tory candi- .date has nevertheless a majority of 792, it is obvious that if the whole of the 531 votes had been added to the total for the Liberal candi- date, he would still have been in a minority. The other factor to con- sider is—how many Liberals have voted Tory? And as to this we are, of course, very much in the dark. Judging from what has happened in other constituencies where, through the Irish vote being less, the problem has been simpler, it is hardly likely to have exceeded zoo; and, if this be the case, it will be seen that the normal Liberal majority, if there be a majority, is nothing like so large as has generally been supposed. Can it be that everybody has been mistaken in regard- ing the population of the Widnes Division as essentially Liberal? We think not, and the conclusion we have come to, after analysing the figures, is that there is an undoubted Inajority of Liberals in Widnes; but that some hundreds of them require as yet to be placed upon the register. These non-electors Swell the Liberal meetings. and hear the Liberal candidate. But they are not in a position to give him a vote. The fact is the total number of electors in the Widnes Division is, in proportion to the population, the lowest amongst the Lancashire Divisions. For comparison, we give the returns as to Population and number of electors of the Lancashire Divisions nearest in size to -Widnes : Population. Electorate. Widnes Division Lancaster Division :North Lonsdale Division... 50,179 9,219 Inca Division „...„ 52,607 Bootle Division 53,167 14,663 It will be seen from the above that there 'ought to be at least r,OOO more voters on the Widnes list, and of this t,OOO it is not un- likely that 750, or three-fourths of the num- ber, would be found to be Liberal. This, as it seems to us, is the weak spot so far as Widnes is concerned, and it is one, therefore, to which attention should be immediately directed. We are not suggesting that anyone is to blame for this anomalous condition of things. We are quite aware that, with a vast extension of the franchise coming close on arrangements, last year, for the General Elec- tion, it was impossible to get all on the register ' Who were entitled to be placed there; and we 'know, too, that there are special difficulties ' in registration where there is a migratory population. But difficulties are things to be overcome, and the difficulty as to the registration of Widnes being apparent, we trust that, before the next election, it will be so grappled with and conquered that the Liberal candidate—with a united party be- hind him—will have a really eood chance of being returned by a large majority.

THE defeat of Mr. BRUNNER in the North- wich Division of Cheshire, is intelligible, if not satisfactory. It is the result, pure and sim- ple, of division amongst Liberals themselves. It is some consolation to know that, if there will be one Radical less from Cheshire, his place will not be occupied by a Conservative. Mr. ROBERT VERDIN is a Liberal, and it is as a Liberal Unionist that he has fought and won the battle. The Tories have voted for him to a man; but that is an operation that they are not likely to repeat; and,. as Mr. BRUNNER said in thanking his support- ers, Mr. VERDIN Will have little chance of being elected a second time, if he does not give evidence of his being a genuine Liberal. It would seem, from the polling return, that between 600 and 700 voters have abstained on this occasion horn exercising the fran- chise; and it is noteworthy that Mr. VER- DIN, although elected, has received 607 votes less than Mr. BRUNNER obtained last year. There can be no question that, with two Liberals in the field, the Liberal party has been more split up than it would have been with a Liberal pitted azainst a Tory. Perhaps, all things considered, we ought rather to be surprised that Mr. VERDIN has not had a larger majority. The election of a Liberal, even if he be of the Unionist type, is no sign, however, of Conservative strength. The Liberals of the Northwich Division may take heart; they have not yet so far gone astray as to return a Tory to the House of Com- mons.

-- Ab-o' th'-Yate's Election Address, which will be found in another column, shows that Mr. Ben Brierley is as fresh, as frolicksome, and as funny as he was a quarter of a century ago. His hits at the Fair Traders are witty, and they are as wise as they are witty.

Let the Sons of Temperance rejoice. Sir Wilfrid Lawson has won a splendid victory in the Cockermouth Division. Defeated last election by a majotity of to only, he has again been in the fight, and has this time come off conqueror; he is returned for the Cockermouth Division with a majority of 1,004.

The Duke of Westminster has made him- self particularly obnoxious by the offensive way in which he has brought his influence to bear at Chester in support of the Tory can- didate. Mr. Gladstone speaks of his action as "a fresh blow at the aristocracy." This is suggestive; it ought to set the duke and other members of the House of Lords a-thinking.

Sir George Errington, in formally tendering his thanks, says :—" I firmly believe that at the next election, which cannot be far dis- tant, we shall, with your assistance, succeed in enlisting this great constituency on the side of popular and Liberal government." This strikes the right note, and will meet with a ready response; the Liberals of Newton are as proud of their candidate as he is of them.

- More evidence of the part drink has played, on the side of the Tories, in the Warrington election: Two men brought up at the Police Court, on Monday, for being drunk and disorderly the day after the elec- tion, admitted that they were supplied with the liquor at Wilderspool, and that they had been "drinking out of buckets !" Could any- thing be more disgraceful to the Tory can- didate and the firm with which he is con- nected?

What of the Corrupt Practices Act? Is it an offence to give a glass of beer before the election, but perfectly legit to supply liquor in buckets after the election? These are questions which ought to be answered in a court of law. If Sir Gilbert Greenall and his henchmen are lacking in regard for decency, would it not be as well to try to make them moral by Act of Parlia- ment?

On the very day these poor wretches were being fitted for the police court, by being deluged, at Wilderspool, with Wilderspool ale, the Brewer of Wilderspool was returning thanks, at the Conservative Club, for his election, and asking his hearers to " let them in their daily life and conduct try to honour God." What a mockery! To quote the elegant language of Lord Salisbury—" it is a wonder the words didn't choke him."

The Orangemen of Belfast have been showing their "loyalty" by maiming and killing the men who are appointed to pre- serve order. After their arrest, and on their way to the Police Office, some of the rioters sang "Rule Britannia," and cursed the Pope, Parnell, and Sexton. These bludgeon-men are "mighty impartial" in alike cursing Catholics and Protestants who happen to differ from them.

The Liberal electors of the Crewe Division have done splendidly in returning Mr. W. S. B. M‘Laren with a majority of 64.5—that is, 163 only less than the majority given to Mr. Latham. Mr. M‘Laren is a nephew of Mr. John Bright, and like Mr. Bright's son, is a Home Ruler. If Mr. Bright had been twenty years younger, he would have been a Home Ruler too. It is once only in a generation that we have a statesma9, like Mr. Gladstone, who is young at 76.

There are 87 magistrates in Flintshire, and not one of them is a Nonconformist! Such is the revelation made by the correspondence between Mr. S. Smith, M.P., and Mr. Hughes, the Lord-Lieutenant of the county. Mr. Hughes suggests that it is solely a matter of " qualification." This is an insult to the Dissenters of Flintshire which they ought to resent. Something would seem to be required for Wales in the shape of Home Rule.

The annual report of the National Society for Women's Suffrage has just been issued, and states that, although the General Elec- tion is not yet concluded, nearly 300 members had been returned to Parliament favourable to the objects df the society. A Parliamentary return which is summarised shows that the proportion of women electors on the muni- cipal lists of voters in Great Britain is i 5 per cent. In some boroughs in Scotland it is as high as 36 per cent.

According to a little story told, on Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, James O'Brien was knocked off a chair by John Narey because he happened to break-down whilst trying to sing a song. It would seem that the poet was right when he said " Music hath charms to sooth the savage breast ; " for as soon as the music ceased, the " breast " (or should it be beast?) ceased to be soothed and the singer was knocked down. That break-down in the song was indeed a " floorer."

Lord Hartington tries to make a point of the Government being in alliance with the Parnellite party, who are in some way, he says, connected with the Fenian organisation. But why does he not apply this mode of reasoning to his present allies—the members of the late Government? And why does he not go a step further and say he will decline to sit in the same House as the Parnellites ? That is the logical issue of his reasoning

Mr. Parnell has promptly taken Lord Har- tington to task for his unwarranted insinua- tion. He says: "I know nothing whatever further than what can be gained by reading the newspapers of the Fenian organisations in either Ireland or America. I have never had any communications with either of these organisations or their leaders, nor have I' accepted any alliance with them. I do not know who the leaders of these organisations are, nor has there been any means of commu- nication, either through the National League, or through the Land League, between me and them." This is a straightforward denial; let Lord Hartington rebut it, if he can. fatigia It is interesting to see how anxious some Tories are to entrap Lord Hartington in a Salisbury Cabinet. Mr. Seton-Karr, having much to thank the Liberal Unionists for, is quite in love with them and Lord Hartington as their chief. The Tories are not quite "the stupid party" they used to be; they are "not in common," Mr. Seton-Karr says, "with that old fossilised party which existed fifty or sixty years ago." Just fancy! "Old fossilised party!" If we were to apply this phrase to Sir Gilbert Greenall—whose politics are those of fifty or sixty years ago —there are people who would say we were using bad language.

If the member for St. Helens, and others ' of that ilk, could look forward as well as backward, it is just possible that they might be led to the conclusion that those who oppose Home Rule to-day will, so years hence, be described by the "young bloods" of the next generation as that "old fos- silised party that existed fifty or sixty years ago." It will seem so absurd to them that their stupid dads should have strug-
gled against Home Rule for Ireland. thus that history repeats itself.
LOCAL NEWS.

OPEN AIR CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—The Mill Brow Brass Band gave the public of Runcorn another treat on Thurs- day evening, when they performed another of their high- class concerts in the Market-place. SUCCESS OF A WIDNES Muslcurr.—Mr. Thomas Sherratt, of Widnes, has successfully passed the Trinity College (London) senior local examinations for pianoforte playing. Mr. Sherratt's playing was most satisfactory, and gained him 66 points. GAME LICENSES AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, on Monday. before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Davies, licenses to sell game were granted to Richard Hulme, High-street ; Eliza Brimelow, Bridge-street ; and Mary Bradbury, Regent-street. A FIST PASSAGE TO RUNCORN.—The German brigantine Manza, of Hamburg, which arrived in Runcorn last week from Rio Grande, made the passage in 45 days, the rate of sailing averaging 61 knots per hour for the entire passage. Seventy days is considered to be a good passage for a sail-

ing vessel. SUNDAY SCHOOL TREAT AT WIDNES.—The children at- tending the Sunday school connected with Hartland Wes- leyan Chapel, Widnes, had their annual treat on Saturday afternoon. Headed by the Goed Templars' Brass Band, about 500 scholars walked in processional order through the town to a field in Lowerhouse-lane, kindly placed at their disposal by Mr. Kilsall. A very enjoyable time was spent

until dusk. ENTERPRIZE AT WIDNES.—The Wi-lnes Foundry Co. have secured a large contract for the ironwork required in the construction of a new subway under the Thames at Lon- don, near the Mansion House. The contract consists of some mammoth cylinders for a shaft in the Ihames, cast iron shields fitted with hydraulic rams, and segments with which the subway is to be lined. The castings, it is stated, will be forwarded' by White's line of steamers from West

Bank Deck. SINGULAR ROAD ACCIDENT AT RtNCORN. - On Thurs- day evening Mr. Britland, of Nelson-street, was returning from Frodeham in his cart, drawn by a pony, when two small birds alighted on the animal's head. The horse was greatly alarmed, and in its violence overthrew the cart, and precipitated the occupant into the roadway. He had several ribs fractured and sustained other injuries. He was con- veyed home in a cab, and is now doing as well as can be

expected. CLOTHE'S LINES AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Margaret Dyke. Maria Mullinger, Elizt Elli- son, Fanny Gerrard, Ann Dalton, Mary Goff, Sarah Moon, and Bridget Burke, married women, were each charged with obstructing the footpaths in the various streets in which they lived by hanging clothes on a line across the street.— Supt. Barker said these cases had only been brought as a caution, and he did not press for a heavy penalty.—A fine of Is, and costs, 7s 61, was imposed upon each de-

fendant. ASSAULT ON AN OLD MAN AT RUNCORN.—EIIen Coffee, a young woman, appeared at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Mon- day, to answer a charge of assaulting Wm. Williams, an elderly man.—lt was alleged that on Saturday evening Williams was sitting on the doorstep of his son's house read- ing the newspaper, when the defendant snatched the paper from his hands and tore it to pieces. She 'smacked" him on the cheek and broke his glasses, and then assaulted him with a water can. This weapon flying from her hand, she seized a chair, with which she struck him on the back.— The defendant admitted tearing the paper, but denied the assault.—She was fined Is and the costs, 12s 6d. NARROW ESCAPE FROlil DROWNING AT DITTON.—EIIen Steadman, five years of age, daughter of Mr. George Stead- man, of Cow-lane. Ditton, narrowly escaped drowning on Monday night. She was playing with several other chil- dren near Mr. Smith's farm, in close proximity to her home, when she fell into an open ashpit, containing about six feet of water. She was in imminent danger of being drowned, and had gone down the second time, when Mr. Smith's housemaid, whose attention had been called by some of the other children, ran to the scene of the accident, and suc- ceeded in getting the little girl out alive, but much ex- hausted. By the kindness of Mr. Smith, Dr. Cooper was soon in attendance. The child is new none the worse for

her immersion. WIDNES' IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE AND MR. BIREHLL'a CANDIDATURR.—At a meeting of the Widnes BI anch of the Irish National League, bald this week, the following resolu- tion was unanimously adopted :—" That this meeting ex- presses its deep gratitude to Mr. Birrell for the manly man- ner in which be has a4vocated the rights of the Irish nation to legislative independence, and its disappointment that he has not been returned as M.P. for Widnes to help in that great work of conciliating the Irish people and redressing the wrongs they have sustained during the last seven cen- turies; but hopes that although he may have met with a temporary defeat it may be of short duration, and that when next he contests the division he will be returned with such a majority as will show that those Liberals who have obtained his rejection only voted against him because they were led astray on false issues, and issues that were only devised to gain power for the Tories with the help of Liberal votes!' RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. Present: Messrs. W. Littler, H. Cole- burn, George Moss, W. H. Rogerson, W. Whittaker, E. Imison, W. Mellor, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary).—On the motion of Mr. Coleburn, seconded by Mr. Rogerson, Mr. W. Mellor was unanimously chosen as the chairman for the en- suing year. On taking the position, Mr. Mellor said be trusted, with the co-operation of the members of the Board, to carry out the duties devolving upon him to the public satisfaction.—Mr. Rogerson was appointed vice-chairman on the proposal of Mr. Littler, seconded by Mr. Imison. Mr. Littler, the retiring chairman, was cordially thanked for his services during the past year on the proposition of Mr. Imison, seconded by the Chairman.—The Secretary reported that during the three months ending June 25th there had been 69 interments in the cemetery, against 102 in the cor- responding period of last year. The fees received were £77 13s, against £96 13s 6d in the corresponding period of 1885. MASONIC INSTALLATION AT RuNconte. The annua I meeting for the installation of W.M. and officers for the year in connection with the Ellesmere Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons, 758, took place on Wednesday night at the Ledge-room, Devonshire-square. The retiring W.M. Bro. George Bell, was supported by Past Masters W. B. Wass, J. Coxhill, E. Marwood, and G. Moss; Bro. Mellor, P.M., P.G.J.D., Bro. J. H. Salkeld, Bro. George Summer- field, Bro. L. Rosenberg; Bro. the Rev. R. Edwards, Bro. T. H. Annett, Bro. Cooper, Bro. Phillips, Bro. T. D. Tim- mins, Bro. Le Coutenr, Bro. J. S. Davies, Bro. Peter Davies, Bro. Jas. Littler, Bro. J. J. Waterwortb, Bro. Joseph Tor- kington, W.M. elect, Jo. The visiting brethren were Bro. Webster Williams, 1609; J. Matthews, W.M., 1384; J. Tunstall, 1.P.M., 1035. Bre. Torkington was presented by Bro. G. Bell, retiring W.M., and Bro. Coxhill, P.M., and in- stalled by Bro. Win. Mellor, assisted by Bro. J. Coxhill. The following officers were than invested by the new W.M. : Bro. Bell. I.P.M. ; Bro. .T. H. Salkeld, S.W. ; Bro. George Summerfield, J.W. • Bro. W. Mellor, treasurer; Bro George Moss, secretary; Rev. R. Edwards. chaplain; Bro. L. Rosen- berg, S.D.; T. H. Annett, J.D.; Bro. Cooper. 1.G.; Bro. James Littler, organist; Bro. J. Le Coateur, almoner; Bro. George Hayes, tyler. During the evening Bro. Bell, 1.P.M., was presented with a Past Master's jewel, along with the Life Governorship of the Cheshire Educational Institution. The brethren afterwards had the customary banquet, when

the usual loyal and masonic toasts were honoured. A Viormwr DRUNKER IRISHNAN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, James Flannigan, a labourer at the Salt Works, but of no settled residence, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting Margaret Stormont, daughter of Andrew Stormont, of Sutton. The prisoner, a strong-looking young fellow, pleaded guilty. It appeared that about half-past six o'clock on Saturday Mr. Stormont, accompanied by his wife and prisoner, were driving through Stockbarn, when the defendant, who was drunk, seized held of the dog cart, and allowed himself to be dragged. Mr. Stormont entreated him to go away, but he used very obscene language in reply, and Mr. Stormont descended from the cart, wrenched his hands off, and threw him into the ditch. Before he could again ascend Into the cart the prisoner was up, and attempted to strike his daughter, who screamed loudly. The prisoner then seized her umbrella, with which he struck her several times, and also struck her on the chest with his fist. He then ran away with the umbrella, and Mr. Stormont pur- sued and caught him, but the prisoner refesed to give up the umbrella, and threw his pursuer to the ground, and threatened that if he bad a knife he would do for him. Eventually the umbrella was recovered, and the prisoner given into custody of P.C. Fryer. The prisoner's foreman gave him a good character.—Mr. Charles Reynolds said such conduct could not be over-looked, and the Bench would have no hesitation in sending him to gaol. For the first offence the prisoner was fined lOs and costs, or 14 days, and for the assault he was sentenced to a fortnight's im- prisonment, without the option of a fine. HALTON LADIES' CLuis.—The seventeenth anniversary of Halton Ladies' Club was celebrated at Halton on Monday. The weather was very favourable for the display, and there were numerous visitors to the ancient village. The members met at the lodge room shortly after 12 o'cltick, and after the usual routine business had been transacted they paraded the village in processional order. At the head was the pony carriage of Lady Brooke. in which was seated Mrs. Elizabeth Barrow, who is in her 89th year, and joined the club on its inception, just 70 years ago. The Runcorn Volunteer Brass Band was the next in order, and then followed the members. Accompanyiu the procession were Lady Brooke, Miss Brooke, Miss Winifred Brooke, Mias Lilian Brooke, the Rev. H. Whytehead (vicar of Norley), Mre. Whytehead, Rev. John Lockwood, Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P., Mrs. Henry Reynolds, Mrs, T.Wright (secretary), and Mr. J. H. Gamon. Lady Brooke and her daughters all wore the white shawls of the society. On arriving at the church, the Rev. H. Whytehead preached a sermon from the words " Render to all their dues," and gave an exposition of the practical uses of such a society as the Halton Ladies' Club. Quitting the church the procession wended its way to the gates of Nor- ton Priory, and afterwards returned to the green within the walls at Halton Castle, where a spacious tent had been erected, and within which the membere partook of tea, pre- pared by Mr. W. Phillips, the proprietor. Lady Brooke, the Misses Brooke, and Mrs. Henry Reynolds presided over the tables. After tea Lady Brooke and Mrs. Whytehead, the Rev. John Lockwood and Mr. C. Reynolds, and Mr. Wright delievered brief addresses. Cheers were given for Mrs. C. Reynolds, Mrs. Henry Reynolds and Mr. Gamon. Subse- quently the members engaged in dancing, the first dance being led off by Lady Brooke and Mr. C. Reynolds.

div.head: FXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 17, 1886
div.p: THE FXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 17, 1886

ROBBERY a'r WIDNEs.—On Thurslay, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Susannah Giblin, a married woman, was brought up on remand charged with having on the 4th July stolen a dress worth 5s from the dwelling-housa of Mary Rley, at Farnworth. The prisoner went to Mrs Riley's house. Mis Riley had occasion to leave while the prisoner was there ; when she returned the prisoner and the dress had vanished. On Monday the prisoner sold the dress to a second-hand clothes dealer named Sarah McLoughlin, at St. Helens.— The prisoner, described as a bad character by :.•• uperinteu- dent Barker, was sentenced to two ,months haid labour. AN ELOPEMENT FROM RUNCORN.— ouring the present week the highly respectible district of Greenway-toad has been thrown into a state of excitement in consequence of the elopement of a married woman with a young man for- merly occupying a position with one of the principal tiades- men in the town. Some time ago the young man was re- ceived into the house of the lady,who is on the shady side of 40, as a lodger; but their commercial relations ripened into feelings of a warmer nature, and the husband having sus- picions, the lodger had to seek fresh quarters. Determined not to be far away from the object of his affections, he took up his residence in the next house, and continued to carry on a clandestine courtship. A few days ago they were both missing, and the husband discovering that several articles of furniture have been removed, has placed the matter in the hands of the police. Ms. Moss AT WIDNES.—On Tuesday evening Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, the newly-elected member for Widnes, ad- dressed a meeting of Conservative workers at the committee- rooms, Victoria-road, Widnes. Major Cross presided. At the commencement of toe proceedings, Mrs Hartland, of Vine-street, appeared and presented Mr. Moss with a neat box, containing a unique and pratty collection of coral (which she said was very valuable) dried leaves, and em- bossed butte, flies. This, said the lady, was a token of her pleasure at his re-election, and regard for him personally. Mr. Moss graciously thanked the old lady, who then retired amid the loud cheers of the audience. Mr. Moss then de-

livered a speech in which he thanked those present for their strenuous and successful labours during the recent cam- paign, and advised them to complete their organisation by the formation of a Primrose League. THE SOCIETY OF CHEMICA.L INDUSTRY AT WIDNES.— Ab4ut 100 members of the Society of Chemical Industry, which is at present holding its annual meeting at Liverpool, yesterday paid a visit to Widnes. They arrived in the town at half•pest nine, and were inet at the statioc by Mr. W. W. Gossage and Mr. H. Timmis. The visitors split up into three sections. One section proceeded to the soap works of Messrs. Gossage and Sons, the precesses and novelties baing shown by the two gentlemen named. A second section was guided so Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon and Co.'s chemical works, through which they were escorted by Messrs. H. W. Deacon, E. Carey, J. Morrison, and Dr. Hurter. The other section visited the Tharais Copper Company's works, where they were received by Mr. Prit- chard and Mr. H. L. Jones. The party left the town by special train at 12 o'clock for Crewe. SUDDEN DEATH OF A WIDNES WORKS MANAGER —The quiet and retired neighbourhood of Deacon-road, Appleton, was sorrowfully disturbed early on Wednesday morning by the sad intelligence that one of its most respected residents had suddenly expired during the night. It appears that Mr. John Roberts, who has been employed for many years as under-manager at the Tharsis Copper Works, retired to rest as usual, about half-past ten, on Tuesday night, ap- parently in his habitual state of health, though he had been troubled for the last two days with indigestion. An hour later' when Mrs. Roberts retired to rest, she heard her hus- band groan. She spoke to him, but the only reply he made was a groan. He appeared to be asleep. Mrs. Roberts's fears were aroused, and she at once sent for their medical adviser, Dr. McCambridge. Mr. Richards attended without delay, and did all in his power to aid the dying man. He, however, expired soon after, the medical attendant pronounc- ing the cause of death to be heart disease. The deceased gentleman, who was of a most amiable disposition, was greatly respected by his employers and a large circle of friends. He was a native of Flint, and had resided in Widnes about eighteen years, and for the last sixteen years had been connected with the Tbarsis Copper Works and all along had borne an irreproachable character. He was a faithful adherent and a warm, though quiet, supporter of the cause at the Cromwell-street Welsh Wesleyan Chapel, and had this week been elected to preside at a coming pub- lic meeting connected with the church. He had attained his 52nd year. His remains will be interred at Farnworth. Mr. Roberta leaves a widow and a young niece to mourn hie loss, for whom much sympathy is felt. EXTRAORDINARY FATALITY AT RUNCORN terday, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, the coroner, held an inquest at the Millstone Inn, Runcorn, touching the death of Robert Henry Hughes, aged 28, a labourer at the docks. It ap- peared that Hughes was assisting to unload the schooner, "St. Austell," which had a cargo of china clay. It was his duty to stand on a scaffold and receive the tubs of clay as they were (lawn up by the windlass. The scaffold was made in a form peculiar to the docks. From the spars of the vessel, ropes were slung to which was secured a pole placed horizontally over the bold. Planks were laid from the quay te the pole, and the scaffold was complete. Whilst Hughes was on this scaffold one of the ropes gave way, and he was precipitated into the hold of the •vessel. Be alighted upon the keelson of the vessel with his face and his skull was fractured, and he was otherwise so terribly injured that death resulted in leis than five minutes. His dead body was removed to the Millstone Inn, where he had lodged for the past 18 months.—Evidence was given by Mrs. Ashbrook, William Garner, of 66, Cooper-street, a dock porter, Thomas Keeffe, of Top Locke, a dock labeurer, and Mr. Blewitt,of Tymarer- drat)), Cornwall, the mate of the vessel. The last-uamed witness, who had superintended the erection of the scaffold, said it was quite secure in the morning. After dinner it was lowered about three inches. After the accident he found that the rope in the strap of the block had slipped, in conse- quence, he thought, of the china clay making the rope slip- pery.—ln answer to Captain Sinnot, the foreman of the jury, the witness said he made a "back hitch."—By another Juryman: He did not put a " mousin " on the rope.—The Juryman said a "mouein " would have made it absolutely refs.—Captain Sinnot said he dare trust his life without a "back hitch," and be never heard of one slipping.—A ver- dict of "accidental death was returned. Mr. J. K. Digges was present on behalf of the Blidgewater Navigation Com- pany. Courry RATES.—At the Quarter Sessions for the Peace for the hundred of West Derby, on Tuesday, an estimate of the rates to be levied on the County of Lancaster for the ensuing half year was submit- ted to the magistrates and approved. Appended are the proportions of the estimate applicable to the West Derby Hundred, which embraces the police divisims of West Derby, Ormskirk, Prescot, Warrington, and Wigan :—General purposes, a rate of 3-16 d. in the .E, yielding £2,494 175.; Nnstic asylums, id. in the .E, £1,663 4s. 7d.; lunatic asy- lums' loan account, id. in the I% £3,326 9s. 3d.; county bridges, 1-24 d., £551 7s. 5d.; general police, 3-16 d. in the .E, yielding £329 14s. 11d, in the West Derby division, £447 151. 4d. in the Bootle division, £254 2s. 11d, in the Ormskirk division, £6lO 18s. Bd. in the Prescot division, £290 10s. id. in the Warrington division, and £2Bl 15s. 6d. in the Wigan division. FAILURE iN THE CHESHIRE SALT TRADE.—A meeting of the ereditOrs of Mr. Josiah Firth, of Chester, and the Island Works, Winsford, salt manu- facturer, was held at the Royal Hotel, Crewe, on Saturday, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Bul- lock, the official receiver. The gross liabilities of the debtor were returned at £10,232 18s Bd, and the assets £1,122, leaving a deficiency of close upon £9,000. The cause of failure was ascribed to depres- sion of trade, unremunerative prices of salt, outlay on works, and bad construction of brine shafts and roofs. The debtor formerly carried on business with his father and brothers, as woollen manufacturers, at Heckmondwike. He had about eight years ago pro- perty which was estimated to be worth about £46,000, but through depression of trade and depre- ciation of property he had lost the great bulk of this, and when he entered upon the business of a salt manufacturer at Winsford he was several thou- sand pounds in debt, mostly borrowed money. The relatives and friends of the debtor, who claimed about £6,700 for money lent, &c., offered to with- draw those claims, and allow the assets to be devis- ible among the other creditors if they would consent to an arrangement for a compromise. It was stated the creditors would then get about 5s in the pound. This arrangement was agreed to, and the official receiver was instructed to realise the estate. SALE OF PROPERTY AT WARRINGTON.—On Wed- nesday afternoon week Mr. Thomas Tunstall offered for sale by auction, at the Golden Grove Inn, War- rington, a freehold farm at Burtonwood, an d free- hold aria leasehold dwelling-houses, corn mill, shop and cottages in Warrington. There was a good company, and some spirited bidding. Lot 1, con- sisting of a freehold farm, known as Lancaster Farm, at Burtonwood, with the farmhouse, out- buildings, yard, and gardens, containing 61a. 2r. 24p., was withdrawn after half-a-dozen bids. Lot 2, being the leasehold shop and premises, No. 64, Buttermarket-street, Warrington, was sold to Mr. Joseph Mounfield, the tenant, for £660, with a ground rent of £lO per annum. Lot 3, a leasehold dwelling-house, No. 6, Academy-street, subject to a yearly rent of £3, was sold for £390, the pur- chaser being Mr. A. E. A. Smith. For Lot 4, con- sisting of four leasehold shops, being Nos. 70, 72, 74, and 76, Buttermarket-street, there was some very determined bidding, notwithstanding the heavy ground rent of £55, and the lot was sold to Mr. Cookson for £645. Lots 5 and 6, two freehold dwelling-houses in Dial-street, Warrington, were offered together, but were withdrawn, as the bid- ding was not satisfactory. For Lot 7, the freehold corn mill, there was no bid. Lots 8 and 9, freehold cottages in Rose-yard and Cockhedge-lane, were sold to Councillor John Brown. Lot 10 was unsold. Lot 11, consisting of six freehold cottages in Buck- ley-street, was sold to Mr. John Wilding for £415. Lot 12, a freehold shop, with outdoor licences for the sale of ale, beer, wines, and spirits, wholesale and retail, were withdrawn, £550 being bid. The solicitors for the vendors were Messrs. Ashton and Woods, Warrington.

RUMOURED PETITION AGAINST SIR RICHARD CRoss.—During the present week a rumour has been widely circulated that the Liberals of the Newton Division have been engaged in preparing a petition against the return of Sir Richard Assheton Cross, who was last week elected by a considerable majority over Sir George Errington as the Parlia- mentary representative of the division. This has been to a certain extent confirmed by a statement in one of the Liverpool papers that it was intended to present a petition, but as yet nothing definite in the matter has been decided upon by the Liberal leaders. BOWLING MAIN AT FIDLERS' FERRY. Mr. J. Johnson, of the Ferry Inn, held his annual bowling main on Thursday afternoon, when upwards of fifty followers of this popular game competed, amongst whom were several well-known players from War- rington, Runcorn, Widnes, Ditton, and Penketh ; the most notable absentee being Mr. G. Ball, of War- rington. The green was in its usual good order, and a fair number of spectators were present. Mr. Johnson gave a sovereign, to which the players subscribed 2s 6d each. The " draw " took place on the Waterloo principle, which is not to .be commen- ded, unless 32 or 64 players compete, and caused dissatisfaction. Mr. Joseph Holbrook (Warring- ton) the winner of the first prize, ..E2 ss, played ex- ceedingly well throughout the contest, his oppo- nent in the final tie being Mr. Price (Widnes) who received the second prize, ..El. S R R. CROSS AT WOLVERTON.—SiT Richard Cross addressed a Conservative meeting at Wolverton, North Bucks, on Monday night, Viscount Curzon presiding. He said that men of all parties were uniting against the Fenian conspiracy as they would against foreign invasion, Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Bright, and Lord Hartington standing shoulder to shoulder with the Conservatives, and showing they could let party differences cease. Mr. Glad- stone's measures were dead because the people of England and Scotland said they would not have them, and were determined that, come what might, even at the call of an imperious and impa- tient Minister, they would not allow the union of Great Britain and Ireland to be disturbed. He

regretted that the Prime Minister had raised the cry of class against mass, and that that cry had been taken up by his followers all over the coun- try. lie denied that the late Conservative Govern- ment ever intended to adopt a Home Rule policy. As a member of the late Cabinet, knowing every- thing that went on in it, he could say there was nothing they would oppose more vigorously, nothing they were so absolutely determined should never be carried, than a separate Parliament for Ireland. _ _ .

"JACOB'S BUDGET".—Under this title, Messrs. Jacobs and Sons, clothiers and outfitters, of Rane- lagh-street, Liverpool, a firm whose name is widely known, have issued an admirably-printed book of 1 74 pages, containing succinct biographies, accom- panied by portraits, of leading statesmen and poli- ticians, and naval and military commanders of emi- nence. There are also several lively literary sketches, with which references to the comprehen- sive business of the firm are ingeniously interwoven. The book possesses an excellent index, and the cover is adorned by finely-executed woodcuts, represent- ing Jacob's establishment in Ranelagh-street, part of the city and river, and the northern part of Lime-street, with St. George's Hall, the North- Western Hotel, the County Sessions House, the Alexandra Theatre, the Wellington Column, and the equestrian statues of the Queen and the Prince Consort. Copies have been sent to the eminent men whose portraits are given, and in most cases letters of thanks have been received. The acknowledg- ment from Mr. Labouchere is characteristic. He says :—" Gentlemen,—l beg to acknowledge book, though I never had such a good .fitting suit of clothes in my life as 1 am portrayed as wearing." The " Budget " will be sold at the nominal price of ' threepence, and sent, post paid, to any address in Great Britain and Ireland for sixpence. THE McComucir BINDER.—Mr. J. H. Newton, of

Lowerhouse-lane, West Derby, who is the sole agent for this world-renowned machine for Warrington and the district, has favoured us with a copy of the fifty-fifth annual illustrated catalogue of the makers, the McCormick Harvesting Machine Com- pany, of Chicago, who claim to be the largest corn and grass cutting machine makers in the world. Besides a mass of information regarding the details and successes of these machines, the catalogue con-

tains a short history of wheat and wheat -reapers, I which will be read with pleasure, bringing out, as I it does, with great force, the progress of wheat cul- tivation. When the reader compares the contents of pages 5 and 24, his mind must be im- pressed with the valuable service that has been rendered to agriculture by the invention and perfection of tl* harvester and binder since the first successful reaper was invented by McCormick fifty- five years ago. This machine was, however, not placed before the public for ten years afterwards, and it is a remarkable fact that while in the year 1841 only two of McCormick's machines were sold, the demand for them last year had increased to over fifty-five thousand. It is also stated as a fact no less remarkable that over five hundred thousand I McCormick machines have been sold throughout the I world, with a capacity of havesting one hundred and fifty million acres of grain and grass, a work that would require an army of fifty million men working with the old sickle and scythe. Appended to the catalogue is an illustrated statement ot the yearly wheat crop in the principal grain-growing countries of the world. The catalogue is through- out admirably compiled, and beautifully and in- geniously illustrated.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at Alforde Chambers on Tuesday under the presidency of Mr. F. H. GossagP, J.P. Present, Messrs. Carey, Handley, Wright, W. W. Gossage, B. Brown, Midwood, Heyes. Taylor, Gaskell, Sadler, Houghton, Dr O'Keeffe, J. T. Allen (clerk), Carr (engineer), Higginson (surveyor), and Dickson (inspector).

A DANGER TO THE NEW OFFICES. Messrs. F. and G. Holmes, architects to the new Public Offices, wrote drawing the attention of the Beard to the fact that the drain pipe from main sewer in front of new building had not vet been put in, and that constcpentiv the water was still standing at a depth of several teet in the cellar under the last wing of the offices. Not only was this very dangerous to the stability of the walls, but it en- tailed considerable expense to the contractors, who had repeatedly pumped the water out of the cellar only to find it filled up again in a few days. It was of the utmost im- portance that this cellar should be dry before the roof, chitnnies, and gables were fixed —Mr. Allen explained that tenders had been invited for this work and would be in on Thursday at noon. Through pressure of work Mr. Hig- ginson had not been able to get the work in hand sooner.

div.head: HOSPITAL LOAN.
div.p: THE HOSPITAL LOAN.

The Assistant Secretary to the Local Government Board intimated to the Board the formal sanction of the Local Go- vernment Board to the borrowing of £3,400 for 37 years for hospital purposes. GAS AND 'WATER COMMITTEE. ..... .

The minutes of the Gas and Water -o-o-tWit-i-ttee contained a report from the Engineer, who said with regard to the waste water meters that a number of inspections had been made in Newtown and West Bank districts during the past month. and the waste had been reduced in the former district to 1 8 gallons per head, and in the latter 1•1 gallons. A new six inch meter had been obtained for Simm's Cross district, and was now being fixed at the corner of Vine-street and Widnes- road. It was recommended that a reduction of 31 per 1,000 feet be made in the price of gas to all consumers, commenc- ing Ist July. The mean rainfall for the month had been 2.120 inches, and the water in stock on the 23rd ultimo was 10,685,726 gallons.—Mr. Gaskell, in moving the adcp- tion of the minutes, referred to the waste water meters, and said that the two now in work had given extremely satisfactory results, saving water of the annual value of £3OO. There was a great waate or improper use of water in the district. Previously, although they might suspect the offenders, they could not Identify them; but now the districts in which waste water meters were fixed, they knew without the shadow of a doubt where and when that waste took place. Those meters showed when a tap was open or closed. There were cases where water was used for gardens, and the taps were left open the whole night, the water running on the ground, and where provision merchants used water for bacon wash- ing. They knew this kind of thing went on before, but could not tell who were the offenders. Now they bad a detective at work day and night, and could tell when and where the waste took place. The committee was anxious to prevent that waste, and gave notice through the Press a prosecution would be instituted in every instance regard- less of the position of the offender. They would not con- sider it any justification because a man was respectable, or anything of that sert. With reference to the proposed re- duction in the price of gas, Mr. Gaskell said the committee wished that minute to stand over for another month. They made that recommendation in the hope that it would bring in some large consumers. At the last meeting Messrs. Sullivan and Co., asked the price at which the Board would supply them with gas, and the firm was not I able to tell them for another month whether this reduction would induce them to become consumers. If they would not at that price it simply meant that the committee would not be justified in reducing the mice so much. They would, however, still make some reduction, but they could not state the amount at present. He (Mr. Gaskell) had seen Mr. Brock, and he thought he would be satisfied. but the matter had to come before his directors.— Mr. Sadler seconded the minutes, which were passed.—The minute relating to the reduction in the price of gas was re- ferred back.
TEIMPHONE POSTS. The Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Company asked permission to erect posts and wires from Stewart's Brook through Appleton, Albert-road, and Halton-view to Cuerdley

beundary.—Mr. Carey said the company wou d put the Board in cem.nunicAtioa with Pexhill, .Stockswell, Belle Vale, and Netherhy, at their own cost, and maintain the wires in repair. The committee thought it would be well to close with these terms, the posts to be erected with proper restrictions for the safety of the public.—The minute was passed.

div.head: HEALTH COMMITEE.
div.p: HEALTH COMMITEE.

The minutes'of the Health Committee contained the re- port of the medical officer, who stated that during June there were 103 births and 48 deaths, being at the rate of 4494 and 20g4 per 1,000 respectively. Zymotic diseases caused six deaths. The nuisance inspector reported that there had been five fatal cases of whooping cough and one of scarlet fever.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. There are, at the present moment of writing, :still 35 members to be returned to the new Parliament. But its composition is already practically deter- mined, and it is pretty well known what forces will meet for contention in the coming session. Liberals, including the dissentients, muster 250, Conservatives 305, and Parnellites SO. The 35 seats yet to be allotted will not materially disturb these proportions. Thus we shall have the Conservatives as forming the largest solid minority of the sections of the House, but still not strong enough to make the position of a Conservative Ministry secure. Even the most enthusiastic partisan cannot claim existing affairs as the result of a Conservative reac- tion. Where Conservatives have won seats it has been due to Liberal abstentions. Mr. Gladstone would be in a minority in the new Parliament only in respect of his "brae Rule Bill. On all questions of fundamental Liberal policy as opposed to Conser- vative policy he would, with the assistance of the Irish vote, be able to place the Conservatives in a minority. This fact has induced some people to urge upon Mr. Gladstone the duty of remaining in power and challenging a vote of the House of Commons. The Premier himself has, as yet, made no sign; but I have reason to know that this proposal finds sup- port among some of his colleagues. The utmost I extent to which they go, however, is to meet Par- ' liament on the sth of August, and thereupon chal- lenge their fate. Mr. Labouchere, behind whom is Mr. Schnadhorst, would go further than this, and talks about bringing in another Bill dealing with , the Irish question. But Mr. Labouchere strangely! omits a consideration which is fatal to such a ' scheme. Mr. Gladstone would have no opportunity of bringing in a Bill. His Ministry would never live that stage. The Conservatives would, of course, move an amendment to the Address involv- ing a vote of confidence, and the Dissentient Liberals would be obliged, in tl.is exceptional case, to throw in their lot with the Opposition. They have won their election as declaring a lack of con- fldence in Mr. Gladstone's Administration, and are logically bound to support it in the House of Com- mons. Whether Mr. Gladstone resigns or meets: Parliament within the next three weeks is a matter of no practical consequence. It does not 'affect I public business in one way or the other, as it was affected when defeated at the polls last November. Lord Salisbury held on till the new year, and inter-1 posed in the working session the delay consequent upon the re-election of \the new Ministry. If Mr. 1 Gladstone meets Parliament on the sth of August,l there will be a few nights debate on the Address, ! the Government will ao out, and the election of new Ministers will take place in good time for the meet-: ing for the despatch of business in October or Feb- ruary, as Lord Salisbury may decide. For there is no doubt it must be Lord Salisbury. The talk about Lord Hutington forming a Ministry; is absurd. At the outside, Lord llartington has not : half a hundred followersnal the new House. His ; personal assistance to a Conservative Ministry is, of course, not to be estimated exclusively by figures.' It is worth a great deal, perhaps as much as the splendid bribe suggested. Lord Harlington's going over to help them would place the Conservative Ministry in a majority, and would give them an im- : mense access of personal influence. But Lord liar- I tington, as he has frequently taken occasion to re- mark, is a Liberal. He has honourably differed with his chief and the great majority of the Liberal , party on a specific point. That aside, he is as much with Mr. Gladstone to-day as he was this time last year. Lord Salisbury will have to form his Minis- j try out of the old elements, a prominent item in which is Lord Randolph Churchill. He will be a; Minister on sufferance, and before the first full ses- sion is out will disappear in some cataclysm, when , we shall have the whole struggle over again, and, I the nation further advanced in education in which ' it has taken such an enormous stride during the past six months, justice will finally be done to Ire- land. It is pretty certain whatever may befall minis- tries that Earl Granville will not continue to take an active part in the (Erection of affairs. He has long been a martyr to gout, but never suffered from so protracted and violent an attack as that which has for some weeks kept him to his room. He has borne his martyrdom with simple heroism and has kept up his spirits marvellously. I had a letter from him the other day' brimful of fun, though the effort of writing with his own hand must have been a most painful one. Lord Granville's retirement will be a conspicuous loss to the Liberal party. It has been the fashion in some quarters to sneer at his conduct of affairs at the Foreign Office as lack- in cr in energy and spirit. But that is not the opinion formed of it by foreign diplomatists, who know that behind the genial smile and Fentle man- ner there is an alert and resolute spirit. Lord ' Granville's political career has in some respects been a disappointing one. He has never actually reached the premiership, though on more than one occasion he has been within reach of it. He has borne these disappointments in the same spirit that he has borne his physical afflictions. I think I mentioned the other week, upon the testimony of a colleague in the Cabinet, that during the trouble- some period of the last six m mths Lord Granville has been one of the most unswerving and reliable allies of Mr. Gladstone. Suspected of Whig tenden- cies, he has loyally and enthusiastically supported the Radical scheme of dealing with the Irish grievance which has proved too much for the country. ' It will be difficult to replace Lord Granville in some of his relations with the Liberal party. In one respect, however, it is pleasant to know that he will have a worthy successor. This will undoubtedly be found'in the Earl of Rosebery. There are many peers on the Liberal side of more venerable years and of longer standing. But there is none who approaches the Foreign Minister in the possession of those rare qualities which go to make a leader of such an assembly as the House of Lords. Lord Granville possessed these qualities in high measure, far exceeding the requirements of Lord Salisbury. Lord Rosebery, I think, will excel even Lord Gran- ville as a leader in the House of Lords. In addition to Lord Granville's geniality, wit, and readiness, he possesses something of Lord Salisbury's impres- siveness. His brief tenure of office as Foreign Sec- retary has greatly strengthened his position in the public estimation. He is popular on both sides, a vary rare position for a Liberal peer. The young Scotch peer is, I believe, destined for even a higher position than that of a leader of a party in the House of Lords. It is true that as time 'advances the chances of a peer becoming Prime Minister under a Liberal regime are greatly lessened. But there may arise a concatenation of circumstances in which it will be convenient to hand the reins of office to a member of the House of Lords, in which case Lord Rosebery is certain to be Prime Minister. The season is still spasmodically kept up in Lon- don, though it is in a halt and maimed condition. Next Tuesday the Queen leaves for Osborne, a pre- liminary to her flight to the Highlands, and a final farewell to London for this year. Then we have Goodwood after which, even in ordinary times, no personage in society with any character to lose would be seen in London. The dissolution un- doubtedly had a lamentable effect upon the season, which is wont in increased degree to rotate round the sittings of the House of Commons. But the fact is that, short as it was, the season has been one of the most lively, not to say riotousof recent years. The presence of the Colonials has been made the excuse for an almost unending series of entertain- ments, some of them given on a princely scale. In addition to these semi-public entertainments pri- vate dinner parties have been got up for the recep- tion of the more eminent colonials_ Thus the aver- age of entertainments has exceeded that of former seasons, albeit the present one has been truncated. Another influence in favour of a lively season has been the personal one of the Queen. Her Majesty suddenly came forth from her seclusion and has shown herself among the people to an extent un- known in former years. All this has tended to- wards the amelioration of the lot of the London tradesman, whose loyalty is much affected by move- ments in the fashionable world, One of the Queen's excursions has not been with-

out its unsatisfactory results. Everybody won- dered when it was announced that one of Her Majesty's rare appearances in public would be de- voted to doing honour to the founder of the Hol- loway Institution. That the Queen should have been secured for such an occasion was cited as the climax of a long and successful career in advertis- ing. Since the Queen went, however, it was ex- pected that something would be done for the owner of the honoured name of Holloway. Nothing less than Sir Martin, Bart., was spoken of. But Martin remains plain Mr. Holloway. There is a general consensus of belief that some- thing is going to be done for Prince Henry of Bat- tenberg. It is a tribute to the belief in the wide range of his capabilities that he is spoken of indif- ferently as being destined to promotion to the army or to the navy. Some authorities say he is to have a commission in the First Life Guards, others with equal confidence assume that he is to have a naval appointment, either under the Duke of Edinburgh or in command of one of the Royal yachts. I think of all the suggestions the last is most probable. The commission in the Life Guards was spoken of some time ago. But some disposition was shown to resent this thrusting upon them of an obscure German princeling who had no recommendations for promo- tion beyond those of a matrimonial and family character. As to the Mediterranean Fleet, the Duke of Edinburgh, like the Prince of Wales, is not so fond of his new brother-in-law that he is likely to make the place comfortable for him. The Royal yacht is the thing, and as there is, of course, a prac- tical sailing master, no harm is likely to come of such an appointment. The prince, a harmless, nice- looking, well-meaning young man, has paid dearly for his connection with the Royal family. Openly insulted by the German Court, who swaggeringly decline to recognise his status as Royal Highness, snubbed by his brother-in-law, and bandied about from pillar to post in the honest endeavour to obtain a status that will permit him to wear a uniform at Court levees and bring in a small salary, he must sometimes pine for a less exalted position.
WARRINGTON. ERILATUM.—In a police case reported in our last issue, a name was given as" Martha Cottam " when it should have been Martha Cotton, of Dial-street,

Warrington. "TITHES."—The adjourned general meeting of the Warrington Farmers' Club is advertised to be held at the White Bull Inn, Horsemarket-street, next Wednesday, wben a paper on " Tithes" will be read by Mr. Wm. Davidson. Punt's BANKING COMPANY.—A general meeting of the directors of this company is announced to be held next Friday, at the Bank premises in Win- wick-street. It is stated that the shareholders will be asked to sanction an interim dividend at the rate

of 15 per cent. per annum. WARRINGTON INFIRMARY.—The secretary, with thanks, begs to acknowledge the handsome dona- tion of £lO from the West Lancashire and Border Towns Rugby Football Union, being part of pro- ceeds of final tie played between Warrington and Aspull at Fairfield, Liverpool. YOUNG THIEVES.—At Liverpool County Sessions, on Tuesday, Thomas Edward Duffield (16) shoe- black, and Patrick Fallon, (16), labourer, were each sent to prison for four months, with hard labour, for committing various thefts at Warring- ton early in last month. The particulars of the cases have already been made public. STREET ACCIDENT.—On Wednesday afternoon an

accident occurred near the Central Station. A horse attached to a trap, belonging to Mr. T. idayhall, of Buttermarket-street, was being driven along Win- wick-street by a son of Mr. Mayhall, when the animal, taking fright, commenced to plunge. The trap eventually collided with a 'bus, and the shafts were broken. Mr. Mayhall's son, and a youth who

was with him, sustained bruises. LA.TCHFORD BAPTIST CllAPEL.—Anniversary ear- 'vices were held in connction with this chapel on Sunday, when sermons were preached in the morn- ing, afternoon, and evening by the Rev. R. Richards, of Liverpool. The collections, which were in aid of the school and church fund, amounted to £24 Ss. It is stated that the Rev. J. W. Varley, of the Man- chester College, has • been offered and has accepted the pastorate of the church. BREWERS' EXCURSION.—The Warrington work- people in the employ of Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, brewers, this year went to Blackpool on their annual excursion. They left Bank Quay Station, about 400 in number, at eight o'clock on Saturday morning, arrived at Blackpool at 9-45, and were back in Warrington shortly after ten o'clock in the , evening. The heads of the various departments oc- cupied a saloon carriage. The weather was fine, and the trippers had a day of thorough enjoyment. ' Besides having his railway ticket supplied, each ' workman was presented with 2s 6d, and a day's wage was allowed. WIFE DESERTION,—A forgeman named Edward Broadhurst, of Lloyd-street, was charged at the Borough Court, on Wednesday, with neglecting to maintain his wife, who applied to Mr. Shearer for relief on Monday. In the evening of that, day Mr. Shearer went to Broadhurst's house, and found that person drunk. The wife, Mr. Shearer said, was not exactly a sober woman, but she was a hard-working one. Prisoner had been employed at the works of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co. Prisoner said he could not live with his wife, who had recently had eight weeks' good, solid "fuddling."—The case was adjourned for a fortnight to allow Broadhurst time to make some arrangement to maintain his wife, and he was ordered to pay us, the cost of the pro- secution. .Two CHILDREN RUN OVER.—Shortly before sir o'clock on Monday evening, an accident took place in Foundry-street, near the railway bridge. A horse and cart belonging to Mr. Rigby, farmer, High Legh, which was being driven by James Stanton, carter, was proceeding along .Bewsey-street, when the sounding of the whistle of a train on the Cheshire Lines startled the horse. The driver did his utmost to stop the animal, which swerved on to the footpath in Foundry-street. Two children, named Sarah and Catherine Hughes, daughters of Patrick Hughes, forgeman, 25, Bewsey-street, were passing at the time, and were run over. They were taken to the Infirmary and attended to. The eldest child, Sarah, was not much hurt, but the younger one was rather severely crushed. A HEARTLESS FATHER. Thomas Garrity, 8. farm labourer, was brought up in custody, at the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, and charged with leaving his three children chargeable to the common fund of the Union. Mr. Shearer prosecu- ted on behalf of the Guardians, and said that the children—aged respectively eleven, seven, and four -years—were admitted to the House in May last. Prisoner bore a very bad character and had been be- fore the Bench on a similar charge some time pre- viously. He had not given his wife any money for sixteen weeks, and when the children were admit- ted they were starving and almost naked. His wife supported herself. When apprehended by P.C. Neill prisoner said that he had got plenty of money "planted," but neither his family nor the Guardians would get it. He was sent to prison for three months with hard labour. ATTEMPTING TO TRICK A TICKET COLLECTOR.— John Vaughan, supposed to be a bookmaker's clerk, was brought before the magistrates at the Borough Court on Thursday on a charge of travelling from Birmingham to Warrington, on the London and North-Western Railway, without having purchased a ticket. Prisoner travelled on an excursion train that was running from Birmingham to Aintree for the races. At Crewe, tickets were examined, and prisoner had concealed himself behind a number of other men. These persons had their tickets snipped, and one of them then slyly handed his ticket to the prisoner. The collector, as the train was then beginning to move, got in the next carriage, and on the arrival of the train at Warrington it was de- finitely ascertained that prisoner had no ticket. He was fined 20s. and fkosts, or a month's imprisonment in default of payment. AN OB.TECTIONA.BLE RAILWAY PASSENGER.—On Saturday, at the Borough Court, a ship's stoker, named John Price, last from Swansea, was charged with riding in a third class carriage on the Cheshire Lines from Garstom to Warrington, without having paid his fare, on the previous night. There was a second charge against him of damaging a carriage window to the extent of 7s 6d. Prisoner, who was "muddled" with drink, stuck his head through the- glass when the train wasnear Farnworth, anawhen he reached Warrington would neither pay the dam- acre nor the fare. The Bench ordered him to defray the damage and pay costs, or suffer fourteen days' imprisonment in default. When the case was be- ing heard, one of the magistrates (Alderman Bur- gess) asked why prisoner was permitted to travel on the line at all, if he was intoxicated. The rail- way officials replied that he was not so much in- toxicated as to prohibit him from travelling, and Alderman Burgess said he would like to know in what state of intoxication a man might be allowed , in a railway carriage. It appeared to him he would be a very objectionable companion in any stage of intoxication.
