div.p: POLIO E TNT ELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.-13ef0ro the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies, and Councillor Greening. CRUELTY TO HORSES.--John Hart, Stockton Heath, Was charged on a warrant with furiously driving two horses, and with ill-treating them, on the 26th of July in last year. Constable Pace was on duty in Mersey-street, and met the prisoner at about midnight on the elay in question, riding on one horse and leading another. The constable, having suspicions, went towards prisoner, who then galloped away. He rode furiously up Manchester-road, and it eras after- wards ascertained that the horse that he rode was so much ill-used that it died on the road a little way out of the borough.—Prisoner, who had just came out of gaol, and pleaded to be lesientiv dealt with, was fined 103 and costs. THEFT OF PIGEONS —Michael Broderick, and John Bro- derick, boys, were charged with stealing six pigeons from a cote belonginz to a boy named Frederick Maddocks, of 19, Orford-lane. Mr. H. J. Longton defended Michael Broderick. The pigeons were seen safe in the cote en the night of the 6th inst.. and were missed the next morning. It was after- wards found that the Broderick s had sold some pigeons, three of which Maddocks identified as his property. John Broderick was ordeied to receive twelve, and Michael six, lashes with the birch rod. BREACH OF THE PEACS.—James Dagnall and Thomas Leyland were charged with disturbing the peace by fighting in Liverpool-road. They were bound over to be of good behaviour.—William Feeney and Patrick Mannion, charged with fighting in Bridge-street, were also bound over. Detusfeseremss.—John Conway, for being drunk and disorderly in Fennel-street, was fined 5s and costa, and Catherine O'Brien, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Battermerket-street, was dismissed with a reprimand.— Bridget Rafferty and Mary Mitchell were summoned for being drunk in Stanley-street, and were each fined 55 and costs.—Mary Mannion, charged with a similar offence in the Old-road, Latchford, was fined a like amount.—Thomas Flannery was fined lOs and costs for being drunk and dis- orderly in Winwick-street. As ABSENTEE —Thomas Lowrey was charged with being an absentee from the North Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Preston, since the 10th July. He was committed to Strangewaya to await escort. PITCH AND Toss.— Thomas Kerry and John Peers pleaded guilty to playing pitch and toss on Sunday after- noon. They were each fined 10s and costs, or 14 day's im- prisonment in default. THROWING HALF A BRlClC.—Margaret Lewis was sum- moned for "throwing half a brick in Beswick-street to the danger of passsngers." The defendant stated that trouble had arisen between herself and neighbours, bat it was all through the election. She was fined 103, including costs. Tratsnex.—Bef ore the Mayer (Alderman Harrison) and Councillor Broadbent. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—MichaeI McMahns and Catherine Riley were charged with aseaulting Catherine Robinson on the 10th inst. Mr. A. Browne defended. Complainant said that Riley's mother called her an Orange Tory, and words followed. Kate Riley then rushed at and assaulted her, and McMahns kicked her. The assault was denied, and it was contended that corcplainant was the aggressive person. The case was dismissed, the Mayor inducing the enemies to shake bands and make the quarrel up. WEDNESDAY.—Before Aldermen Chandley and Pickmere, Councillor Greening, and Mr. J. Fairclough. DRUNEENNESS.—MichaeI Morris, charged with being drunk in Stanley-street on the previous evening, was dis- charged with a caution. STEALING Boars.—James Henderson and John Fletcher, strangers, were charged with stealing a pair of blucher boots, value 12s 6d, the property of Mr. R. Roberts, boot and shoe dealer, Bridge-street, on the previous day. The hoots were hanging outside the shop on Tuesday. secured with nails and wire. Between eleven and twelve o'clock in the morning prosecutor saw the prisoners loitering about. and shortly afterwards he noticed that a pair of boots had been taken, and he at once communicated with the police. One of the prisoners afterwards offered the boots in pledge whilst the other stood outside the shop. The man who en- tered the shop asked for 4s, and, in response to a question, said that the boots were his, and that he bought them at Mr. Roberts's shop in Bridge-street.—P.C. Monaghan said he saw one of the prisoners in Mersey-street on Tuesday wearing a new pair of blucher boots similar to those pro- duced, and shortly afterwards he received information to the effect that a pair of boots h-ad been stolen from Mr. Roberts's shop. Witness went in search of the prisoners, and found them near to Mulholland's lodging-house in Mersey-street. They were taken into custody, and one of the men was very violent, and assistance had to be obtained to bring him to the police reation. Prisoners were under the influence of drink, and on being charged later on in the day with the robbery, one of them replied" You cannot charge two of us with the same thing," whilst the other denied any knowledge of the boots.—Prisonets were each sent to gaol for two months with hard labour. THORSDAY.—Before Major Litton. DRI'WEENNESS.—Mary Coyne, Catherine Connolly, and Mary Connolly, were each fined 5s and casts, or seven days' imprisonment in default of not paying the fine, for being drunk and disorderly on the previous eveniog.—Catherine Dogherty, similarly charged, was dismissed on promising to behave better. A VIOLENT FELLOW.—Thomas Foy, a young man, was fined 103 and costs for being drunk and disorderly in But- termarket-street on the previous night, and was sent to pri- son for a month for kicking and otherwise assaulting Police- constable Turner. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynold., Dr. Gomel!, and Messrs. John White, and Robert Garnett. THEFT OF RABBITS.—Edward Massey and Fred Humt, lads, were chargsd with stealing two rabbits, value is 61, the property of Frederick Hough, 22, Ashton-street, arid pleaded guilty. Massey was ordered to receive 10 strokes with a birch rod, and Hunt was ordered to pay a fine of 53 and costs.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Alevsrs. F. H, Gossage and John Brock. DISOUDERLY CHARACTERS.—Lawrence Mulroy and Anthony McGlovne were each fined for being drunk and disorderly.—For committing a breach of the peace, Johanna Quinn, of Water-street, was bound over in the usual surety. TUESDAY.—Bpfore Mr. T S. Timmis.

COUNTERFEIT Cors.—John Williams,-w—ITO-;;id he came from Liverpool, was charged on remand with uttering twe counterfeit half-crowns and having a third in his possession. —The prisoner was again remanded. TRURSDAL—Before Messrs. John Brock and T. S. Timmis. DRUNSENNESS.—MichaeI Tansev, Thomas Tansey, David Rogers, Mary Ann Fox, and Mary Mullarkey were each fined for drunkenness. BEGGING.—WiIIiam BaylPy was i.entenced to seven days' hard labour for begging ar Ditton. DESERTER.—George Kinsey was convicted of being a deserter from the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, and was given in custody of an escort. BREACH or THE PEACE —John Townsend and Catherine Townsend were each ordered to pay casts for committing this offence in Tavis-etreet.—Ann Griffin was dealt with in like manner.—Mary Burke was ordered to pay costs for as- saulting Elizabe:h Kilmartin.

NEWTON PETIT SESSIONS. SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Houghton, C. Pilkington, T. J. Gillespie, A. C. McCorquodale, and W. F. Goocb. DEUNIKENNESS.—• deorge Jackson was summoned for being drunk and disorderly in Market-street, Earlestown, Os the 3rd inst.,and was fined 53 and costs.—Owen Cain, for drunKenness in Viaduct-street, Earlestown, on the rd inst., was fined 5s and costs. REFUSING TO QUIT —George Cosgrove, who was stated to be " up" in the militia, was summoned for refusing to quit licensed premises. the Griffin Inn, Earle-street, when requested, on the 30th May.—Mrs. Cosgrove appeared for her son, and asked the Bench to inflict a small fine.—De- fendant was fined IU3 and costs.—Wm. Montgomery (My- dock), Andrew McLoughlin (Haydock), and Joseph Pen- nington (Golborne), were each fined 53 and costs for similar offences.

Hugh Brooks, " alias " Maxwell, who was to be executed on August 27 for the murder of Mr Arthur Preller, has ap• pealed against the sentence' and a respite until October next has therefore been granted. It is annoenced in a telegram from New York that Colonel Gilder, who, as he was aboat to start on a Polar exo,dation, was arrested on a charge of misappropriating a bond of which he was trustee, has been released on hatl. The Liverpool Cup was run for no Wednesday at Aintree. Mr. L. de Rothschild's Middlethorpe and Mr. A Benhohn's Perdita 11. making a deed heat for fl-st place, and Mr. W. Gilbert's Sailor Prince being third. Fourteen ran. SAD BOATING FATALITY —At Dunbar, on Monday, a boat containing 13 men and women engaged in the fi•thing in. dustry was crossing the bay, a distance of four miles, when a squall broke over it just as the harbour had been c'e ,red and the sails hoisted. The boat capsized, and the parry were all thrown into the water. Only four persons were saved. The coast is rocky, and the water at the time was tough.
NORTHWICH DIVISION ELECTION, MR. BRUNNER'S CANDIDATURE.

MASS MEETING ON RUNCORN HEATH. On Saturday afternoon the Liberals of Runcorn gathered in large numbers on Runcorn Heath, to take part in a meeting in favour of Mr. Brunner's candida- ture. The proceedings were very enthusiastic, and Mr. Brunner, who was accompanied by Mrs. Brun- ner, had a splendid reception. Mr. B. Kniveton pre- sided, and he was supported on the platform by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, Mr. Schwan, M.P. for North Manchester, Mr. W. Summers, M.P. for Huddersfield, Messrs. Jas. Handley, J.P., S. C. Beckett, P. Speak- man, J. Bridgewater, and W. Handley. The CHAIRMAN delivered a brief speech, urging the audi- ence to increased efforts in Mr. Brunnet's behalf, and ex- pressing himself confident as to the result. The Rey. J. D. THOMAS moved a resolution expressing unabated confidence in Mr. Gladstone, and pledging the meeting to work heartily to secure Mr. Brunner's return. The support that Mr. Brunner had given to the Premier had been so steadfast and consistent throughout that they rose and fell together. (Hear, hear.) Approval of one was approval of the other, and cendemnation of one was con- demnation of the other. The Irish policy of our great and noble Premier had been out on the field of war. It had been sorely stained and riddled by the fire of the enemy, hnt those who fougtbot under it desired none otuer. (Cheers.) They were satisfied that the banner which had inscribed upen it, "Justice to Ireland," "Home Rule for Ireland," was the banner under which they would yet achieve a glorious and enduring vietory. (Cheers.) Mr. P. SPEAKMAN seconded the motion with very great pleasure. He believed with Mr. Gladstone that it was far better to govern Ireland in love and unity than by coercion. (Cheers.) If they stuck to their text and returned Mr. Brunner to Parliament, they would aid that enlightened policy. A scheme of Home Rule for Ireland, whether formulated by Mr. Gladstone or the paper Unionists, or Lord Salisbury. Mr. Gladstone bad laid the foundation stone, and as sure as that stone had been laid a superstruc- ture would rise upon it and would be to posterity a memo- rial of that grand old man. (Loud cheers.) Mr. C. E. Scaweam, M.P., who was loudly cheered, said they had got a good candidate, he had got a good leader, and his leader had got a good cause. (Cheers.) He should be ashamed of the men of Cheshire if they allowed such good things to go begging. They bad the franchise given to them by Mr. Gladstone at the last election, and they then returned such a trump of a candidate in Mr. Brunner that it would be a disgrace if they did not repeat it on the present occasion. (Hear, bear, and cheers.) If they returned these Unionists they weakened their (the Liberal) party, and would find that the Tory party would probably have a large majority at the end of the election. That meant foreign wars, increased taxation, and stoppage of business; and when it came about they would remember the day they did not stand true to the cause of Liberalism. (Hear, hear.) Those gentlemen were getting weak upon this one question which was agitatieg their breasts, and that was to give to Ireland a good measure of self-government by consolidating the union which exists between Great Britain and Ireland. He dared say they had seen some of those flags posted about the town with the harp taken away. Well, it had only been taken away by Mr. Gladstone to be repaired, and would be placed back again tun,cl and in good circler. (Cheers.) Ireland was a black spot on the great fame of England, but Home Rule for that country, whether it was granted by the Liberals, whether Mr. Gladstone bad time to carry his measure to a fulfilment, or a measure similar to it was brought in by the Tories by one of those dodges which they had heard of before, of stealing the Liberal clethes—they had claimed the credit of the Liberal Franchise measure—whether they carried it or not, it was probable that, soc tier or later, and probable sooner than later, some measure of self-government would be granted to Ireland. (Cheers.) He was sure tha English people were not willing to return to coercion. They had had coercion long enough. The time bad come for them to tarn over a new leaf, and he looked to the men of Cheshire to maintain their old character by returning Mr. Brunner to Parliament, and they trusted that a new dawn of peace and a new era of posperity would exist between England and Ireland. (Cheers.) Mr. W. SUMMERS, M.P. for Huddersfield, who was loudly cheered on rising to address the melting, said before he came up there he was under the impression that they were having a fair and square stand•up fight between the Liberal candidate on the one hand and a Tory candidate on the other. But since he had come amongst them he had been somewhat enlightened. He had been told that Mr. Verdin had found the name of Tory inconvenient, and therefore for that occasion was coming out as a Liberal-Unionist, a Liberal-Conservative, or a Conservative-Liberal, which ever they liked. (Laughter.) Well, now, it seemed to him that that term Liberal• Conservative or Conservative-Liberal was a contradiction in terms. It was just like talking of a white negro— (laughter)—or ‘f a sober drunkard. (Renewed laughter.) Depend upon it, Mr. Verdln was a Tory. (Hear, hear.) He was only taking the name of Liberal in order to catch the votes of unwary Liberals, but they were much too wide awake to be taken in by that device. They would vote, he had no doubt, for the truly Liberal candidate, his friend and their late member, Mr. Brunner. (Cheers.) Now what was the issue at present before the electors of the United Kingdom ? They had te ask themselves this question, Would they have Mr. Gladstone or Lord Salisbury as the Prime Minister of this country? Would they apply to the future government of Ireland Liberal or Conservative prin- ciples, a policy of conciliation on the one hand, and coer- cion on the other? (A Voice: "Conciliation.") Well, there could be no doubt about this, that the Tory policy at the present moment was a policy of coercion* (Hear, hear.) He described the Carnarvon - Parnellite I contract previous to the last election, and said the Act of Union had been in existence for semething like eighty-six years. Through that period of time the Imperial Parliament had been busy in passing some eighty-six Co- ercion Bills, and the very first time that Ireland was ap- pealed to after household suffrage had been granted to her she sent them, in answer to their eighty-six Coercion Bills, eighty-six Nationalist members, asking that Ireland should be allowed to manage her own affairs. (Cheers.) They had to ask themselves whether there was anything in it in- consistent with the common interests of the United King- dom as a whole ; and if they believed that it could be safely granted, it was their duty to make the concession. (Hear, hear.) Well, now, he held that it could be granted, not only without detriment, but With very great advantage to the common interests of the United Kingdom. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) The demand was not a demand for separation. (Hear, hear.) When Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill became law, as of. course it would become, or something very like it in a very short period of time, Queen Victoria would continue to reign over Ireland just as she reigned over Great Britain. Their Army and Navy, and all the forces of the Crown, would remain in the bands of ties Imperial Ministry at Westminster, and would not be given over to the hands of the Irish Ministry at Dublin. (Cheers.) They were the proper Unionists. (Hear, hear.) They wanted to bring about a living, a real, and a practical union between the mind and sentiment of the English and Irish people. (Cheers.) The motion was carried unanimously and enthusi- astically. Mr. BRUNNER received a splendid 'ovation on rising to address the meeting. He thanked them for the unanimous vote of confidence in Mr. Gladstone, and their support of him. He had attended a great many meetings, and the men who bad held up their hands against him could sit com- fortably on that lurry—(laughter)—and if he could trust that the opinions were to be freely expressed on Tuesday, he should not have the shadow of a doubt as to the result. (Cries of "No traitors here," and "Keep your heart up.'') But mind this, that there were many hundreds of their fel- lows scattered over the constituency who dared not say they were Liberals. ( Hear, hear, and a voice: "They are cowards, net men.") Don't blame men weaker than them- selves. It was not because they were not men, but because circumstances were stroneer than they were. (Hear, hear.) There was many a man serving under a squire, and un ler a noble lord who dare not say he was a Liberal, and if they did nothing else record their votes on Tuesday against that t ranny. (Cheers.) Alluding to the Irish question, Mr. Brunner said wherever the English people had trusted any other set of people to manage their own affairs they had good results—(hear, hear.)—and wherever they had refused the people that right the results had been bad. (Hear, tlear.) They had done what they were now asked to do for iprieeleatndresusltesv,eraanld tthime ems nstoysetc,ikinangd of wtiht the many cases was that of i'anada. In Canada they had a large majority o f l?o m majority a neawyjneCdhr were ttißhtaonl lmiwikeaaesn.s o cf Tbatehthcheaeyoul because Fen. sir ,et :Inch:he that the In oGvAloormvenleeoarrnuni cdrmiat Government 1 ele its: to gwereet al- together, eo r, m backed by an insane old king, George 111., persistently and cruelly refused to allow the people of North America to set- tle their own affairs that they fought against them and beat them. In 1766 they made their Declaratien of Independ- ence, and that country, as part of the British Empire, had been lost. Twenty-nine years after the loss of the United States, the English Government came to the conclusion that if they refused to Canada the right to manage its own affairs they might lose that country too, and in 1795 they granted Canada a Parliament; but, it was a very bad sort of Parliament, just like the Parliament in the last century. The mi-take in Ireland was that they did not give the Roman Catholics a right to vote or a right to sit in that Parliament. In Canada they formed two Houses, the Caper and the Lower. The former was appointed by the Government in London, and the latter by the people. To the Upper House was given the right to veto any measure which was passed by the Lower House, so that from 1795 to 1840 the Canadian people were con- tinually rebelling against England. In 1835 the English Government sent out the Earl of Durham, who was a strong Radical like Lord Spencer. He was the pluckiest man in the world, like Lord Spencer, and he put deem rebellion with a firm hand, like Lord Spencer. (Cheers.) The Tories talked about their " firm and resolute " government. but if they wana d to learn something about coercion im- posed with a strew and imperious will, commend him to Lord Spencer. During the last five years, Lord Spencer put a thousaid leaders of the Irish nation in gaol, and held them there without trial. (Shame.) Lord Durham, after putting the rebellion down, gave the Cana- dian peoole a large measure of Herne Rule, but he did not give them enough—he did not allow them to manage their , own affairs entirely. They went on grumbling, and occa- sionally blood was shed, until the year 1867, when we finally I allowed the Canadians to elect in the freest fashion the i

Lower and the Upper Houses, and since that time Roman Catholics and Protestants—rich and poor—had been put on absolute equality, and they had had perfect friendliness and the utmost loyalty to the British Empire. (Cheers.) Did they think, if they continued to refuse to the Irish Roman Catholics what they had granted to French Roman Catho- lics, that they would support them in the hour of difficulty as the Canadians had done? He asked them to do to the Irish as they had done to the Canadians, and they would be as firm friends as the Canadians. (Hear, hear.) Would they do something, the results of which he had described to them, when it was asked for, in a respectful constitutional and friendly fashion by the Irish? (Hear, hear.) There ought to be no fear in any man's mind of any harm whatever coming to England, and that nothing but good would result to the Irish people. (Cheers.) His opponent, continued Mr. Brunner, called himself a Liberal. A Liberal, to his mind, was a politician who put the in- terests and feelings of the men he wished to represent be- fore his own and not after them. (Oheers.) When Mr. Robert Verdin was 'More the Liberal delegates last year he was asked which he put first, the salt trade or his Liberal politics, and he said he was first a salt manufacturer and next a Liberal. (Laughter.) Mr. Verdin was then asked why he did Rot support Mr. Latham, who, if ever there was a Liberal, was a Liberal—(cheers)—in the year 1880. His reply was " Do you think I would support a man that would not support me." (Laughter.) Mr Verdin told the delegates this without any feeling of shame that he did net support Mr. Latham because Mr. Latham, being one of the trustees of the Weaver Navigation, had voted against the interest?' of Joseph Verelin and Sons in a private b.isiness matter in a private business meeting at Northwicb. ("Shame.") What was the price that they had to pay for Mr. Verdin's advocacy of their political feelings and their rights. It wag this, that unless they supported Joseph Verdin and Sons he would throw them over. (Laughter and a voice: "He will not throw them over here." Cheers.) Don't get on his back, and then. (Laughter. "We will have you again." Cneers.) Replying to a question what Home Rule would cost, Mr. Brunner asked What sort of a politician was Dr. Mackie ? (" Tory " and laughter.) There was no shade of politics Dr. Mackie had not advocated in his time—(laughter and cheers)—and there was no blessed religion on the face of the earth that De. Mackie had not advecatea in his time. (Renewed laughter.) It would cost England, Dr. Mackie had stated, to give Home Rule to Ireland, 150 millions. He (Mr. Brunner) had been once for his sins a director of Mackie and Co. (Load laughter.) It was not for very long, and he was very sorry he was ever there. (Loud laughter.) But when he was there he found he was to the full as good a financier as Dr. Mackie, and he (Mr. Brunner) was not in it with Glad- stone. (Hear, hear.) What Dr. Mackie said would cost 150 millions Mr. Gladstone said would not cost, half that sum. (Cheers.) He (Mr. Brunner) knew as well as most men the difference between investing money and spending money. He had invested a good deal in h's time and spent as little as be ceuld. (Laughter.) He contended that the money under the Land Purchase Scheme would be invested on good security, and that by Homo Rule England would save three millions a year in the reduced expenditure neces- sary to maintain the country. (Cheers.) He appealed to them to stand by Gladstone, and not be misled by the Tories, who told them not to trust Irishmen. Two years ago it was the English people who were not to be trusted with the franchise. (Hear, hear.) Remember the words of their dear old chief that Liberalism meant trust in the people, tempered with prudence, but always to trust in the people. (Loud cheers.) The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 17, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 17, 1886.
MR. ROBERT VERDIN'S CANDI-
DATURE. MEETING AT RUNCORN.

A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Robert Verdin was held on Monday night in the Public Hall, Runcorn. When the proceedings com- menced there was but a sparse attendance of electors, many ladies being present, but as the meeting pro- gressed there were considerable additions, and the body of the room became filled. The gallery was al- most empty. Mr. Charles Wigg presided, Fad he was supported by Dr. McDougall and a number of Tory gentlemen. The CHAIRMAN said they had a momentous question be- fore the country. It was the disruption of the Empire—an Empire which our ancestors had built up and maintained by enormous sacrifices, and maintained against nearly all the world in arms. (Hear, hear.) They were now asked to sever a portion of that Empire to gratify the ambition of one man—(hear, hear)—to retain him in power. If they could only get rid of the incubus of Mr. Gladstone's Gov- ernment, they would have a firm Government, free from the agitating excitements of the last six years; confidence would revive, and, as a natural consevence, they would have better trade, higher wages, and increased happiness all round. (Applause.) Mr. PERCY GLASS, whom the chairman introduced as a Liberal, moved the usual resolution that in all legislation relating to Ireland, the supremacy of the Imperial Parlia- ment and the Union must be maintained, and that the Irish loyalists meet be protected. In supporting the motion Mr. Glass attempted to prove that Ireland had been more pros- perous under the Uuion than previously, by showing that the tonnage of Irish ships had increased many fold and consumed a tremendously larger amount of sugar. tea, and coffee, and that the deposits in the savings banks were con- siderably greater. In a commercial aspect the Union had been of great advantage to Ireland, and also in a social, re- ligious, and political aspect. (Applause.) Mr. J. LOWRY, of Liverpool, seconded the motion. He denied that Ireland as a nation, one people, one race, had ever existed, and certainly did not exist new. (Applause.) There were two nationalities in that country, one prosper- ous because loyal and industrious —(applause)—and the other disloyal and lazy. There were two millions happy and prosperous, and three millions who detested the Eng- lish breed, seed, and generation. He admitted that there were 86 Nationalist members, but in Ireland the Qneen's writ bad ceased to run, the Land League ruled, free speech was in abeyance at present, and in the provinces of Leine- ter and Connaught a Loyalist dare not appear as a candi- date. (Applause.) He drew a black picture of the crime in Ireland; and said what was wanted was not justice for Ireland, but justice in Ireland. (Applause.) He described Mr. Gladstone's bill as a miserable contemptible rag of a bill that he would not pick out of a gutter, and argued that it did not really give Ireland Home Rale, because her customs and excise would be under the control of a receiver general. He asked Englishmen to reject this nefarious scheme, and to say to these infernal wretches who went against the unity of this country—No, a thousand times no kCheers.) Mr. t. C. RAYNOR supported the resolution, and con- tended that the Parnellites did not speak the national senti- ment ef Ireland, and that Mr. Gladstone had by his con- cession of Home Rule raised dynamite, gunpowder and bullets, and brutal outrages, to the level of political argu- ment. (Applause.) He asked those present to give their vote solid for the unity of the empire, and then to coerce these who would not obey the law. Mr. W. H. Verdin, who was cordially greeted, apologised for the absence of his brother who was attending three meet- ings in other parts of the division. He expressed his own and his brother's deep regret that any attack had been made upon Mr. and Mrs Brunner. (Applause.) It had pained and distressed his brother very much that Mr. Brunner should have been attacked, and he need not assure them that there bad been no instigation on his (Mr. Robert Ver- din's) part' (Hear, hear.) On the contrary everyone must have observed that throughout the contest he had guardedly restrained from mentioning even Mr. Brunner's name. (Ap- plause.) It was insinuated in one print that the attack upon Mr. and Mrs Brunner was at a place called Moulton, with which they (Messrs. Verdins) were intimately associa- ted. There was considerable feeling there, and for this rea- son, They in Runcorn had no idea of the intense bitterness , there had been in that part of the constituency during the last few months. When he told them that even in the very house of God men had been pursued and attacked they would understand why it was tuere was some feeling of re- , sentment in Moulton. A man some months ago went in the Moulton Church, and a working-man's wife had the cour- tesy to offer him a bymn book or a prayer book, and be- cause she did that—because she happened to be a woman of dark complexion—she was likened to the devil. They would thus understand why the women of the village bad a feeling of resentment. He did not say for one moment that they had been justified in attacking Mr. and Mrs Brun- ner, but he mentioned thia to show that the fault did not lie entirely with the inhabitants of Moulton.
_ The resolution was put to the meeting and carried with- out dissent.
Mr. H. COBH moved, and Mr. YERBURGII, M.P., secon- ded, the customary resoletion to support Mr. Verdin's re- turn, and it was enthusiastically carried.
On the proposition of Dr. McDouGALL, seconded by Mr. J. G. FLETCHRR, a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, and the meeting broke up.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS
div.p: GENERAL NEWS

Sir Samuel Ferguson, president of the Royal Irish Acad- emy, is seriously Mr. Childers has returned to town from Scotland, and resumed his duties at the Home Office. Mr. Jesse Collings is obliged to go abroad in consequence of ill-health. He will be. absent several weeks. Mr. Henry George, 4".er investigation, reports that the miners are the worst-paid working-men in the United States.

On Monday night 20 ruffians entered the houses of men named Walsh and SuHinter; near Kanturk, and severely maltreated the inmates. It is understood that the Marriott-Chamberlain libel case which was referred to the arbitration of Lord Se(borne, has been abandoned by mutual consent. Mr. Andrew Carnegie has offered to erect a free public library and music hall in the town of Alleglaany, Pennsyl- vania, at a cost of net less than £50,000. Of the 207,232 farms in New England, only 17,596 are rented, the remainder being farmed by the owners. In the Southern States 1,047,505 farms are occupied by emancipated coloured tenants. lhe Kingston-on-Thames Working-men's Club and Insti- tute, consisting of an extensive range of buildings, was entirely destroyed by fire on Monday night. No lives were lost, nor was anyone injured. Margt. IVeston, the woman who attempted to drown her four children and herself at Wolverhampton, last week, has been committed for trial. The prisoner pleaded that she had "had trouble with her husband." Mrs. Mary Ann Lord, 43 pairs of ago, attended a poliele eal meeting at Barbridge, Leioestarshlre, on Saturday night. She had been in excellent health, but became excited with the proceedings, Was as zed with a fit, and died in a few minutes. ' At Spiddale, a village about 15 miles from Galway, Dr. Brodie, a dispensary doctor, shot his wife while suffering from the effects of drink, to which he had been much addicted. He has been takenlto Galway in charge of the police. FATAL ELECTION FIGHT.—At Poplar, London, on Sun- day, two labourers named Hawkins and Mundy, while drinking at a public-house, quarrelled over electioneering matters and went outside to tight. In the course of the en- counter Munday received a blow which caused his death. Hawkins has been arrested charged with manslaughter. FOURTEEN BRITISH SEAMEN DROWNED.—A sad disaster has occurred to the crew of Her Majesty's ship Goshawk, while off Hayti with the North American squadron. A boat containing 17 of the crew was capsized, and only three of the men were saved. The news was communicated by sig- nal, and no details of the disaster were known to the other ships of the squadron. MURDER IN A LODGING•HOUSIL—A desperate affray took place in a lodging-house at Hanley on Saturday night, in which the keeper of the house, a blind man named Hall, was killed. Some lodgers were fighting, when Hall and his wife attempted to separate them. Two of them, named Richards and Brown, knocked him down and jumped upon him, inflicting such internal injuries as resulted in his death. DEATH OF AN EX-MAYOR OF BOLTON.—On Tuesday morning Mr. Richard Stockdale, an old Bolton inhabitant, died at he age of 77. He was Mayor of Bolton from 1864 to 1866, and during his mayorality the public park was opened by the Earl of Bradford, and he cut the first sod of the waterworks which supplies the town with water. He was boroagh magistrate, and was highly respected in the te wn. STRIKE DISPUTES IN Duoroete—On Tuesday David Scott and Ed. Burrett, indicted for assaulting men who re- placed the labourers of the Dublin and Glasgow Steam- packet Company on strike, at North Wall, Dublin, pleaded guilty, and were allowed out on bail, on their own recog- nisances. It was stated that the men struck in obedience to the Emmet Labourers' Society, now dissolved. The funds have disappeared. FATAL AFFRAY.—Late on Saturday night a fatal affair took place at Matlock Bridge, Derbyshire. A man named Lawrence Reeder, aged about 50, was walking home with Fred. Wilegoose, a retired soldier, when the latter dealt him a severe blow on the neck, inflicting injuries to the jugular vein. Reeder was removed to his home in a dying condition, and be expired on Sunday morning. Wildgoose delivered himself up to the police. LYNCHING A MURDERER. A despatch from Detroit, Minnesota, states that William Kelleher, alias "Reddy," the gambler, who killed officer Convey while the latter was try- ing to arrest bim for shooting at another gambler, was taken from gaol by a large crowd of disguised men and hanged to the limb of a tree in a neiehbouring grove, and his body riddled with bullets. Sheriff Pinney attempted to defend his prisoner, but was overliowered. ATTEMPTED MURDER ANG SuICIDE.—At Plymouth, on Monday night, an artisan named Oliver, in consequence of jealousy, upbraided his sweetheart, a servant girl named Jenkins, and shot her twice with a revolver. She fell in the street, and believing he had killed her, Oliver rushed off and killed himself by discharging the remaining bullet through his forehead. Jenkins is expected to recover. One bullet lodged in her chin, and with the other her right ear was blown away. RECRUITING FOR THE ARMY.—Recruiting for the regular army is now going on satisfactorily, and it appears probable that the rate for 1885, when just 40,000 were obtained, will be nearly, if not quite, sustained during the current year. But it will -squire Quite that number to carry out the pro- ject of increasing the army at home, as well as the European force in India, each by 10,000 men. As regards the Indian establishment, the increase already made amounts to about 7,000 on the establishment of last year. THE UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH AAIEMBLY The annual assembly of the United Methodist Free Churches opened in Sheffield on Tuesday morning. The election of president for the ensuing year was early pro- ceeded with, the following being nominated T. Sherwood, Rev. J. S. Balmer, and Rey. T. M. Myers. On a vote being taken the Rev. T. Sherwood, Cennexional secre- tary, was elected, and Mr. Balmer was promoted from cor- responding secretary to Mr. Sherwoed's late position. MURDER OF A SWEETHEART.—At Burtori-on-Trent. On Saturday, John Jeffries was charged with the wilful murder of Ann Jane Willis. The deceased, a young woman who had previously kept company with the prisoner, was out walking with two other girls late on Friday night, when, as is alleged, the prisoner came up and so brutally kicked and assaulted her that she had to be taken to the infirmary, where she died on Saturday morning. The prisoner is also stated to have assaulted the deceased's companions, who Interfered to prevent the assault. THE ROYAL VISIT TO TATERPOOL.—With the special sanction of the Queen, an official record of the Royal visit to Liverpool, prepared by Sir James Picton, has been for- mally entered in the civic records. Sir Jaime stated on the occasion that it was the wish of her Majesty that every per- son who had taken part in the proceedings, on the part of the City Council, should be individually mentioned, as she was desirous to give honour to those to whom honour was due. The Council also decided to furnish the Queen with copies of an idition de luxe of the Pictorian report. ATTEMPTED MURDER BY IRAMPS.—At Garisha, county Kildare, the cottage ef a labourer was found on Saturday to be on fire. An entrance was effected, and the occupier sent for. When he arrived he discovered his wife lying on the floor in a pool of blood and moaning feebly. 'rhe flames were extinguished with difficulty, and the poor woman removed to an outhouse. The man next found that £22 had been stolen. The police believe that some tramps entered the cottage, and having attacked the woman and left her far dead, stole the money, set fire to the place, and then locked the door. The woman is in a dying state. A MAN'S HEAD CUT OFF.—On Monday morning, at Bardsley, Henry Taylor, a retired soldier receiving a pen- sion, whose place of residence is unknown, was seen to throw himself in front of the train which left Church Fen- ton at 8-20 about 200 yards on the Leeds side of the Bards- ley Station. The wheels passed over his neck, completely severing the head from the body. On one ef the leaves of a pocket book found on the body of the deceased was written, "Died of a broken heart, unable to find employment." The deceased is supposed to have hidden himself behind the Thorner Bridge, which crosses the railway, and waited for the train. AN AFFECTING INCIDENT.—An incident of mach interest arose out of Mr. Irving's visit to Oxford. in his address at the University he spoke of the last days of Edmund Kean, whe died without a ten-pound note. A few days after, Mr. Irving received it letter from Mr. Robert Browning. enclosing the purse, of slightly faded green silk—found in the pocket of the great actor after his death, "without a sixpence therein." It was given by Charles Kean to John Forster, and by him to the poet, who now sends it to the actor in due succession. "How can I more worthily place it," gracefully writes Mr. Browning. "than in your hands, if you will do me the honour to take it, along with all res- pect and regard ?" THE WESLEYANS AND THE REV, W. ARTHUR. An "Ardent Wesleyan" writes to the "Daily News" as fol- lows respecting the action during the election of the Rev. Wm. Lord Henry Lennex's creditors on nursday accepted a NM of £2,500 in full satisfaction of Lord Lennex's debts, wbich are returned at £11,500.
Major General Sir E. Bulwer, Mr. Le Poer Trench, Q.O and Mr. Richard Adams, barrister, hAve been appointed to inquire into the Belfast dots.

The Queen, accompanied by Prince and Princess Elinry of Battenberg, left Windsor on Thursday morning for Lon- don, where her Majesty paid her third visit to the Colonial and Indian Exhibition, returning to Windsor after about two hours.

At Dorset Assizes, on Wednesday, John Gerrard King, a pilot, was sentenced to death for the murder of Alderman Hamilton, at Poole. The prisoner sh.t the deceased with a revolver on account of a supposed injustice done him in his °opacity of pilot.

In the Divorce Court, on Wednesday, Baron Henry de Worms, M.P., applied for a divorce from his wife, on the ground of adultery with Baron Moritz Ritter on Leon There was no defence, and the Court granted a decree nisi, with costs and custody of the children.

A Great Conference of British and Colonial Temperance Advocates was held on Wednesrlay in Prince's Hall, Picca- dilly, London. Dr. Temple, Bishop of London, an enthusi- astic temperance reformer, presithd, and the attendance, which was large, included thirty colonial delegates. At noon, on Thursday, a labourer named Ralph Dodd, employed at the Chorley Flooroloth Works, was engaged in placing cloth between some rollers, but did not stop the machine, and his head and right arm were dragged between the rollers. The machinery was stopped and Dodd released, but death was the result.

On Wednesday, a fatal boat accident, by which one man was drowned, occurred on the Mersey, between New Brighton and the opposite shore. The boat contained two men, and when it capsized in a squall one of them clung to It until rescued. The other man, named John Henry Rowe, not being able to swim, sink immediately. WomsN's I'I3FFRAGII.—Mrs. Fawcett, who presided on Thursday at the annual meeting of the National Society for Women's Suffrage, said the election now in progess led them to look forward with confidence to the speedy settle- ment of the long struggle that had taken place on the sub- ject, and a belief that the measure would be carried by the concurrence of opinion the beet men and women on all sides in politics. The adoption of the report was moved by Sir R. Lethbridge, M.P. NONCONFORMISTS AS MAGISTRATBS.—A remarkable cor- respondence is proceeding between Mr. Samuel Smith, M.P., and Mr. Hughes, Lord-Lieutenant of Flintsbire. Mr. Smith wrote that the Flintslaire magistracy consisted of 87 gentle- men, not one of whom was a Nonconformist, and asking if some two or three Nonconformists could not be appointed. The Lord-Lieutenant replied that of 87 magistrates he was responsible for 35. Of the whole bench nine were Liberals and two doubtful. His object, adopting Blackstone's ad- vice, had been to eppoint men the most worthy and of the best reputation. When Mr. Smith's experience in Flint.. shire was enlarged he would be able to judge whether among his constituents there were any who came up to his requirements or were otherwise possessed of the necessary qualification. The Lord-Lieuteeant concluded by saying "I shall continue to make these appointments at my own discretion, uniefluenced by the public agitation with which you threaten me." A PIT-BROW WOMAN KILLED.—Mr. Brighowe, coroner, held as inquest at Blackbrook, on Monday, on the body of Mary Birchall, 39 years of age, widow, who was employed on the pit-brow at Queen Colliery, Havdock, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. Mr. H. Hall, government inspector of mines, and Mr. B. B. Glover, general manager of the collieries, were present.—Mrs. Sarah Garner stated that deceased was her daughter, and since her husband bad died had lived with witness at Garner'a-houses, Blackrook- road. On Friday morning she left home in good health, but was brought home dead later in the day.—By Mr. Hall : Deceased was satisfied with the work she had to do. —Peter Rimmer, beowmen, said he SAW deceased go to the empty end of a waggon which was in motion,to get off, and he saw her crushed between the waggon and the spout. Witness immediately called for someone to pull the waggon away. He took hold of deceased, and she died in his arms. —George Brown, day wageman, stated that deceased ordered him to lower a waggon to the screen to receive coal, and he did so. She was standing on it. He heard a scream and found that she had changed her safe position to one of danger, and was crushed against the spout.—Mr. Hall said his impression was that the man who lowered the waggon had not given her sufficient time to get into a safe place. No doubt there was some misunderstanding. but he thought that was the real cause of the accident.—The Coroner said it seemed to him that the woman was in a place of safety to begin with. There were two places of safete, but she went into the only one of danger.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. Mn. GLADSTONE AT HAWAEIDEN.—Mr., Gladstone read the lessons at Hawarden Church, on Sunday morning, for the first time since his return from London, the occasion being the annual church parade of the HAvvarden Rifle Volunteers, who are going into camp on Conwary Marsh next Saturday. Mr. Gladstone's voice was again clear, and quite free from huskiness. Mr. Gladstone, with Mrs. Glad- stone and Miss Helen Gladstone, left Hawardeu Castle about three o'clock on Wednesday afternoon. There was a considerable gathering of Liberals on Chester platform, and as the salon was drawn up to the train Mr James Tomkin- son, the Liberal candidate for the Eddisbury division, en- tered in and engaged in conversation with Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Tomkinson said he did not wish to be too sanguine, but he had reason to believe that there were very good hopes of a Liberal victory in the Eddiabury division. Mr. Glad- stone said be knew that Mr. Tomkiuson was doing splended work in Eddiebury, and that the enthusiasm of those who were with him was beyond all praise. The combination against Home Rule in the country generally had been tre- mendously formidable, and it was too much to have ex- pected to secure a complete victory at the first, but ultima- tely victory was certain to be their reward. Mr. Tornkiri- son had carried on a grand work of political education in the Eddisbury division, and he wished him most F,eartily success in his arduous fight. The train then moved out of the station, and hearty cheers were raised for Mr. Gladstone by those assembled. On arriving at Euston, Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone drove to Downing-street in an open carriage, ale riving at the official residence shortly before nine o'clock. A large crowd which had assembled in Downing-street loudly cheered the right hon. gentleman and passed around the carriage to shake him by the hand. The Premier, who was looking well, acknowledged the greeting by bowing from the carriage and doorstep. After giving more cheers for Mr. Gladstone the crowd dispersed. THE ASHTON POISONING CASE. On Saturday, Mary Ann Britland and Thomas Dixon were again before the Ashton-under-Lyne magistrates, and some additional evi- dence was given in connection with the three cases• of Alleged poisoning, but neither of the two barristers engaged for the defence of the prisoners was present. Police In- spector John Snell deposed that when he arrested the female prisoner and charged her with poisoning Mary Dixon, and also on suspicion of causing the death of her hasband and. daughter, she replied, "Are they bringing that against me and all? It it something I don't understand. You said lam charged with it. lam innocent of that." He also apprehended Thomas Dixon, who replied to the charge, "I can only say, as I have said before, that I have had nothing whatevee to do with it in any shape or form." On Monday, Mr. Charles Estcourt, analyst, stated that he had made some physiological experiments with the strychnia re- covered from the body of Mary Dixon. About 100th of a grain was given to a mouse, and after showing a little pre- vious uneasiness it dropped dead sudeinnly within two miuutes. About half that quantity given to another mouse brought on tetanic convulsions, and it died in less than three hours. lie had made further experiments, whiee be could describe if necessary. He had not made any ex- periments with arsenic.—The case was again adjourned.-- On Wednesday the Ashton magistrates commmitted Mary Ann Brigand for trial. The magistrates now discharged Thomas Dixon, holding that there was not sufficient evi- dence to incriminate him at present. The Coroner's inquest in these two cases and that of Elizabeth Hannah Britland, daughter of Mts. Britland, was also concluded on Wednes- day. It resulted in the committal of Mrs. Britland on the charge of murdering all the deceased. The jury added to their verdict an expression of their opinion that more strin- gent regulations should be adopted in regard to the sale of " vermin killer," and asked the coroner to bring the matter to the notice of the Home Secrerarv. . div.head: SHIP CANAL SCHEME.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME.

It is stated that the Manchester Ship Canal Scheme will be a nnounced early next week. The capital spoken of is £8,000,000 in £lO shares, of which .£1 will be at once paid up. The "Times,' in announcing that the prospectus of the Manches- ter Ship Canal will be issued next week, says that a contract for the construction of the canal has been signed with Messrs. Lucas and Aird for con- siderably less than the Parliamentary estimate. Another account says that as the first definite step towards the commencement of the undertak- ing the contract for the whole of the works con- nected with the construction of the Ship Canal has now been let to Messrs. Lucas and Aird for the round sum of £5,750,000, which is .E 560,000 less than the Parliamentary estimates. These works include the cutting of the canal from Manchester to the outlet at Eastham, the building of the docks at Manchester and Warrington, thc construction of the necessary locks with the swing aqueduct at Barton, and the carrying out of the whole of the required railway deviations. The whole of the work is to be completed within a period of four years after the actual commencement of operations, and if from any unforeseen circumstances the work be not completed within that period, the contrac- tors subject themselves to heavy penalties in the shape of the payment of interest until the comple- tion of the work at the rate or 4 per cent. per an- num on the amount of capital which shall then have been called np. On the other hand, if the con- , tractors complete the work within the specified period they will receive a bonus on their contract equal in amount to the interest which the company would, during such period as the work may have been complated within the specified time, have paid on the called-up capital. It is estimated that the working plant for carrying out the undertaking will require about 6,000 railway waggons and 300 lo- comotives, and that employment will be found for something like 20,000 men. It is the intention of the contractors to commence operations by laying down a line of railway along each side of the route, and to cut the canal in sections, operations pro- ceeding simultaneously in each section. The whole of the capital required, which is spoken of as £8,000,000, is to be raised in £lO shares, and the floating of the scheme has been placed in the hands of Messrs. Rothschild, who will issue the prospec- tus, and have undertaken the financial portion of the scheme at a commission of 1 per cent.

div.head: ORANGE MOTS AT BELFAST. THE CHIEF CONSTABLE SHOT. FOUR PERSONS KILLED AND MANY INJURED.
div.p: ORANGE MOTS AT BELFAST. THE CHIEF CONSTABLE SHOT. FOUR PERSONS KILLED AND MANY INJURED.

Disturbances commenced on Tuesday night with collisions between political parties, and resulted in conflicts between the police and the public. The police, it is alleged, in attempting to quell the dis- turbance were fired on by some of the mob, and this allegation is borne out by the fact that several of the police are seriously injured by pellets, and at least three of the officers have been treated for bul- let wounds. The disturbances commenced early in the afternoon. Large numbers of members of the local Orange lodges assembled for the purpose of attending the ceremony of laying the foundation stone of a new Orange Hall at Ballynafeigh, and , the attack, led by the Nationalist roughs, upon one of the parties who were proceeding to the scene of the ceremonial, was the direct cause of the first out- break. However, with the assistance of three policemen the Orangemen succeeded in compelling their assailants to beat a retreat. Things for a short time assumed a quiet appearance, when suddei4 a mob appeared in Grosvenor-place, which is situated between Leeson-street and Grosvenor-street. They commenced to shower stones across Grosvenor-road, Leeson-street, and Cullingtree-road. A number of police came on the scene, and owing to their posi- tion between the cross-firing many of them were struck by paving stones and badly injured. They succeeded, however, ih dispersing the mob. The houses opposite Cullingtree-road and Leeson-street have scarcely a whole pane of glass left. The noise of the disturbance soon brought large numbers of people from the Shankhill-road, many of whom were workmen just returning from their day's labour. These took the part of their co-religionists, and a desperate encounter ensued. The police on duty in this locality at the time were thirteen mounted constables under Head Con- stable Hamilton, and fourteen King's County Constabulary under District Inspector M'Clel- land. Only ten of the latter were armed with rifles. The mounted men and other police charged the crowd repeatedly, and after a desperate effort succeeded in separating the parties, though not till several of their number had been struck with stones and severely injured. The lives of some, of the men are despaired of. They dis- persed the less desperate of the mob for a time, but many hundreds of them still held their position and defied the police, some of them even inviting the police "to shoot for Tipperary dogs." The position of the constables seemed desperate, the mob grow- ing more excited and more desperate with each shot. Just at this juncture—news of the disturbance having been sent to head-quarters—large reinforce- ments of police arrived under the command of Col. Forbes, R.M., Town Inspector Carr, and District In- spector Hoggin. This fresh body charged the mob, who, however, met them with the greatest deter- mination, flinging volleys of stones an firing several shots, which, however, did not wound any- one. Many of the men, however, were struck with bricks and " pavers," and some of them were very seriously injured. Sergeants Forster and Macmalion were among those whose wounds were dressed by Dr. Harkin at the barracks, both having received severe lacerated wounds from sharp stones. Colonel Forbes, being unable to disperse the mob, read the Riot Act. At the lower portion of the brickfield stone throwing still continued, and revolvers and gun shots were discharged from time to time at the police. Town Inspector Carr at length ordered his men to fire on the crowd. They were, however, it is stated, first put into kneeling position in order, if possible, to warn the rioters off, but this had not the slightest effect upon the inflamed and des- perate mob. The constabulary then fired a number of rounds, and two unfortunate men were killed and upwards of thirty wounded by their discharges. Meanwhile, word having been sent to the military barracks where the men had been kept under arms for several days past, a strong body of military was sent down to the Brickfield, arriving shortly before eight o'clock. After the arrival of the military the Percy-street and Beverley-street crowd gradually dispersed, although one or two revolver shots were tired, but happily did no harm. It was desperate work while it lasted, and the police themselves speak with horror of having had to use firearms on the crowd, but add that it was, under the circum- stances, unavoidable. There was also bad work on the Shankhill-road side. M`Glade's public-house was wrecked, and a number of boys, the eldest not more than 15, were brought down to Davis-street Barracks. They were, it is stated, arrested while taking part in the outrage. All of them seemed utterly defiant and desperate. The military were kept on duty all night with the exception of the Dragoons, who were withdrawn to the barracks about 11 o'clock. Charges of police, armed with batons, had to be made from time to time to dis- perse isolated parties of stone throwers and roughs, who were endeavouring to wreck houses. Three men were killed during the rioting, two being constables, and twenty were wounded, of whom four are policemen. Sergeant Itfl`Gee was severely injured. At the police court on Wednes- day morning, before Colonel Forbes and Sir John Preston, several persons were charged with rioting. They were sentenced to terms of imprisonment , -varying from one to six months. Two men named Joseph Walker and john Walker were also charged, /the former with the wilful murder of Private Hughes, of the West Surrey Regiment, and the latter with feloniously firing a revolver by which it is stated Head Constable Gardiner was dangerously wounded. From the evidence given in the last- named cases the riot evidently originated in a desire for revenge arising out of the loss of life that occurred on the recent occasion when the police fired on the people in the Shankhill Road dis- trict.

Another death has occurred as the result of Tiles,' .day night's rioting. Head Constable Gardiner, who was shot during the melee, died on Wednesday in the Royal Hospital. Additional troops and consta- bulary have been drafted into the. town, which is in a very excited state. A ,special meeting of magi- strates wat held on Wednesday afternoon to devise means for restoring order. Though a great deal of excitement prevailed no serious rioting took place on Wednesday. The more serious part of the riots occurred at an early hour on Wednesday morning, and it Was net until five a.m, that the military were withdrawn from the disturbed district.. In the course of a des- perate encounter Head Constable Gardener, of. the Waterford force, received a fatal bullet wound in the neck. A private of the West Surrey named Hughes perceiving that the head constable had been disabled and that his assailant was likely to

escape, rushed forward and endeavoured to arrest the person who had fired the shot. No sooner, how-- ever, was his action perceived than he himself WO-- shot, and he fell dead close to where the head c.ou- - stable lay insensible. On Thursday Belfast continued in a tranquil state; but boilies of police were still posted in the disturbed districts, and the military were confined to their quarters, so as to be in readiness if their services were required. Those who were wounded are progressing favourably. An address "to the Nationalists of Belfast," telegraphed from Dublin by Mr. Sexton, M.P., has been extensively posted, es- pecially in the district now represented by gr- Sexton. He urges the Nationalists by no act or word to excite bad feeling, and to remain as much as possible within their own homes, especially alter nightfall.

THE PROGRE-S OF CHEMICAL INDUSTRY. SPEECH BY MR. E. K. MUSPRATT. The annual meeting of the Society of Chemical Industry was held at Liverpool University College/ on Wednesday. Mr. E. K. Muspratt, J.P., of Wil nes, the president of the society, occupied the chair, and delivered an address of great interest to the,, inhabitants of those centres of chemical industry ' St. Helens and Widnes.—After welcoming the Mop' bers to the city, Mr. MUSPRATT said that more thall 50 years ago Liverpool contained several soap au' glass works, and here the manufacture of alkali Iva! first carried out on a large scale, but the town itsem had long ceased to be the principal seat of these manufactures, which had migrated to the neigh; bouring towns of St. Helens, Widnes, Runcorn, all' Flint, and, together with large works for the ex- traction and smelting of copper, formed the staple industry of this portion of the county of Lancaster. Considering that, with the exception of sulphur,th,e prices of the several raw materials were not materl' ally different from what they were -50 years agO great improvement must have been made in the chemical operations to enable the manufacturer tie sell soda ash at present prices, even taking Intl3 consideration the aid afforded by the increased cell' sumption of the chlorine products. Great econonlY, had, for instance, been effected in the production 0' sulphuric acid. Attempts had often been made tO supersede the costly leaden chambers by Ear_ere economical structures without success, but provements had been made in the mode of Or, struction of the plant, and a cheaper source sulphur had been found in the cupreous pyrites el- Spain and Portugal. The most important improve; meat had been the substitution of pyrites for silt; phur, and the econmny of nitrate of soda and f11e,14 by means of the Gay Lussac absorbing column ae", the Glover Tower. The suicidal policy of the of Naples in granting a monopoly of the trade 13 Sicilian sulphur to a French firm, which raised tbe,l price of sulphur from £5 or £6 per ton to £l2 an' £l4, roused the English manufacturers to seek el substitute, which they found in the Wicklow Welsh pyrites, and it was in this neighbourhood was first used on a large scale, for in the years 1639 and 1840 large quantities were burnt by his fathe.s at his works at Liverpool and Newton. The use e' Irish, pyrites in place of sulphur was soon general adopted by alkali makers in the Lanca3hire district; but sulphur still continued to be used on the TYlle' and so late as the year 1852 7,580 tons of sulphl_lr were consumed in that district, when none Wu.' used in Lancashire. The effect of improve" ments in copper extraction had been to bind mere closely together the manufacture of alkali with the production of copper, sometimes by the same fire 39 and sometimes by the shares in the copper OM" pany being largely held by alkali make It had long been known that the copper precipitate produced from the Spanish and Portuguese ores con: tamed both silver and gold, but as the amount or silver present in the burnt" ore was exceedingl/ small, and even the whole of this small quantity le not obtained in solution, a simple and expeditioue method was necessary, if its extraction could he made remunerative. In the year 1870, Mr. Claudet introduced his beautiful process at the works of th, e Widnes Metal Company, • and since then about 24 millions of ounces of silver and 11,965 ounces of geloi had been extracted from the burnt pyrites. By !Jr' Claudet's process all the -constituents of the pyritee were practically made available: the sulphur for the production of sulphuric acid, and the iron, copper, silver, and gold in the extracting works, Unforto• pately, all the salt used in the calcination process, amounting to over 20,000 tons per annum, was present lost, and was run away as sodium sulphate in the waste liquors. This drainage from the ex- tracting works, coming in contact with the chloride of calcium, the waste liquor from the Weldon Pre: r cess in alkali works, deposits large quantities gypsum, obstructing the drainage, which gave rig° to a long and expensive lawsuit in the Widnee district. The present generation could hardlY • form an idea of the intensity of feelini and prejudice aroused against chemical alkali works during the first 40 years 0-`• their existence, namely, up to the passing of the Alkali Act in 1863. Hardly an assize! passed without an action for nuisance or damages and, as this litigation continued without absolute ruin to the manufacturer, the public believed the -profits to be fabulous, and many people without chemical knowledge commenced to decompose salt' - sometimes selling the salt-cake to soapmakers to INO converted by them into black ash, or, as tl..e demalla for -alkali continued to increase, converting tbe salt-cake themselves into soda ash. With an iry creasing demand for alkali, much more acid wile produced than could be easily disposed of, and the - alkali manufacturer was gradually led to manufae" ture bleaching powder for the purpose of utjljsiflg' his hydrochloric acid. With its allied industries copper and chlorine product, the alkali industry 01. this neighbourhood had, of course, attracted rotuid it other industries such as the manufacture of glass and soap; but these were now principally in St. Helens, Warrington, and Widnes, whereas in Liver' pool, where there were seven or eiAht soap work , in 1827, there were now only two small ones. •At St. Helens, in 1829, the first alkali works was ereo- ted, and there were then only five small glass works' - now there were eight Alkali works and nine large glass works, four of them manufacturing plate glasg. Of copper-smelting works there was only one in 18; to-day there were five, and two copper-extractiq works, and the population had increased from 14,25J' to 61,472 at the last census. In Widnes the pro' gress had been still greater, as its rise as a mana'' facturing town dated from about 1848, and it novi contained 15 alkali works, most of them of larget size, four copper works, and the large soapworks o Messrs. W. Gossage and Sons. All this was noW placed in jeopardy by the advance of chemical ill' dustily. France, since 1860, has seen her supreme/ in this particular direction rudely shaken by Get" many, which had made enormous strides id al) chemical manufactures. The records of the progreSe of the alkali manufacture showed that most of the processes now used were old, and that it was in the apparatus employed that the greatest improvementS had been made; but while a few of our manufae: turers had shown that they fully recognised this, was very difficult to find, a mana,er who had knowledge of engineerins, combined with a knovir• ledge of chemistry. Such men must be educatedf and it was only now, after the Germans and the French had shown the way for 40 years, that 'CV! were beginning to follow in the path. (Hear, hear.) The laboratory in which they were met was but sign of the movement that was in progress, all" their Chair of Engineering in Liverpool had onli been founded one year, but he looked forward tc.: the not distant day when, by means of improve secondary education, and the work of institutiong like Owens College and University College, Liver pool, our manufacturers would be able to find ready to carry on, with even greater success thaff in the past, a. large portion of the great cheraiea' industry of the world. (Loud applause.) Sir HENRY ROSCOE, P.R.S., M.P. in moving Tote of thanks to the president for Ilk able and ill; teresting address, said it was indeed a matter congratulation that they should on the present neal casion have Mr. Muspratt as their president. (kr plause.) The name of Muspratt, as they all knevfi had been intimately connected with the birth an with the rise and progress of this great industrit and perhaps Ile might be allowed on behalf of the society, to offer to their president their sincere con" dolence with him on the death of his father, grci James Muspratt, the well-known and respect originator and founder of the Leblanc industrY . this district. (Hear, hear.) .11 Mr. DAVID HOWARD seconded the proposal, w_h IC. was carried by acclamation.

Ririe-naive canes.—Hurrioanes. If you find you cannot succeed—succamb. Dissolving view.—A Parliamentary break-up. A cyclone is an ill wind that blows no good. When is a teapot like a kitten?—When your teasin' it (tea's in it). A local wag defines nothing as being a bung hole without a barrel. "The wedding ring is often love's last offering," says an Cid:bachelor. The telephone is an arrangement by which two men can lie to each other without becoming confused. An enterprising reporter, writing of a wreck at sea, stated that no less than fourteen of the unfortunate crew and pas- sengers bit the dust. BEEAD !—An Irish editor, apologising for a rather serious blunder in his paper, said, "I never saw the manuscript till It was in print." A yeast manufacturing company have placed a large gilt atar above their works as a sign, and it is occasionally re- ferred to as the star of the yeast. An Indian named "Man Afraid of Nothing" married a white woman in Montana recently, and in one week after his wedding applied to his tribe to have his name changed. Benevolent old lady, who has just given a penny to a Small rustic: "Now, my dear, what do you say ?" Small rustic, with native politeness: "Give us another !" Collapse Cf old lady. "Rachel, my tear, I pring you a vine engagement-ring." "But, Isaac, it's a !marl, mad beans are onlucky—ain't it ?" "Don't say a vord, Rachel. I tought of dot, mid so I take me an imitation von out of stock." Master of the house, writing a letter: "My dear friend, I cannot write you as freely as I would like, as my new secretary is impertinently looking over my shoulder—" Secretary, indignantly, from the rear: "I'm doing nothing CI the kind, sir !" A teacher asked one of her pupils the other day to give her the sum of five and six. " 'Leven " was the reply. " You shouldn't say "'even,' " she said; "say 'eleven' always. Next boy—how many are five and seven ?" "B-twelve?' was the prompt reply. FOR THE Mustangrs.—Why does the historical p'cture, Meeting of Mary Queen of Scots and James 1.," remind the spectator of a celebrated actress? Because it was "'Mary and 'en son." What is the difference between a railway brakeman and a dancing master? One couples trains and the other trains couples. What is the difference between a celebrated beauty and a woman paying court to a man? One is a fair woman and the other is a woo-man affair. IT WOULDN'T QUITE Do.—Scene—Mansion at South Kensington' social gathering. Accidental guest, to casual acquaintance, whom he finds " doosid agreeable": Hang this equalling! Let's go and have a weed in the Exhibi- tion.—Casual acquaintance: Nothing I should like better this hot weather; but, as it's my wife at the piano, and I'm the master of the house, I'm afraid it wouldn't quite do! "Mother," said a City clerk's young wife, "would you Itind cooking the dinner to-day? It would please John, I know. He complains so much of the new servant that I shall discharge her the moment I can get another." " Cer- tainly!" replied the old lady cordially. At dinner John said innocently to his wife, "Mary, that new servant of yours Seems to be getting worse and worse 1" Tableau! SHOCKING PROFANITY.—Dr. SUlldel was a society-man Who liked to air his Latin. Be has taken an acquaintance to call en Mrs. Parvenu, and the man had never called again, and, when the lady saw the doctor, she asked him about it. "Ah, doctor," she said, "where is you friend?" " Not my friend, madam," corrected the doctor; "he was . merely a quondam acquaintance." "Sir," exclaimed the c lady, in horrified amazement, "I don't know the relation existing; but, if you cannot express yourself in ladies' company without profanity, you had better follow your friend." "Yes, yes," said the landlord; "but what toddy do you Want? For we have three toddies here. Two glasses of hot water to one glass of whisky makes a very good toddy in. ; then one glass of hot water to one glass of whisky makes Heelan' toddy; but one glass of hot whisky to another glass ef hot whisky makes the real Heelan' tartan toddy, and any shentleman might be proud to drink it whateffer." - "Bring me a tumbler of the real Heelan' tartan toddy, then," said the stranger, giving a resigned glance round the room to see which was the nearest road to his apartment. A traveller, jest at the close of the American Revolution- ary War, was cros3ing the Fishkill mountains at the time when it took about a hatful of Continental money to buy a breakfast. He had no money; but he had a copy of a famous England Primer, which contained the Shorter Catechism of the Scotch Church. It was a little book; but it had nictures with rhymes, such as, "In Adam's fall we Binned all." He counted out a number of these pages, after eating his breakfast, and handed them to the old lady who had served him. She did not know much about reading; but she took them, looked at them closely, spelled out a few pious words, and said, "That's all right! I ara so glad that Congress has at last got some money with a little religion

In An eminent French art collector once bought at the Hotel Dronot a landscape by a noted ,s impressionist," which he showed, with much pride in his purchase, to an artist-friend. "But I think," quoth he, "that the picture lacks animation ai-it wants personages. Now, if you would paint for me a MB or woman on that road that runs through the middle • of the landscape, it would greatly improve the picture." "That is ea-41y done," ss.id the artist; so he carried off the painting, and sent it back in a week or two with a figure of an old peavant woman going to market with her basket and her red umbrella introduced on the road in question, to the great satisfaction of the picture's proprietor. Meeting shortly after with the " impressionist " who had painted it, the artist remarked, "1 had the audacity to alter a landscape of yours belonging to M. X. the other day. I painted an old peasant-woman walking down the road." " Down the road? I remember no work of mine with a road in it. I should like to see the picture and judge of the effect of your alteration ' SJ the artist carried him off ta M. X.'s, and they speedily stood before the landscape. The " impres- sionist" turned perfectly green with wrath and horror. .4 miserable man," he shouted," what have you done? That Is not a rod that runs through the centre of my work; it 18 a river!"
