An old North Sea skipper who was asked to buy a number of life-belts for his vessel's use waxed eloquently in the sub- limity of his contempt. "Take 'em away !" said the old "salt." "Don't let me see such long-shore rubbish on my decks. I don't want no life-belts, nor no smelling-salts, nor no eau-de-Cologne, nor no feeding-bottles or fans abroad of me. Them as mils in my ship has got to stick to her as I do; and, if she goes down, why, I expects them in duty bound to go v.loeg with her !" HINTS TO YOUNG MEN "WHO WANT TO MARRY. Select the girl. Agree with the girl's father in politics, and with her mother in religion. It you have a rival, keep an eye on him; if he is a widower, le,rep two eyes on him. Do not assure the girl that you have no bad habits. It will be enough for you to say that you never heard your, self snore in your sleep. Do not put too much sweet-stuff on paper. If you do, you will hear it read in after-year, when your wife has some special purpose in inflicting upon you th, severest punishment known to a married man. Go home at a reasonable hour in the evening. Do not wait till the girl has to throw her whole soul into a yawn that she cannot cover with both hands. A little thing like that may cause a coolness at the very beginning of the game. If you sit down on some molasses-candy that little Willie has left on the chair while wearing your new summer trousers for the first time, smile sweetly, and remark that you do not mind sitting on molasses-candy at all, and that "boys will be boys." Reserve your true feelings for future reference. If, on the occasion of your first cail, the girl upon whom you have placed your affec- tions looks like an iceberg and acts like a quiet cold wave, take your leave early and stay away. Women in her hours of freeze is uncertain, coy, and hard to please. In cold wea- ther finish saying good night in the house. Do not stretch it all ths way to the front gate, it there is a front gate, and thus lay the foundation for future asthma, bronchitis, neu- ralgia, and chronic catarrh, to help you to worry the girl to death after she has married you. Do not be too soft. Do not say `• These little hands shall never do a stroke of work while they are mine," and "You shall have nothing to do in our home but to sit all day long and chirp to the canaries " —as if any sensible woman could be happy fooling away valuable time in that sort of style!—and a girl has a fins re- tentive memory for the soft things and silly promises of courtship, and occasionally in after years, when she is wash- ing the dinner-dishes or patching the west end of your trou- sers, she will remind you of them in a cold sarcastic tone of voice.—American Payer.

div.head: PASSAGE OF THE NIAGARA
div.p: PASSAGE OF THE NIAGARA

RAPIDS. The Philadelphia correspondent of "The Times" telegraphed on Monday night ;—A successful pas- sage through the rapids and whirlpool of Niagara was accomplished, on Sunday afternoon, by Mr. C. D. Graham, an Englishman by birth, now residing in Philadelphia. Graham, who is a cooper, con- structed a barrel shaped like a buoy, seven feetiono., 33 inches in diameter at its widest part, 23 inches the top, and 18 inches at the bottom. It was built of one-and-a-quarter inch oak staves, bound with iron hoops, the barrel weighing altogether 2501b5., and carrying 2401b5. Sand ballast was so disposed as to keep uppermost the side of the barrel which Graham faced. Inside of this machine Graham stood in a canvas hammock made like a -suit of clothes, holding on by means of iron handles fixed in the sides. He could live, he found, for half an hour without fresh air, and a small air hole fitted with a plug, by which a supply could be renewed. Gra- ham, confident that he could thus shoot the rapids, started from the American side, just below the falls. His barrel shot swiftly along, made somersaults, and twirled like a top; but it generally kept floating with the widest part uppermost, as intended. It took about one hour to complete the journey, and was picked up at Lewiston, five miles below the starting place. Graham was taken out uninjured, excepting that he had a slight bruise on the arm and was suffering from want of air. Half an hour afterwards, having recovered from his exhaustion, he thus told his story :—" I was that rattled with getting off in a hurry that I didn't plug the air hole. and when I tried to do it afterwards I couldn't do it. I couldn't see, of course; but I could feel. Lord! how that river drops under the bridges • I felt mighty queer when I struck that place. When I got to where the water breaks; and went under, it just poured in at the open air-hole. It was awful hot in there. While I was drifting slowly up above I thought I'd die; but the water cooled me, and didn't wet me very much—for you see I was inside the canvas. When I got to the whirlpool I took off the cover and could see out ; but 1 was carried along so fast that I Put it on again in a hurry. Then I got dizzy with rolling over, and pretty sick in my stomach. In the Devil's Hole rapids I got the worst shaking up. Then I was all right enough until they pulled me out. I never want to try it again for fun. I'll do it again for money pretty quick." His journey was made without notice, so as to avoid arrest ; and few persons witnessed it. Another account of the affair is supplied by the New York correspondent of the "Standard' who telegraphed as follows ;—A man named Carlisle D. Graham, a cooper, of British birth, resolved on the day he heard of Captain Webb's death to attempt to pass through the rapids of Niagara River. He suc- ceeded in his rash enterprise on Sunday. The only precedent is the escape of the steamer Maid of the Mist from the Sheriff's pursuit in 1861, by shooting the Rapids below the Falls. Several thousand per- sons assembled to witness the feat, which was al- most prevented by Graham's arrest. He was, how- ever, released because there was no legal reason for detaining him. He started from below the Falls at 3-53 p.m., passed the Whirlpool at four o'clock, and reached Curston, a town on the east bank of the river, and the limit of steamboat navigation for Lake Ontario, at 4-26. The course of the barrel was very erratic, as may be imagined. After it was sub- merged it was scarcely ever upright, and was dashed about with tremendous violence, but escaped being driven upon the rocks or being detained in the Whirlpool, where Graham even ventured to open the manhole. When his dangerous journey was over he emerged dizzy but unharmed. He de- clares his confident belief that he can go over the Falls themselves with safety.

MR. PETER RYLAND& M P. AND THE BURNLEY CONTEST. The following is a copy of a letter addressed by Mr. P. Rylands, M.P., to Alderman Greenwood, his op- ponent in the recent contest at Burnley. " Massey Hall, near Warrington, July 12th, 188 G. "Dear Mr. Alderman Greenwood,—I was glad to learn from our friend Mr. H. Nutter that you disapproved of the publication during the late election of extracts from my private letters addressed to Mr. W. Collingo at the time of the change of Government last January. Whoever sanc- tioned such a proceeding was guilty of a dishonour- able and ungentlemanly act. I have the more reason to complain because a meaning was falsely attached to my letters which, at the time they were written, never entered into my mind. "Let me recall too circumstances attending the for- mation of Mr. Gladstone's Government at the end of January. Lord Hartington, Sir Henry James, and other distinguished Liberals declined to join the Government. There was a serious split in the party, which necessarily weakened Mr. Gladstone's position, and we had all to seriously consider what course we ought to take. I decided upon acting with Mr. Cham- berlain and Mr. Trevelyan, who, I knew, were as much opposed to a separate and independent Parlia- ment in Dublin as I was. They agreed to take office. It was no doubt presumptuous on my part to imagine (although so many held aloof from .51r. Gladstone) that my assistance might be of some service. At least, I may excuse myself by the fact tkat it was generally believed in the House of Commons, and was also mentioned in the press, that I should be asked to take office. I therefore decided that if I were so ap- plied to I would render such assistanceto Mr. Glad- stone as might be in my power. I communicated this confidentially to Mr. W. Collinge to prepare him for the possibility of my having to stand for re-election, but I never gave him or anybody else the slightest reason to suppose that my support of Mr. Gladstone depended upon my being offered office. I had no such idea. On the contrary, my being left out of the Government made no dine' ence in my actions, and, as an independent member, I continued to give Mr. Gladstone my loyal support so long as I had reason to believe that the Irish measures would be of a moder- ate and prudent character; but as soon as the policy was announced, and it was propot.ed to establish a separate and iridependent Irish Parliament, which I hai denounced during the election contest in Novem bar, and which (as was well known in the House of Commons and elsewhere) I continued strongly to op- pose, I at once entered into active efforts to defeat the Government measures. "In confirmation of the correctness of my recollec- tion, I may mention that whilst the Government was being formed I had conversations with Sir Ughtred liay•Shuttleworth, Mr. Heneage, and other friends who had been offered office, and I said to all of them , they were justified in giving Mr. Gladstone their as- -Isistance in carrying out what I hoped would be a I wise policy in relation to Irelan,=l, but that if any each jschemes as those rumoured in the papers, and which I did not credit, were proposed, I took it for granted they would leave the Government. Had I been hon- oured with a seat in the Ministry, I should certainly have retired with Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Treve- :Van. No office could have induced me to stifle my conscientious convictions; and I should have been degraded if I had allowed myself to be bribed to

violate my pledges and to support measures which I believed to be so dangerous and unjust. And now, after this explanation, can any reasonable man sup. pose that the extract from my letter justified the im- putation cast upon me P I have no copy of the letter, which, I believe was dated January 28th. I am obliged to trust to the words as given in the extract circulated, which are as follow It is not unlikely that the present crisis may end in a split amongst our leaders. lam disposed to assist Mr. Gladstone, if he thinks fit to offer me office, although the prospect of the immediate future in politics, owing to the difficul- ties of the Irish and other qusations, is not , A misrepresentation of this innocent passage was made use of in the last hours of the contest, when no refutation was possible, to deceive ignorant electors into the belief that my opposition to Mr. Gladstone entirely arose from disappointment at not, having been asked to serve in his Government; and, under this false impression, many votes, I AM told, were recor- ded against me. One of my Burnley correspondents calls it a 'dastardly trick,' and so it, was. " Bolieve me, yours faithfully. PETEIt RYLAND& "Mr. Alderman Greenwood, Burnley."

MURDER IN lIIELAND.—Mirtin Nee, of Recess, County Galway, who was brutally beaten while returning from Roundstone Fair in the same county on the 14th ult., died on Saturday from his injuries. The police have effected some arrests. The offence is not agrarian. A TALKING CORPSE.—A singular store comes from Clin- ton, Kentucky. George 0. Daniels, of that place, had been 11l for several months, and at length, to all appearances, died. The body was put in a coffin, where it remained for 20 hours, awaiting the arrival of relatives to attend the funeral. At midnight on Thursday the watchers who sur- rounded the coffin were startled by a deep groan emanating from it, and all but one, a German of the name of Wabbek- ing, rushed from the room. Wabbeking remained, and as the groans continued he raised the coffin lid and saw that Daniels was alive. Seizing the body he placed it upright. A few spasmodic gasps, a shudder, and the corpse spoke. The relatives returned to find the man sitting in a chair, and conversing with reasonable strength. Mr. Daniels claims to have been perfectly conscious of everything which passed around him, but says he was unable to move a muscle. He heard the sobs of his relatives when he was pronounced dead by the doctors, and noticed the preparations for the funeral. He is about 80 years of age. ALLEGED ATTEMPT TO DEFRAUD TEE RUSiIAN GOVERN. WENT—At the Mansion House, London, on Monday, Gar- sien Czarnichouski and Abraham Myers were charged with having had in their possession, without authority, three wooden blocks bearing an impression of a Russian 25-rouble note.—The City Solicitor, who conducted the prosecution, stated that the prisoners called on Mr. Gasceyne, an en- graver, and instructed him to prepare three blocks for the engraving of a 25 Russian rouble note. Mr. Gascoyne com- municated with the police, and proceeded to make the blocks. The prisoners were afterwards arrested. The case was a serious one, as it had been contemplated that there should be an issue of 50,000 of these notes, representing £125,000. He (the City Solicitor) had communicated with the Russian Government as to whether they would like to conduct the prosecution but they replied that they were so satisfied with the action of the city police in the matter that they preferred to leave it in their hands.—Some evidence in support of the charge having been given, the case was adjourned. TER TWELFTH OF JULY IN IRELAND—The Orangemen of Ulster had their annual carnival on Monday, and there was little or no rioting in Belfast part of the province. At Newtownbreda, adjacent to Belfast, a huge meeting was held, presided over by the Rev. Dr. Kane, Grand Master of the Orangemen of Belfast, and resolu- tions were adopted expressing heartfelt thanks to God for His manifest interposition on their behalf at this crisis as seen in the decision of the late House of Commons, and more evidently still in the results of the General Election, whereby the disloyal, unpatriotic, and cowardly scheme of the Prime Minister had been effectually defeated. They renewed their solemn determination never to be deprived of their rights and privileges as citizens of the British Empire, and to maintain (if necessary by force of arms) their independence of the "League of Hell," of which the traitors who call themselves Nationalists are the leaders. -At Scrabo, near Newtownards, a very largely attended meet- ing was held, Colonel Waring presiding. The following resolutions were there adopted :—"That we, a monster meet- ing of the Orangemen of Newtownards and of the surround- ing districts, recognise with gratitude the exertions of our brethren in time past, and declare our unalterable determin- ation to stand or fall by the principles of our Order in de- fence of her Majesty the Queen and of the British Constitu- tion." "That we deplore the Irish policy of Mr. Gladstone, foreseeing that if carried out it will be the deathblow to the prosperity of Ireland, and a signal for the renewal of those scenes of anarchy and bloodshed from which we were provi- dentially delivered by William 111. and the heirs of his principles." "That we desire to express the highest ad- miration of the manner in which Colonel Waring, our mem- ber, has discharged his Parliamentary duties ie the present crisis, and at the same time to tender our heartfelt gratitude to the Liberal statesmen who have so nobly and so success- fully resisted the disruption of the Empire." Resolutions of a similar character were passed at largely attended meet- ings at Armaeb, Banbridge, Coleraine, Portrusb, and other places throughout the North of Ireland. NORTHW ICFI DIVISION ELECTION. THE ELECTION. The contest for the honour of representing the Worthwich Division in Parliament was brought to a conclusion on Tuesday, when the election took place. Mr. J. T. Brunner, the late member, and a follower of Mr. Gladstone, was opposed by Mr. Robert Verdin, of the firm of salt manufacturers of that name at Northwich, who claimed the suffrages of the electors as a Liberal Unionist. At the last election, after a protracted and severe struggle, Mr. Brunner gained a decisive victory over his Tory opponent, Mr. W. H. Verdin, brother to the present member, and it was considered that the seat was rendered unassailable in future. Within eight months Mr. Brunner has had to rally all his forces against the attacks of another Verdin, whose politics are of a different colour and complexion to those of his brother. During the pre sent campaign some doubt has been thrown upon Mr. Verdin's description of himself as a Liberal, and at his meetings in all parts of the division he was fre- quently saluted as a "Tory." Of Mr. Brunner'e Liberalism there is not the shadow of a doubt. The party of progress in Cheshire have always been pleased to number him amongst their ranks Its a robust Radical, and he has justified all the confi- dence placed in him. He has been ever ready to spend time and money in the cause of the demou.racy, and his generous spirit is shown by the statement in a Liverpool journal this week that it was from his hand the cheque for £l,OOO went to Mr. 41 W. Latham to pay that gentleman's election expenses at Crewe last November. BIOGRAPHIES. Mr. Brunner comes of Swiss and Manx stock, but by birth and education he is a Liverpool man. He entered mercan- tile life in 1857 with the Liverpool house of the firm of JoshuaScholefield and Sons, of Birmingham. Between 1861 and 1872 he resided for the most part at Widnes, where he was connected with the chemical trade. During a memor- able strike which took place during his stay at Widnes Mr. Brunner rendered invaluable service in preserving tranquility amongst the excited population. In 18.7-2 he entered iuto partnership with Mr. Ludwig Mond and Mr. C. M. Holland, and established on a small scale the now extensive alkali works at Northwich. The firm, having the exclusive right to certain valuable patents. attained an extraerdinary suc- cess. The works are now owned by a limited liability com- pany, in which Mr. Brunner is the chief shareholder, and are said to be the largest of the kind in the world. Mr. Brunner has always taken a great interest in public affairs, and especially in the spread of knowledge amongst the people, free education being one of the articles of his political treed. He has been a large contributor to the funds of the Liverpool University College. and is one of the guarantors of the Shipperies Exhibition. The Farnworth and Witton Grammar Schools have been supported very liberally by his generosity, scholarships worth.tso per annum having been established by him in connection with the last-named school_ Although a Nonconformist, he has always con- tributed handsomely to Church funds, one of the last ex- amples being a donation of £3OO towards the recently com- pleted restoration of Witton Church. Mr. Robert Verdin is the eldest surviving son of the late Mr. Joseph Verdin, of Hightield House, Winsford, was burn In 1435, and educated privately. He is senior partner in the firm of Joseph Werdin and Sons, salt manufacturers, a magistrate for Cheshire, a Commissioner for the Upper Mersey, and chairman of the Salt Chamber of Commerce, of the Salt Association, and of the Winsford Local Board. Mr. Verdin, in coajunetion with his brothers, founded in 1883 an institute at Moulton, Cheshire, for the benefit of his workpeople, which, besides including a library, has also jarge billiard and lecture roosts. THE CAMPAIGN. Beth candidates have conducted a most arduous cam- paign. Each part of the constituency has been visited, and in Runcorn and Northwich. the two lupe towns of the division, several meetings have been held in supnort of each candidate. The last three days of the contest were very lively. On Friday evening there was are Irish meeting at Runcorn in favour of Mr. Brunner's candidature, Mr. BrIln.• ner addressed meetiags at Halton and Aston, and Mr. Robert Verdin spoke to an open air assembly at Weston Point, held under the presidency of Ceptain Clark. On Saturday. an enthusiastic meeting was held on Ransom Heath. and addressed by Mr. Brunner and others, and on the evening of the same day a capital meeting was held at North svich in import of Mr. Brunner. Oa Monday evening Mr. Verdin held meetings at Runcorn, Northwich, and Winsford, and there were Liberal meetings at Ityncorn and Weston Point held in the open air. Mr. Arthur O'Connor, of Chester, a clever young Irishman, and Mr. W. B. Kennedy, of Liverpool, were the principal speakers at the 'Runcorn Liberal meeting, and a resolution of confi- dence in, and support to, Mr. Brunner was carried with enthusiasm.

ELECTION LITERATURE. Notwithstanding the brief period of battle, literature, both mural and otherwise, has played a somewhat prominent part, The walls were covered with placards, and handbills were issued almost daily. Under the heading of "Wesleyan* and the Elections the following letter, tcrMr. Simister, of Runcorn, from the Rev. Charles Garrett, ex-president of the Wesleyan conference, was spread broadcast, and it was thought would have considerable influence upon the result: —"I heartily hope that you will succeed in returning Mr. Brunner for •Northwich division. Mr. Gladstone is fighting for justice to Ireland, and for the true unity of the British • Empire. Every true patriot should feel it to be an honour to be able to assist him in his noble work. Besides, the friends of temperance should take care their voices should be distinctly heard in the new Parliament. Help Mr. Brun- ner all you 'can." The Unionists replied by calling atten- tion to the resolutions passed by the 'Wesleyan Methodists in Ireland, and asked the electors not to have their co- religionists to despair. "Who goes straight" was the ques- tion asked, and the doubtful colour of Mr. Verdin's politics was shown by his speech to the Liberal Council in 1885, and his oppertition to Mr. G. W. Latham in 1880. The ,electors choice, said a handbill, lay "between a true Liberal and a•sham one." A retort was issued consisting of ex- tracts from speeches by Mr. Brunner, who had described his opponent as "as straight as a die," and had stated -that no person ever lost anything by trusting Verdin. The Union Jack was a very popular emblem with the Unieniste, and the people were abjured to "Rally round the old flag," and to vote for Verdi°, one Empire,one Parliament, one queen." Mr. Brunner based his claims to support, however, on other principles besides Home Rule, and the electors were asked to "Vote for Brunner, the work- ingman's friend, who supported the Manchester Ship Canal 'He advocates Free Trade, which brings increased wages.' He also advocated the union of hearts and of hands. A 4liegraceful cartoon was issued by the Unionists representing Mr. Gladstone as the Pope, and endeavouring to stir no re- ligioneobigotry and prejudice, and it called forth almost universal condemnation. The Liberals issued a cartoon re- presenting Ireland ccntented and happy under Home Rule, and as the victim of evictions and vielence under the pre- sent system. The latest issue was the declaration of tbe Crewe election, which put renewed vigour into the Liberal workers.

THE POLLING AT RUI`ICORN. The Spelling was commenced promptly at eight o'clock ou Tuesday morning at the several polling districts. There were very few vehicles in use on either side, and the polling was very slow all through the day. At. four o'clock under one half of the electors had voted in Rancorn, and reports from other parts of the division showed a similar state of things. From half-past five to eight o'clock matters were I very brisk, and the committee rooms of both parties were scenes of busy activity. About noon Mr. Verdin, accom- panied by his brothers, Mr. W. H. and Mr. J. Verdin, drove through the town in a carriage and pair, but his reception in some places was not of a very encouraging nature. Later in the day Mr. and Mrs. Brunner arrived by train and were driven to the Liberal committee room in Mr. R. Shaw's car- riage. Mr. and Mrs. R. Shaw and Mr. J. Simpson occupied seats in the carriage. In the committee room several of Mr. Brunner'a enthusiastic admirers seized that gentleman and carried him to the" big lamp" on the Market Ground, cheered during his progress by the assembled hundreds. i Mr. Brunner delivered a brief speech n which he said he had had another proof that Runcorn Liberals were sturdy, streng men. (Cheers.) As they knew the Grand Old Man's schemes for the benefit of Ireland were temporarily de- layed, and their duty remained to return him (Mr. Brunner) in outer te prevent the adoption of that abominable old policy of coercion for Ireland. (Cheers.) The Liberal policy was truth, right, and justice, and mercy before all, and it should prevail. (Cheers.) Last year the Liberals of Northwich Division had before them the question— "Should a man be returned to Parliament on account of principles, or on account of trade." They decided that it was to be principles first and trade second. (Cheers.) Now the fight this time was between truth and con- sistency and a man whose sole object was to get an advan- tage for himself. (Cheers.) He believed they were straight- forward and wanted a straightforward man to represent tbem—(bear, hear)—and in that full confidence he should go home and tell his friends and neighbours in Tiorthwich that they could trust to Runcorn. (" Three cheers for Branner " were heartily given). Mr. R. Shaw also spoke a few words. He described Mr. Verdin as a wishy-washy politician, while Mr. Brunner was. a man of honour and integrity and a man desirous to do justice to the multitude. Therefore they must do their best to place Mr. Brunner at the head of the poll. (Cheers.) In the evening, just previous to departing by train, Mr. Brunner was drawn through the town in a carriage by a number of men, and he received an ovation all along the aaDrite.

The polling arrangements were similar to those of last y.ear, and were admirably carried out. At the Market Hail there wen four booths. In the first Mr. E. S. Giles, of Cheater, was the presiding °nicer ; Mr. W. Brookes, poll clerk: Messrs. E. Marwood and A. Riley, personation agents. Ne. 2: Mr. A. Linaker, presiding officer; Mr. E. Marshall, poll clerk ; Messrs. R. Wright and W. Fisher, personation agents. No. 3 : Lieut.-Colonel Ashton, presid- ing eke Mr. W. Sutton, poll olerk ; Messrs. Edward Key and J. D. Jones, personation agen:s. No. 4: Mr. F. A. Lake, presiding °Meer ; Mr. W. Pownall, jun., poll clerk ; Messrs. W. Littler and T. Sharrock, personation agents. At Greenway-road Board Schools there were two booths. In the first Mr. Raymond Harris, Chester, was presiding officer; and Messrs. T. C. Williams and J. Collier, personation agents. In the other Mr. Cann Hughes, Chester, was pre- siding officer ; and Messrs. Thomas Cooke and T. Johnson, p.rsonation agents. The poll clerks were Messrs. F. B. , ,Idason and R. Williams. both of Chester.

The town was very quiet all the day with the exception I of the noise made by a number of youths and boys, who de- lighted to cheer and groan the respective partisans as they recognised them. Superintendent Hollingsworth had aug- mented the police force coßsiderably, but happily their ser- vices were not required. The poll closed at eight o'clock.

div.head: DECLARATION.
div.p: THE DECLARATION.

The ballot boxes were conveyed to the Central Hall. off Witton-street, Northwich, where the counting up com- menced at eleven o'clock on Wednesday morning. A num- ber of politicians from Runcorn travelled to Nortbwich to hear the result, which was declared to a large crowd about two o'clock, as follows:
R. Verdin (U) J. T. Brunner (L)

Majority The declaration was received with mingled cheers and groans. Last November the numbers were :—Mr. Brunner (L), 5,023; Mr. W. H. Verdin (.:), 3,995; majority, 1,028. Before departing from the hall, where the leading poli- ticians in the district had assembled, Mr. R. Verdin proposed a vote of thanks to the deputy high sheriff (Mr. Tatlock) for the courteous and efficient way in which he had fulfilled I his deties in connection with the election. Mr. Verdin re- ferred to the admirable polling arrangements. Mr. Brunner seconded the motion with pleasure. He had something more to say. He had to thank his friend Mr. Ver- din for the way in which he had conducted that contest. He began it by saving that he would not speak a word to hurt his (Mr. Brut:meets) feelings, and he had stuck to that decision in a way that did him henour. (Hear, bear.) He (Mr. Brunner) had a confession to make, and it was this: That be bad made a like promise, and he had not kept his word; and he had to leave it to their Christian charity to say whether the provocation he had received was sufficient to justify him. He was very much pleased with Mr. Ver- din and congratulated him heartily. (Applause.) The defeated candidate and the new member then shook hands, amid cries of "Bravo." The motion was carried with acclamation, and Mr. Tatlock suitably responded. Mr. A. Fletcher and Mr. J. H. Cooke and the Liberal an Conservative agents respectively spoke of the admirable and courteous way in which Mr. Tatlock had conducted the election. _ _

Mr. R. Verdin said he hoped that all the electors belong- ing to both sides would be as good friends to one another as Mr. Brunner and he were that thy. (Applause) He had a single responsibility in connection with being their mem• ber, but it would be his study to carry out the wishes of the constituency to tha utmost of his power. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that the good feeling existing that day would continue for days to come. (Applause.) MR. BRUNNER ON HIS DEFEAT.

Mr. Brunner, upon leaving the building, was sur- rounded by several hundreds of his supporters, who accompanied him to the house of Mr. Mendes, hat- ter and clothier,Witton-street, cheering and waving their hats in defiance of their defeat. Mr. Mendes iaTited Mr. and Mrs. Brunner, Miss Brunner, the Rev. W. Gelly, Mr. Robert Shaw, Mr. A. Fletcher, and several other gentlemen into his sitting-room on the second floor. The crowd remained outside, and when Mr. Brunner appeared at the window they set up a cheer which was prolonged for several minutes. Mr. Verdin passed by at this time, and was greeted with groans. Quietness being re- stored, Mr. Brunner said: Gentlemen, I have been beaten. but I have not bet heart. (Cheers, and cries of "You will go again," "Keep up your heart," renewed cheers.) I ant far too good a Liberal to lout pluck. (Cheers, an I a voice, "You will not turn your coat," and cheers.) You know that, although Mr. Verdin has been elected by the Tories, nevertheless he cells himself a Liberal. (Groans.) Now, I have hopes, and I entertain those hopes on your behalf that in his conduct in Parliament Mr.Verdin will prove him- self a Liberal. (Cries of " Never," and cheers.) I heartily trust that your feelings will be represented to your con- tent in Westminster. (" Three cheers for Brunner," given heartily.) If Mr. Verdin does not act as a Liberal— (" He is no LPeeral ")—next time depend upon it be will get no help from Liberals, and you will be certainto have a true Liberal in. (Cheers.) lam sure that after yesterday's work, the Tories have killed theirebance in this division. Now lam going to be your neighbour, I trust, for many a , day, and I can assure you of this that so far es it lies in my power I will be at good a neighbour to every man anti wo- man as I have be.eo. (Cheers.) I want to say a word for , the men who have worked for me. I tell you the exertions they have made have been absolutely beyond praise. The self-denial and self-sacrifice that bai been gone through on my behalf are something that is beyond my power of ex- pression. I thank them with all my heart (Cheers.) There is many a face down there that I know, faces of men who have sacrificed a great deal in the Liberal cause. ("And will again.") I trust they will keep their bearts up as I shall mine. (Cheer%) I have another word to aay,.and that is I am very proud of the way that my wife has aupported me. (" Three cheers for Mrs.,Brunner," loud cheers.) low, gentlemen, good-bye for to-day; (Cheers.) I ask you be- fore we part to keep up the good name of Northwich. and don't let us have any disturbance. (Cheers.) The Rev. W. Gelley then addressed a few remarks tl the assembly. He asked them to go quietly home, and not to create any disturbance. They bad fought a strong battle, but had lost it. As they had learned t•.) be honourable in victory, let them learn to be fair and honourable in defeat. (Cheers.) It was only a defeat by a twofold source. They had had to tight not only their enemy the Tories, but they had had to tight some that once belonged to their own ranks. (Groans.) When the fight came between Toryism and Liberalism this division would be found soundly Liberal. He thought they would all keep the peace, take their de- feat as calmly and as good naturedly as Mr. and Mrs Brunner had done. Let them have no unneighbourly acts. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner then drove away to Winnington Hall, ac- companied by his wife and daughter and Mr. R. Shaw. Mr. R Verdin also addressed a large number of his sup- porters from the Angel Hotel. MR. ROBERT VERDIN ON HIS VICTORY.

Amid the mingled cheering and hooting of the assembled populace, the newly-elected :member and his party drove through the town to the Bull and Ring. Speaking from his carriage, Mr. VERDIN, M.P., said: Fellow-electors and fel- low-townsmen—(cheers)---I thank you mostleartily for the high and honourable position in which you have placed me to-day. (Cheers.) It is ,a great plea- sure to me to have been elected as your represen- tative in Parliament—(cheers)—and I trust the confidence you have reposed in me will .never be forfeited. (Cheers.) I further trust that .you will always find me promoting any measure that will tend-to promote the welfare of this town .and this division. (Cheers.) This contest has been fought in a good spirit, and I hope that one and all will SOparttto good friezias—ohc,cisi- -I trust that if we should have to fight on any future occazion in this division the battle will be conducted in:as friendly a spirit as this has been. (Cheers.) I again beg to thank you for the great trust you have placed in me.. (Loud cheers.) The carriage was then driven on to Porockhurst, Mr. Verdin's residence. Mr. VERDIN again addressed the assembly. He said he could scarcely express in words the grati- tude which he felt; but he assured them that it would be his constant study to do all he could to further the interests of the working classes of the community generally. (Cheers.) He took the op- portunity of heartily thanking the band of hard workers in the division who had been so largely instrumental in bringing about so triumphant a success for the Unionist cause. (Cheers.) They had had very little time for organisation. A month ago no one thought of a candidate who would have to fight for the cause of the Union: but he was proud to find that the people of that division had in their hearts so warm a love for their country. (Cheers.) He hoped that Englishmen would al- ways consider country before party, and country before self-interest. (Cheers.) Their forefathers had shed their blood for their country, and it would be a disgrace to Englishmen if they did anything -which .would lead to the disintegration of the em- pire which they had inherited. (Cheers.) He thanked them for the splendid reception they had aiven him as their representative; but he must say 'hat he had a strong objection to being drawn about by men—(laughter)—because it was not his wish that wen should make of themselves beasts of bur- den. (Laughter and cheers.) His anxiety was, and it would always be his aim, to raise his fellow-men and improve their position in life. (Cheers.) He once more thanked them for their cordial welcome. (Cheers.) Speeches were also delivered by Messrs. W. 11. Verdin, T. Ward, Dr. Moreton, and Dr. McDougall. The latter said that as a Liberal he was heartily proud of the share .he had taken in the contest. He was quite sure that Mr. Verdin would be a credit to the division, and would do his duty as a kind neighbour to them all. (Cheers.) Mr. Jos. Verdin and Mr. J. H. Cooke also spoke, andthe crowd hav- ing sung the National Anthem separated,

CoNsERTATIVE MEETING AT EA.RLESTOWN%—A meet- ing of Conservative workers was held at the Club, Earles- town, on Monday evening. Captain Seton, chairman of the District Registration Committee, presided, and was sup- ported by Mr. T. Pearson and Mr, C. F. Boron. The Chairman said they bad all been asked to attend there that night, in order that he might thank them most heartily for the way in which they had worked at the elec- tion, and with such success. The majority of 816 was one to be proud of, and he thought they had put such a spoke in the Radical wheel that they would not ha able to get out in a burry. (Cheers.) He had received a letter from Sir Richard Cross, dated from Warwick-square, London, in which he desired him (the speaker) to thank the workers heartily for returning him at the head of the poll, and said that he would take an early opportunity of thanking them personally. Routine business having reference to the com- ing reyisi:n was then transacted,

FRODSHAM. SERVICES AT PRESTON BROOK.—OR Sunday the Rev. J. Cansland, of Runcorn (superintendent minister of the Pres- ton Brook station), preached the annual sermons of the Sunday school to very large congregations. Special hymns were sung by the children and choir, assisted by friends from Greenway-road chapel, (Runcorn, from Latch- ford, kc. SIINDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY—The anniversary ser-
mons in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist Sun•

day school at Five Crosses, were preached in the Wesleyan Chapel, Five Crosses, on Sunday, by Mr. T. Simister, of Runcorn, and on Monday evening a sermon was also preached in the same chapel by the Rev. Thomas Champ- . .
ness, of Bolton. A collection was made at the close of each service in aid of the Sunday schools, and amounted to £2l 5354

OPEIN AIR CONCERT.—On Saturday evening the Prod- sham Braes Band gave their seeond open air concert op- posite the Town Hall, which was duly appreciated. The movement has so far been successful, and the band is de- serving of every encouragement. During the week pro- grammes had been freely circulated through the neighbour- hood, and as a result a large crowd assembled near the band stand. The programme was short, but contained attractive pieces. The band, which has only lately been formed, played in a very creditable style. The position of the band stand is being changed each week, and on Saturday it will be occupied by the Runcorn Mill-brow Brass Band, which will consist of 2$ members. The programme is to be a long one, and it is expected that it will also be an interest- ing one. Lizettar, MRETING.—A crowded and enthusiastic meet- ing of electors in the Frodsham polling district of the Eddis- bury Division was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Tuesday evening, in support of Mr. James Tomkinson, the Liberal candidate. Mr. Samuel Rigby, J P., of Chester, presided.—Mr. Chadwick, a workingman, moved the follow- ing resolution :—"That this meeting expresses confidence in the candidature of Mr_ Tomkinson, and pledges itself to use all legitimate means to secure his triumphant return le, Parliament."—This motion was seconded by Mr. Joseph Corker, another workiergman, and carried with a few dissen- tients.—The meeting was also addressed by Mrs Tomeinson, ' Dr. Foster, and Mr. Tomkinson, the Liberal candidate. The newly-returned member for Blackfriars, Glasgow, also gave an address on the Home Buie question.—A vote of thanks ' was accorded to the Chairman, on the motion of the Rev. A. Mills, seconded by Mr. Peter Harrop.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 17, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 17, 1886.

Xetters to the t Moe. _ - - -- BATHS FOR RUNCORN. Sir,--I hope you will oblige me this once by inserting this small letter in your valuable paper. Just a word or two for bathers. There really ought to be Publie Baths in Run- corn. On a nice summer night if you want to take a walk on "no man's laed," you see nothing but a lot of naked lads bathing. I think this nuisance ought to be stopped. I de- clare it is worse on a Sunday than any other day, and there is always some one getting drowned. If a decent fellow wants a swim, he has to pay 6d and go to Widnes.—Yours truly, Runcorn, July 14th5 1886. - - THE GREAT POLITICAL PLOT. Sir,—l am fully aware that anything I may write touch- ing the contest that has been waged between true Liberalism and that bastard sort, the offspring of Chamberlain, Hart- ington, Bright, and Co., can now be of little avail; yet. better late than never. The country has been made to resound of late with a few leading, or rather misleading, war cries, which were—" The Unity of the Empire." "Roman Catholic Ascendancy," kc. These cries very soon I got vapid; but the latter has done its mean work. The dis- reputable coalition, has created a considerable amount of surprise throughout the British dominions, and through- out the civilised world. But it is not generally known that the High Church party belonging to tbe Roman Catholic Church, viz., the Jesuits, were and are much opposed to Home Rule; and seeing the Jesuits are the most influential party belonging to the Catholic Church, they must, inevit- ably, exercise the greatest power over the members of that churoh. Under these circumstances there is a secret under- standing between the Jesuit party and the Coalition : and allow me to tell the readers of your paper that as a re- sult the bulk of the Irish Catholics in this coentry have not voted for Home Rule. The Catholic priests have been play- ing a double came; whilst Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Parnell have been working and suffering for "righteousness sake,' they were under the impression that the Roman Catbolie Interest was in their favour, whilst, and at the same time, the priests have been working with all their might in the interests of the Coalition. In the face of such a gigantic sham as this, what will honest-minded men think in future of those clergymen who have been giving out warnings from the pulpits, in nearly every parish through the land, as to the overwhelming danger of Roman Catholic ascen- dency, which it was said Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Parnell were seeking to establish. I think it is high time that British working-men and the trading and agricultural com- munity open their eyes to this great plat that has been worked with some success amongst the enemies of liberty as against the upholders of Home Rule.—Yours, BUS f ICUS.
DECENCY.

div.head: BAZAAR :-A_ MARQUEE BLOWN DOWN
div.p: BAZAAR :-A_ MARQUEE BLOWN DOWN

On Wednesday a bazaar in aid of the Frodsbam Tower Restoration Fund was opened at Frodsham by Mr. Clarke Aspinall, of Liverpool, in the presence of a large number of the gentry of the neighbourhood. It had been intended to hold the bazaar in a tent that was erected in a field adjoin- ing the vicarage. The bulk of the goods had been arranged on the stalls, but at ten minutes past six on Wednesday morning the nightwatchers, consisting of Messrs. H. G. Lineker, T. H. Kitchen, H. E. Heywood, S. Davies, B. A. Rigby, J. J. Wilkinson, R. Rogers, and Roberts, were alarmed by hearing a loud crash, and in two minutes the bazaar was a complete wreck, the tent having been blown down bya gale which had been raging for some hours. Many of the goods were broken. The gentlemen named, who had been in charge of the stalls all night, rendered all the assist- ance they could, and prevented further damage being done, the goods being taken without delay to the bore school, where it was decided the bazaar should be held. Later on in the morning the stallholders and other ladies, who had been apprised of the accident, set to work with great energy and determination, and in a few hours the goods were ar- ranged on stalls in the schoolroom; andeconsidering the short time at their disposal, in a very creditable manner. Five years ago when a barter was being held to raise funds to complete the restoration of the church, a tent was erected, and was blown down by 41 high wind. Since the ,completion of the restoration of the 'church, some three or four years ago, at which time funds did not admit of its being restored, the tower had shown unmistakeable signs of giving way, and great fears were entertained as to its safety. After a careful examination of the tower, a meeting of parishioners was held, when it was resolved to at once remove the bells until the structure could be either taken down and entirely rebuilt, or so restored as to place its strength beyond question. Funds not being forthcoming for the former object, the majority of the parishioners, at a subseqaent vestry meeting, decided in favour of a restora- tion, instead of an entire re-building. It was resolved to place the matter in the hands of Mr. Samuel Davies, archi- tect, Frodsham, who was instructed to report upon the matter, and to prepare plans and specifications, and obtain tenders for a complete restoration. The committee con- sisted of the following gentlemen :—The 'Vicar, Rev. H. B. Blogg (chairman). Mr. Alfred Thomas, J.P. (hon. secretary and treasurer), and Messrs. Henry Linaker, john Robinson, Robert Ashton, Robert Holland, and Ralph Bate, who were appointed to raise funds and generally to carry out the work of restoration. The plans having been approved, tenders were advertised for, and the work was ultimately entrusted to Mr. Thomas Davies, builder and contractor, Frodsham. The estimated cost of the work at present authorised is about £1,200, and about two- thirds of this sum has been subscribed. The expedient of a bazaar was resorted to to meet the deficiency, and to collect additional funds for the improvement of the south aisle and the interior ef the churcb, and for the provision of two new belle, to increase the present peal of six bells, to eight. The restoration will comprise the complete repairing of all fractured and defective masonry, and other repairs necessary to place the tower, which dates from the 15th century, in a state of absolute safety. At the opening of the bazaar there were present, amongst others, the Rev. H. B. Blogg ',vicar), the Rev. A. Chorley, Mr. and Mrs C. Reynolds, Mr. and Mrs H. Linaker, Mr. C. E. Linaker. Mrs Reynolds, Mrs Simpson, Mr. John Simpson, Mr. W. H. Linaker, Mies Cope, Mr. Beamont (Warrington), Mrs John Ashton, Mrs H. Reynolds, Miss C. Reynolds, Mr. Riley, Mr. P. Nickeon, Dr. Robinson, Mrs Aman, Mrs and Miss Stubs (Chester), Mr. H, S. Limiter, Mr. H. E. Heywood, Mr. V. Davies, Mr. E. Cresfield. ittc...Acc. The sale was declared open by Mr. Clarke Aspinall, who said that he bad visited Frodsham before, but net on an errand like the present. and he liked to come amongst them because everything about the place and the people was to him very attractive. The parish church of Frodsham was, of course, a magnificent one. The parish churches of England were one of the boasts • of their country, and no parish church could be more in- teresting, either in its old and 'unreetored condition or re- stored, than theirs had been made by the great architect, Mr. Bodley. He did not wonder that they took a great in- • terest in it, and were minded to keep it in thorough and complete repair. They spent a few years ago what one ' could scarcely think about without being filled with sur- prise, something like £lO,OOO upon their church. No one • could examine it, especially internally, without seeing that they had got their money's worth, but still they did spend that very large sum and thatvite recently, and they did . what was not frequently accomplished, they re-opened their church., if be remembered aright, out of debt, and they knew the old saying,' Out of debt, out of danger." (Applause.) , how they found themselves in the throes of another effort in restoration. and another bazaar, the purpos., of it being to obtain at least £5OO to carry out the work, which was considerably advanced already, and partially paid for. He , hoped when the tower was itself again that it would &give them all full satisfaction, and he had no doubt it would be solidly and safely and well done, without undue economy, because if things were done cheaply they were often done badly. It was a very grateful sensation to him to come into a parish like theirs where the church was so splendidly kept, and its services so efficiently ordered, and its people so hearty, and its clergy so faithful. (Applause.) He was • ole enough to remember the time when some of the parish churches in England were really in a very sad state, and when the people seemed careless. In those days pluralities were tolerated, and the hopeless condition of many parish churches within his knowledge made him uncomfortable, even as a matter oft memory, to think about or reflect upon. Happily, there seemed to be more earnestness now, more vitality, more religious vigour, and he hoped —for this was a necessary condition to healthfulness —more spirituality in the land. (Applause.) These constant restorations were an outward proof tbat the English people were determined that in God's service they would work sagrudgingly, and that all they dedicated to him ehonld be the best they had. He wished to refer to a singular circumstance which had occurred that morning. At six o'clock, when, of course, the Frodsham people were all up and doing, being an active people, the tent blew either up or down, and their arrangements, which they bad matured no admirably, were all scattered literally to the winds. (Laughter.) It was remarkable that notwithstand- ing that sad accident the present bazaar had been so beauti- fully arranged and the room sd neatly decorated and ordered. But many hands made work light, and cheery hearts thought nothing of trouble, and what English people: were minded to do they could always accomplish. The blow- ing up or blowing down of the tent bad leeen little more than a pleasurable iccident, which had varied the monotony of their proceedings in a somewhat cheerful fashion. (Laughter.) It was, however, possible to have too much of a good thing, and, strange to say, many in that room would remember that on the occasion of their last bazaar the same calamity overtook them, and it looked as though it was to be their chro- nic condition. (Laughter.) He had great plea- sure in declaring the bazaar open. (Applause.) —The Vicar then presented Mr. Aspinall with a handsome tea pot as a tribute of regard from himself and the par- ishionere, and in recognition of his services in opening the bazaar.—Mr. Aspinall suitably returned thanks, after which the sale of work was proceeded with. div.head: IRELAND FOR THE IRISH.
div.p: IRELAND FOR THE IRISH.

Sir,—! hope vou will forgive me if I betray a strong de- sire to keep the Irish question before the public. It is quite clear that the process of educating the public on this question is not yet ended. The human animal is to-day, as he has always been, a stupid one, determined to run against every stone wall that may come in his way. But that the consequences are widespreading, one might quietly stand by satisfied to see the weakest go to the wall. A simple measure of justice is sacrificed to the prejudices of the ill-informed an the upper classes, and the true British workman is left stranded, unable to help himself. It may be that Mr. Bright, Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Tre- velvan, and Mr. Bylands are right in the opinions they hold; most certainly they are wrong in the manner of their enforcement.; and they will find to their dismay how ruinous a path it is that is trod by the foot of a rene- gade. I suspect that it would be impossible for a Tory Minister to bring in a bill, and find himself deserted by his best men. However bad the bill might be, they would at least help it into committee, and try to lick it into shape. Nay, they have proved that rather than lose place and position in the House they would take any number of leaps in the dark.

Referring to Ireland, I take it that the interpretation given to the remelt of the polls will be that England is de- termined that the Union shall be maintained. Good; I have never heard a statement made to the contrary, and yet the position taken by Mr. Gladstone is a reasonable and just one—viz., that the living body—England—shall not drag along with it-the dead or dying body—lreland—any longer without endeavouring to instil into it that healthy vigour so necessary to the life of the whole. The Tory party are jubilant; their satisfaction is so great that am almost compelled to say— Bring me cotton! the cheers Will split open my skull, and play hell with my ears." And what is it all about'? Simply to maintain the Union on dishonest lines. What is the history of the last eighty- five years? Fox at the time .of the Union warned his countrymen that they ought not to presume to legislate for people with whom they had no empathy. "The whole scheme " (of .Union), said the great Whig statesman, "goes upon the false and abominable assumption that we (the Eng- lish) could legislate better for the Irish than the Irish could de for themselves." Besides passing a Coercion Act of some sort.or other for every year since the Act of Union was passed, we have passed 43 Acts in acknowledgment of the ruin and despair that have haunted all sorts and conditions of Irishmen.

'During the short time the Tories were In power a number of deputations waited upon Lord Salisbury asking for more stringent measures, and protesting against "the policy of successive concessions." Could a fatuous people go fur- ther? The Irish grievance is agrarian; it differs only from the English grievance in that it has been hastened cn by an absentee landlordism. What is stifling Irish agricultural life to-day will, before very long, bring sorrow and ruin to many an English hearth. A little bit of history may be here given. Fifty years ago Ireland's wrongs were to the fore then, as now, Toryism stood in the way. A complete parallel to the present political situation in Ireland was set ep by the Tory land- lords in 183.5. when Lord Mulgrave (afterwards Lord Nor- manby) was appointed Ticeroy, with Lord Morpeth (after- wards Earl of Carlisle) as Chief Secretary. and Mr. Thomas Drummond as Under-Secretary. The new Liberal Adminis- tration came into office with the feeling that something should be done for Ireland by remedial legislation. The conciliatory and impartial action of the new Viceroy and his colleagues sent Toryism Into a frenzy, and reports of agrarian outrages .multiplied to an extent that created •quite a panic. Lords Lismore and Glengall and thirty other Tory magistrates visited and memorialised the Lord Lieutenant. It was in reply to these same magistrates that Lord Mulgrave returned the memorable reply in 1838, in which he said: "When the character of the great majoritY of serious outrages occurring in many parts of Ireland is considered, it is impossible to ,doubt that the causes from which they mainly spring are connected with the tenure and occupation of land. . . . Property bas its duties as well as its rights. To the negkct of those duties in times past is mainly to be ascribed that diseased state of society in which such crimes take their rise; and it is not in the enactment or enforcement of statutes of extraordinary severity, but chiefly in the better and more faithful performance of those duties, and the enlightenea and more humane exercise of those rights, that a permaeent remedy for such disorders is to be sought." As an answer to this advice, Lord Mulgrave's life was ' attempted in the Theatre Royal, a bottle being hurled at him; and Lord Roden succeeded in having a committee ap- pointed to inquire into the conduct of the Mulgrave Ad- ministration in Ireland. I should add that Lord Donougb- more acknowledged before the committee that he concealed the answer of the Lord Lieutenant from the public after its receipt, on the ground that he conceived passages in it to be "dangerous;" and when asked by the chairman to mention the passage he believed to have that tendency, he replied that portion which referred to "property having its duties as well as its rights." Immediately on the evidence of Lord Donoughmore becoming known, Mr. Hume moved that the letter above ,quoted be laid on the table of the House of Commons, and it was then sent in fly-sheets over the conn-

try. It was subsequently shown from official returns that during the Mulgrave Era—as it was styled— there had been a marvellous decrease in agrarian crime. Thus we see there has always been a class of people blind to their duties, and the present outcry against Home Rule, is based upon nothing less than ignorance of the subject, and if I may presume to give advice to the Home Rulers of Warrington, Englishmen and Irishmen alike, I would urge that they at once set about forming a Home Rale Associa- tion, with weekly meetings; and, independent of any politi- cal club, set about getting the names of every voter, so that at the next election., which may not be far off, a sufficient number of pledges may be in hand to carry the candidate. Already I hear steps are being taken for the retirement of Sir Gilbert. Another titled brewer is to step in, paving his way with a magnificent gift to the town in the shape of a Free Library. Surely the educational movement can be made successful without the town being hampered with another Lord of Gin Palaces.

The failure is announced of Messrs. R. Harris, Goodwin and Co., general merchants, London and Birmingham, with £108,817 of liabilities, and assets £23,862. A WOMAN COMMITTED FOR WILFUL MURDER.—Eliza- beth Bruton, wife of a labourer, has been committed for trial for the wilful murder of Mary Maloney. The evidence was that the prisoner, while under the influence of drink, saw the deceased pass near where her husband was standing. In a fit of jealousy she rushed up to Maloney, and asked her if she was talking to her husband, and then knocked her down. The unfortunate woman's head came in contact with the kerbstone, and she died from the injuries She received by the fall- THROWING WATER ON A GIRL AT TUE TIILCAN. Before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, A. C. McCorquodale, and W. F. Gooch, Richrnul Wilcock, was summoned for assaulting a girl named Annie Dash- wood, on the 2nd July. Mr. H. J. Longton appeared for the defendant. The girl stated that she lived next door to the defendant in Warwick-row, Vulcan. On the date named she was going to the water tap for water, and when she was returning the defendant threw a bucket of water over her and followed her into the house and beat her.—ln reply to Mr. Langton, complainant said her mother died about 12 months ago.—The defence was that Mrs Wilcock had behaved as a mother to the complainant, who had re- paid her by annoying her in every possible way, and calling her names. It was stated to have been only a trivial affair, and that Mrs Wilcock had only chastised the girl by shak- ing her,---Ellen Coop and Margaret Smith gave evidence that the girl bad annoyed the defendant, and the Bench dismissed the ease on the payment of the costs by the defendant, They also cautioned the girl as to her future conduct,

CRWlLET.—Anstralians versus Steel's Eleven at Liver- pool; Australians made 142 in first inniegs. The Central News statement respecting the new Anglo- American extradition treaty is officially confirmed from Washington. THIE BRITISH AND COLONIAL TEMPERANCE CONGRESS. —Archdeacon Farrar, who presided, on Friday morning, over this congress, in Lonion, gave a dispiriting account of the spread of drinking habits among inferior races of the globe, and said we bad girdled the world with a zone of drunkenness. Papers were read in reference to the drink traffic in Canada and New Brunswick, and on Friday after- noon the discussion was directed to other colonies. FOUR AT A BIRTH. The wife of Daniel Robinson, a labourer, of Milton, near Northampton, has just given birth to four children. The first survived only a few hours, the others were still-born. The mother expired the same ' day. Upon the particulars of the case being reported to the Queen, by Mr. J. A. Bennett, relieving officer and regis- trar, the sum of two pounds was immediately forwarded by Sir H. F. Ponsonby, for which the poor man is extremely grateful.

div.head: CRAWFORD DIVORCE CASE.
div.p: THE CRAWFORD DIVORCE CASE.

In the Divorce Court, on Friday, the case of Crawford v. Crawford (Queen's Proctor showing cause) came before Sir Jas. Hannen and a special jury. The case excited great interest, and, despite special precautions taken to avoid the court being overcrowded, every seat was occupied lone be- fore the jury was enpanelled. Sir Walter Phillimore, Q.C., and Mr. Bargrave Deane appeared for the Queen's Proctor; Mr. Henry Matthews, Q.C., M.P., Mr. Inderwick, Q.C.. and Mr. R. S. Wright for the petitioner (Mr. Donald Crawford, M,P.); and Mr. Lockwood, Q.C., for Mrs. Crawford. Mr. Murphy, Q.C., watched the case for an interested party. Mrs. Crawford. Mrs. Ashton Dilke, and Mr. Crawford were accompanied with seats at the solicitor's table. Sir Charles Dilke, whose name did not appear in the case, and who was unrepresented by counsel,also found a seat in the well of the court. Sir Henry James, Q.C, M.P., and Sir Charles Russell, Q.C., M.P., were also in court, holding briefs, it is understood, on behalf of persons whose names did net ape pear in the cause list. Sir Walter Phillimore, in opening the case for the Queen's Proctor, recapitulated the history of the suit, already published, and justified the intervention on the ground that the evidence which had been suppressed at the original trial was material to the case. Dealing with the statements alleged to have been made by Mrs Crawford in her confession, he said there was no doubt that the house in Tottenham Court-road at which she was alleged to have met Sir Charles Dilke by assignation in February, 1882, was 65, Warren-street, Tottenham Court-road. In regard to the evidence which he should lay before the court, the learned counsel said the footman at Sir Charles Dilke's house, who was alleged to have let Mrs Crawford in, would state that the only two occasions on which she called at Sloane-street were times when visitors were in the habit of calling on Sir Chas. Dilke, between 10 and 11-30 in the morning, and that on those occasions the interview took place in the breakfast or other rooms, which were perfectly open to all corners. The woman Sarah, who was alleged to have been referred to by Mrs. Crawford, and whose name was Sarah Grey, would also be called. Sarah Grey, who was stated to have assisted Mrs. Crawford to dress on the occa- sion of one of her visits to Sir Charles Dilke, and who was housekeeper for many years in the employment of Sir Charles Dilke, would state that it was entirely untrue that she ever saw Mrs. Crawford in the house, or that Mrs. Crawford ever entered Sir Charles's bedroom. Sarah Grey's evidence on this head would be corroborated by the under. housemaid. In regard to the woman described at the last hearing as Fanny, and who was supposed to be Fanny Grey, the sister of the housekeeper, it would be proved that no such familiarities as had been alleged could have taken place. Fanny Grey was in the service or Sir Charles Dilke some years ago as under-housemaid, but she left Sloane-street when Sir Charles's son went abroad many years ago. From that time forward the only re- lation she had to Sir Charles Dilke's household was an occasional visit to her sister. She was now mar- ried, and her name was Fanny Stock. Every attempt had been made to get her to come as a witness, but after she was seen with tbat view by Sir Charles Mike's solicitors, she and her husband disappeared, and there were no means of ascertaining where she now was. Mrs. Craw- ford bad been subpeenaed and was in attendance, so that her version of the matter could be heard in the witness-box. There were certain discrepancies in Mrs. Crawford's state- ment, and enquiries instituted thereupon by the Qneen's Proctor had elicited the informatice6, which would be given on oath, that Mrs. Crawford had never been to 65, Warren- street. Evidence would also be given to prove that it was absolutely impossible for Sir Charles Dilke to have been at Warren-street on the day named. In reference to the allegation and as to adultery being committed at Young-street, the residence of Mrs. Crawford, Sir Charles Dilke would give an absolute denial, and his coachman, who, when waiting for Sir Charles outside the house, could see from his elevated position on the box all that took place between his employer wad Mrs Crawford, would testify to the fact that no impropriety took place so far as he could see. Mrs Rogerson, an old acquain- tance of Sir Charles Dilke's, who was alleged to have acted as an intermediary between Sir Charles and Mrs Crawford, would deny the statement. The learned counsel added that afterahe shorthand notes of the last trial had been read he would call Mrs Crawford. Sir James Hannen said that must be left to him. Sir Walter Phillimore said he would then ask his lord- ship that Sir Charles Dilke be examined.' Sir James Hannen : I must say I cannot assent to that. The issue lies upon the Queen's Procter. He must lay before the jury such evidence as he deems necessary to sub- stantiate his case.

The shorthand notes of the last trial were then read. Sir Charles Dilke was then called and examined by Sir W. Phillimore. He said he had known the family of Mr. Eustace Smith since IE6B, and his brother, Mr. Ashton Dilke, married a daughter of Mr. Smith. Before Mrs. Crawford's marriage he did not know her except As a younger member of the R,.stace Smith family. During the lifetime of Sir Charles's grandmother he believed some of the younger children of Mr. E. Smith were in the habit of calling at Sloane-street. He , did not remember calling ea Mrs. Crawford at j

VERY IMPORTANT CONSIDERATION. _ A A most important consideration for all at this season of the year is how best to rid the system of tt e disetties induced by the trials of winter. In many cases it seems as though the seeds of consumption had been planted in the sTstem by the trying weather we have gone through. The symptoms may have commenced with a slight cold, a little sore throat and hoarseness, then come, perhaps. a feeling of weakness, or chil- liness, ace, mpanied or followed by aching of the limbs; now and again a hot, dry, feeling of the skin; gen.ral feverishness ; tightness in the chest, with difficulty of breathing ; a little cough, short and dry, then some expectoration; the weakness increases, and friends become anxious.

In other cases various forms of Liver or Kidney Complaints are develop, d ; the lassitude becomes nervous weakness; the sleep is uneasy, and troubled by unpleasant dreams; and ne patient, instead of waking refreshed, gets sip with a feeling of weight and ,anguor, and every action seems a burden. Others again begin the spring with what appears like con- firmed Indigestion; headaches, bile, loss of appetite, a u flaw ing sensation at the stomach, a sense of fulness and oppression, pains in the breast or bowels, or in the region of the heart, are all so many signs that the stomach is out of order. These are a few only of various form of complaints from which you may be suffering. You need not continue to suffer, as I shall show. The system is more liable to thesm attacks in the spring and early summer, as the bodily powers have been reduced by the trials of winter. It is of the greatest impor- tance to pay attention to the general health at this season. This is why doctors prescribe so generally a good tonic medicine to be taken during the present months. And it is because some people laugh at these signs, and neglect to take the proper reme- Biattner a s.vuersyefsuilmapnAs Simple dies in time, that they break down later on in the summer when any unusual demand is made upon thrir bodily powers. How then can the danger be averted? bmeannenfiecira'l atNril'sGeawsolitYrsmo h Evans' Quinine year, Is simply ievaluable Though it is not food In itself, it enables the stomach to ao- cent food readily, and not only to digest it without pain and suffering, but to extract from every morsel of food eaten, the greatest possible amount of nourishment. Altrincham, was fined 2s 6d and costs for being drunk disorderly at Lymm on the 18th ult. FURIOUS DRIVING.—Joseph Massey, veterinary Stirgeoll; was summoned for furiously driving a horse and UM) Lymm, on the 24th ult.—P.C. 38 said that he saw defer dant driving at the rate of 15 or 16 miles an hour.—A ness named Read, a groom, called for the defence, said En 7. the defendant was not driving at a furious rate.—The Be131'" dismissed the case. A MAD Dog AT LAMM—Thomas Hatton, for allowing a dog to stray, in contravention of an order now in force, fined 2s 6d and costs ; and for a similar offence Willi Gibson, Thel wall, was fined 5s and costs. During the beat' lug of the case, Sergeant Harrington said that a dog, or posed to be mad, was loose in the village' and had bittell several other doge. The police had on the day before nee!! looking for it with the intention of shooting it.—Super_T- tendent Leighton said that two dogs that were certaiwi mad had been destroyed since the order was made, on° g Roston and the other at Ringway. A NEGLIGENT DRIVER.—Josepb Rawlinson was fitied:sB. and costs for not haying proper control of horses that wet' under his charge on the 22nd June. SWINE FEVER—Joshua Slater: miller, Warburton, Wag summoned for neglecting to notify to the police that We: pigs in his possession were affected with swine fever. Pg. of the pigs died and the third was killed. Afterwards tbu bodies were exhumed, and subjected to an amination by Mr. Martin, veterinary surgeon, Allgrili; cham, who said that the animals had, without deny been affected with the disease. Defendant said that he 101 not aware that they bad been suffering from swine fever. Superintendent Leighton told the magistrates that Oil fever was worse at present in that division than ever known it before. It was spread by pig dealers.--3A Bench imposed a fine of £1 in each of the three cases, iD 44 12s. div.p: THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTHWICH DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. ONXTIMIEI7,—I write in heartfelt sorrow for the disap- Peintment suffered by the men who have fought so gallant battle on my behalf against the tremendous forces opposed to them. They have well deserved success, and will assuredly achieve It when the unhappy differences now parting them from old friends shall have disappeared. To myself personally the loss is less, for the reason that I Could not look forward with any degree of hope to the doing ai much good work for the happiness and well-being of the People in a Parliament containing so large a number of reac- tionary politicians. Mir action in the last Parliament and during the late contest 'WU guided by strong and conscientious conviction, and I had rather today be defeated on account of having stood by my Principles than elected by the enemies of the people's rights and Is :Ming my seat at their mercy. It is abundantly clear tnat the •Liberal party in this divi- eon is in a vast majority, that the Tory party cannot win in a fair fight, and that your member must support Liberal prin- CiPles, or suffer defeat at your hands at the next election. My short experience as your member has been a very plea 'ant one, and I shall always cherish the recollection of many kindnesses received from you. Your faithful servant, JOHN TOMLINSON BRUNNER. Winnington Old Hall, July 14th, 1886.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTHWICH DIVIBION. GY.l4Thinlnf.—lt is with sinew e plesuure I most heartily thank those Electo,s of this Division who, by recording their votes In my favour, have placed me in the honourable position of member for this Division—a Division so conspicuously asso- cieted with the town of my birth and the work of my life. , My especial thanks are due to the large numbs - of arduous lott, workers who have so successfully aided r*y own personal efforts; of these there are many friends and volunteers whose labours cannot be snißeently valued. Ma., I now be permitted to ask that all feelings of animosity and displeasure shall be buried, and—the battle being over— Opponents and friends—all Englishmen alike—will conscien- It tiousiy believe that it will ever be my honest endeavour to discharge without partiality the serious and responsible duties anposed upon me. I am, gentlemen. Your obliged and faithful servs,nt, ROBERT TERDIN. The Brockhurst, Northwich, July 14th. 1886.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE WIDN ES DIVISION OF THE COUNTY OF LANCASTER. GErrxxium—Permit me to take this opportunity of thank- ing those of you who supported me, bath by their work and their votes at the recent election, most heartily for so doing. The diminished majority of my Tory opponent is good ground for the b, lief that some day soon you will be repre- sented in Parliament by a Liberal. Our whole party being now agreed that as much self-goTern- ment must be given to Ireland as is consistent with the unity of the Empire, the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament, and the safety of the Protestant minority, we must, for- getting former differences, press steadily forward to that mark. Persorally, however, I shall always rejoice that during the contest I upheld before you an Irish policy at once just and cauragwus, and no less sympathetic than sensible. I am, Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, AUGUSTINE BIRRELL. 37, Addison Gardens North; London, W.

rib o THE LIBERAL ELECTORS OF NEWTON DIVISION or LANCASHIRE. GENTLEMEN,—I hasten to tender my most 'earnest and sin- sere thanks to the large and inluential body of Electors who have so generously supported me in the recent conteet. Fought under circumstances of exceptional difficulty. its re- sult offers the most gratifyirg eacrouragement and assurance of our success in the near future. We have been contending for justice and right. for the real interests of the Empire, for the principles of true Liberalism, and I firmly believe that at the next election, which cannot be far distant, we shall, with your assistance, succeed in enlist- ing this great constituency on the side of popular and Liberal , government. 'thanking you once more respectfully for your kindness. I am, Gentlemen. Your obedient servant, G. ERRINGTON.

He went there and was told that the female , had taken prosecutor's purse, and handed it to the male prisoner, but the purse was given back to Leigh before the officer arrived. Riley, who was drunk, was taken to the police station, and was seen to have a shilling in his hand. Prosecutor, who at the time was also considerably the worse ' for liquor, swore that when the purse was handed to him some silver had been taken out of it, and the boy Jenkins gave evidence to the effect that he saw the purse taken and handed to Riley by Gib- bons. Both prisoners denied the offence. "Such a crime," Riley said, "is not written in my coun- tenance." He added that he saw Leigh early in the morning and they had some ginget beer together, Leigh then expressed a wish to be introduced to some girls. He (pri- soner) spoke to two girls who promised soon after- wards to meet Leigh. They, however, disappointed him and he appeared to be "regular Cll6 up about it." During the morning they got into the com- pany of others, girls and men, and had eight pints of rum and whisky, and three half-gallons of beer, shared between six or eight of them. He (Riley) was drunk and had no knowledge of how the purse came to be in his hand. He was not inclined for thieving, although he had been in good company and might have made a few pounds that way. They had been drinking together all day and prosecutor spent his money fast enough. Questioned by Chief Constable Hunt, prisoners and friends of theirs who were in court, resolutely declined to say where they purchased their liquor on Sunday morning. The female prisoner also protested her innocence.— Alderman Davies (to prosecutor) : Are you married? No.—Alderman Davies: You had better get married and have a little Home Rule.—The Mayor: You seem to have been, from what I can hear, frequently a victim—by robberies perpetrated on you by women? I cannot tell you, sir—The Mayor: Have you never charged a woman before with robbing you? Yes, one or two. Only two, I think.—Mr. Hunt: You have been here once before, and once in Cheshire? Yes.—Mr. Hunt: You are a single man with plenty of money? A little—The Mayor said that prosecutor had acted in a disgraceful manner, and deserved the punishment he had had. Having regard to his conduct they were not inclined to deal severely with the prisoners. Riley would be fined lOs and costs for drunkenness, and Gibbons 58 and costs for the theft.

He might have called on Mrs. Crawford about the begin- ning of the session of 1882, but he made no assignation with her between February 20th and 23rd of that year. The elder sister of Mrs. Davis, who lived at 65. Warren-street, was his nurse, and Mrs. Davis herself had been in the ser- vice of the Dilke family, and had been pensioned off by them. The Court adjourned for luncheon, and Sir Charles Dilke afterwards proceeded to show that, from his official engage- ments, Mrs. Crawford could not have visited him at his house as stated. He was afterwards clesely cross-exam- ined, and asserted his belief that the charge against him was the result of a conspiracy on the part of Mrs. 1 Crawford and others to screen other people who were guilty.—The case, which was adjourned, is expected to last several days.
